org.scicloj/plotje {:mvn/version "0.18.0"}


 - to visualize plots with Clay. Follow Clay documentation for recommended usage. You may find the videos useful. It is recommended to set Clay up using the Setup for your specific IDE or editor.
 - for the RDatasets collection



(ns plotje-book.quickstart
  (:require
   ;; Rdatasets -- standard datasets
   [scicloj.metamorph.ml.rdatasets :as rdatasets]
   ;; Kindly -- notebook rendering protocol
   [scicloj.kindly.v4.kind :as kind]
   ;; Plotje -- composable plotting
   [scicloj.plotje.api :as pj]))

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Your First Plot
Load the classic iris dataset and scatter two columns:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

rdatasets/datasets-iris loads the classic iris dataset from the RDatasets collection as a Tablecloth dataset with keyword column names.
pj/lay-point shows each row as a dot (scatter plot).

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Plain Data
You do not need to load a CSV – Plotje accepts plain Clojure data and coerces it into a dataset internally. A map of columns works directly:

(-> {:height [1 2 3 4 5] :weight [2 4 3 5 4]}
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight123452345
When the dataset has few columns, you can skip the column names – Plotje infers them from the dataset shape. The first column goes on the x axis and the second on the y axis, so here :weight is on x:

(-> {:weight [1 2 3 4 5] :height [2 4 3 5 4]}
    pj/lay-point)

heightweight123452345
Auto-inference covers 1-3 column datasets. With 4 or more columns no column is read by default – pass column names like (pj/lay-point data :height :weight).
See Core Concepts for more input formats.
String column names also work – keywords are conventional but not required:

(-> {"height" [1 2 3 4 5] "weight" [2 4 3 5 4]}
    (pj/lay-point "height" "weight"))

weightheight123452345

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Color
Map a column to :color to color points by group.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
More Chart Types
Each pj/lay-* function adds a different chart type.
Histogram – pass a single column for automatic binning:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))

countsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00510152025
Bar chart – count occurrences of a categorical column:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-bar :species))

countspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica05101520253035404550
Horizontal bars – flip with pj/coord:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-bar :species)
    (pj/coord :flip))

speciescount05101520253035404550setosaversicolorvirginica
Line chart – connect points in order:

(-> {:day [1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8]
     :visits [3 5 4 7 6 8 7 9]}
    (pj/lay-line :day :visits))

visitsday123456783456789
Boxplot – compare distributions across categories:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-boxplot :species :sepal-width))

sepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica2.02.53.03.54.04.5
See the Layer Types chapter for the full list of chart types.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Inference
pj/pose declares which columns to plot without committing to a chart type. When a pipeline ends at pj/pose (no pj/lay-*), Plotje picks the chart type from the column types. Two numerical columns produce a scatter plot:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
A single categorical column produces a bar chart:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :species))

countspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica05101520253035404550
A single numerical column produces a histogram:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length))

countsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00510152025
See the Inference Rules chapter for the full set of rules.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Multiple Layers
Use pj/pose to set column mappings for a pose, then add layers with pj/lay-*. All layers on this pose inherit the pose’s mappings. Here (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}) sets the layer’s stat (the computation applied before rendering) to a linear model, adding a regression line per group:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Titles and Labels
Use pj/options for the title and the axis labels:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/options {:title "Iris Petals"
                 :x-label "Petal Length (cm)"
                 :y-label "Petal Width (cm)"}))

Iris PetalsPetal Width (cm)Petal Length (cm)speciessetosaversicolorvirginica12345670.00.51.01.52.02.5

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Panels
The layers of a pose share one panel. For a panel per category of a column, facet the pose by that column:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/facet :species))

sepal widthsepal length682.02.53.03.54.04.56868setosaversicolorvirginica
For a panel per column, write the column the panels share on the pose, add a layer that names no columns, and facet over the other columns. Each panel draws the layer on its own column:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}))

sepal width2.02.53.03.54.04.5petal width4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00.00.51.01.52.02.5sepal length
The Faceting chapter teaches both kinds of facet.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Dashboards
Combine multiple plots with pj/arrange:

(pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
             (pj/lay-histogram (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :sepal-length {:color :species})]
            {:cols 2})

sepal widthsepal length682.02.53.03.54.04.5countsepal length56780246810121416speciessetosaversicolorvirginica

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
Getting the SVG
The examples above auto-render in this notebook because Clay recognizes Plotje poses and visualizes them. In an interactive workflow with Clay (or another Kindly-compatible tool), you rarely need the SVG explicitly.
When you do want it – to inspect the hiccup or embed the plot in a webpage – call pj/plot:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/plot)

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
The result is a hiccup vector starting with :svg – a Clojure data representation of the SVG markup. The notebook auto-rendered it as a plot above because Clay has built-in hiccup rendering. To see the hiccup value itself rather than its rendering, wrap with kind/pprint:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/plot
    kind/pprint)

Export
Save a plot to SVG with pj/save. It writes the file and returns it as a java.io.File:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/save "/tmp/iris-scatter.svg"))




For PNG output, (pj/save pose "x.png") writes a raster image via the Java2D backend; see the Cookbook for other export paths.

title: 2  Quickstart
text:
What’s Next
On a first read, follow these chapters of Foundations in order: Datasets, Poses, Core Concepts, Panels and Specifying Aesthetics. Together they teach what Plotje reads, what a pose is, how a mapping and a layer combine, where panels come from, and how to write a mapping. The rest of Foundations is reference to come back to when a question needs the precise rule.

Datasets – what kinds of data Plotje accepts (Tablecloth datasets, maps of vectors, sequences of row maps)
Poses – the mental model behind composable plotting
Core Concepts – data formats, marks, stats, color, grouping, coordinates
Panels – where panels come from, and which forms draw two things inside one panel or across panels
Specifying Aesthetics – how to write what a mapping means, in full or in shorthand
Relationships – scatter plots, regression, density, and SPLOM
Cookbook – recipes for common multi-layer plots
Configuration – themes, backgrounds, palettes, and other plot-level defaults
Gallery – many more chart variations with side-by-side code

title: 3  Datasets
text:
Plain Data Works
You do not need to know about datasets to plot with Plotje – you can pass plain Clojure data (maps, vectors of maps) directly. But understanding datasets is recommended background for four reasons:
This chapter gives a brief introduction. For full documentation, see the Tablecloth and tech.ml.dataset docs.
Plotje accepts plain Clojure data – a map of columns or a vector of row maps. No dataset wrapping needed:
This is all you need for quick plots. The rest of this chapter covers datasets, which become useful as your data grows.

title: 3  Datasets
3  Datasets
text:
What Is a Dataset?
A dataset is a columnar table backed by efficient typed arrays. It is the Clojure equivalent of an R data frame or a Python pandas DataFrame.
The core implementation is tech.ml.dataset. Tablecloth is a higher-level wrapper with a more convenient API. Plotje uses Tablecloth internally and in its documentation.

(The :key-fn keyword option converts CSV string headers like "Sepal.Length" to keywords like :Sepal.Length. Without it, column names remain strings.)


Column names
A column name can be a keyword, a string, or – for a dataset built without names – an integer. Plotje reads all three, and derives an axis title from the name whenever you do not supply one.
A keyword cannot hold a space, so hyphens and underscores in a keyword stand for word breaks. The derived title is spaced rather than punctuated:

(-> {:sepal-length [5.1 4.9 4.7 5.0]
     :sepal_width  [3.5 3.0 3.2 3.6]}
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal_width))

sepal widthsepal length4.74.754.84.854.94.955.05.055.13.03.13.23.33.43.53.6
A string is left as written. A string can hold a space, so a hyphen in a string name was written on purpose, and replacing the hyphen would change the name:

(-> {"sepal_length"       [5.1 4.9 4.7 5.0]
     "Cost-Benefit Ratio" [3.5 3.0 3.2 3.6]}
    (pj/lay-point "sepal_length" "Cost-Benefit Ratio"))

Cost-Benefit Ratiosepal_length4.74.754.84.854.94.955.05.055.13.03.13.23.33.43.53.6
Set :x-label and :y-label through pj/options for a title the column name does not give.
Given no :column-names, tc/dataset names the columns by their place, 0 and 1:

(tc/dataset [[1 2] [3 4] [5 7]])


:_unnamed [3 2]:



0

Plotje plots such a dataset from its inferred mapping, and titles the axes with those names:

(-> (tc/dataset [[1 2] [3 4] [5 7]])
    pj/pose)

1012345234567
Plotje reads an integer name wherever a mapping is written, so (pj/lay-point ds 0 1) and (pj/lay-point ds {:x 0 :y 1}) both plot those two columns:

(-> (tc/dataset [[1 2] [3 4] [5 7]])
    (pj/lay-point 0 1))

1012345234567
The data decides which of two readings a number takes: a number the data carries as a column name is that column, and any other number is a value to place a mark at. So the same code can mean different things on differently named data – Known Limitations has the detail, and writing {:x {:column 0}} or {:x {:value 0}} chooses the reading in the mapping itself. Renaming the columns is the other remedy:

(-> (tc/dataset [[1 2] [3 4] [5 7]])
    (tc/rename-columns [:height :weight])
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

title: 3  Datasets
text:
Datasets and Plotje
When you pass plain data to Plotje, it is coerced to a dataset internally. You can also pass a dataset directly – the result is the same:
Plain data:

(-> {:height [1 2 3] :weight [4 5 6]}
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight123456
Dataset:

(-> (tc/dataset {:height [1 2 3] :weight [4 5 6]})
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight123456
Both produce the same plot. Use whichever is more convenient for your workflow.

Plotje reads long-form (tidy) data most directly: one row per observation, with categories and groupings in their own columns. Real datasets often arrive in wide form – each measurement in its own column. tc/pivot->longer is the canonical reshape:

  (tc/dataset
   {:month   ["Jan" "Feb" "Mar"]
    :tokyo   [3 5 9]
    :paris   [4 6 11]
    :nairobi [22 23 24]}))

title: 4  Poses
text:
A pose describes a plot
Plotje is a composable plotting library inspired by Wilkinson’s Grammar of Graphics and Julia’s AlgebraOfGraphics.jl. Its operators are shaped by Clojure idioms – threading, merge, plain maps – rather than a custom DSL.
Plotje calls the value at the heart of each plot a pose. The word is photographic: a pose is the arrangement you settle into before the picture is taken. In Plotje, the same shape is a plain Clojure value – which columns become axes, which become color, which chart-type layers sit on top – that you build, inspect, and recombine until you call pj/plot and capture it.
This chapter introduces the pose value step by step. Each section shows a rendered plot followed by the printed pose value, so you can see both what the library produces and the data structure underneath.
The composition functions – pj/pose, pj/lay-*, pj/options, pj/scale, pj/coord, pj/facet, pj/arrange – all take a pose and return a pose, so plots build up through ordinary -> threading. When the pose is ready, pj/plot renders it. (pj/plot is one of a few output functions that turn a finished pose into a rendered result; the Architecture chapter walks the full pipeline behind it.)
The simplest pose carries some data and picks columns. With no explicit chart type, the library infers one from the column types:
Two numerical columns produced a scatter. And because a pose is plain data, you can inspect it with kind/pprint:
A pose is a plain Clojure map. The dataset lives under :data, the column mapping under :mapping, chart-type layers under :layers (empty here, since none was attached), and plot-level options under :opts.

title: 4  Poses
text:
Poses carry mappings
An aesthetic is a visual property of a mark: :x and :y (where the mark sits), :color, :size, :alpha and :shape. A mapping says which column, or which written value, an aesthetic takes. We mapped columns to :x and :y above; the pose also accepts mappings for :color, :size, :alpha and :shape:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    kind/pprint)

 :layers [],

title: 4  Poses
text:
Poses carry layers
A layer is a layer type placed on a pose. The layer type is a chart-type recipe made of a mark (the shape drawn), a stat (the computation applied before drawing) and a position (how marks of different groups share space, such as bars stacked on one another or dodged side by side). The pose says what to plot (its mapping picks the columns); the layer says how it is drawn (points, a smooth, error bars). Several layers attached to one pose share its mapping and coordinate system, so a scatter and its regression line are drawn as one picture. This split – mapping for what, layer for how – runs through the rest of the library. Written as a literal map, pj/pose accepts the nested-map shape directly:

(def multi-layer
  (pj/pose
   {:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :color :species}
    :layers [{:layer-type :point}
             {:layer-type :smooth :stat :linear-model}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))

title: 4  Poses
text:
Layer order is paint order
On a leaf pose, layers paint in the order they are added: the first lay-* call renders first, and each later one on top of it. When layers overlap, the order of the layers decides which marks stay visible – so add the layer you want on top last. (On an arrangement, a layer added to the arrangement as a whole is drawn under each cell’s own layers – see Panels.)
Two points at one spot. The large one is added first and the small one second, so the small dot reads on top of the large one:

(-> {:height [1] :weight [1]}
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:size 30 :color "#a6cee3"})
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:size 12 :color "#1f78b4"}))

weightheight012012
The same rule lets a value label sit on a bar: add the label after the bar so it paints on top, and use :align-x :right so the label sits inside the bar’s end rather than past it. (Bars and pj/coord are covered later; anchoring is in Placing Marks, and the Cookbook has a value-labels recipe.)

(-> {:species ["setosa" "versicolor" "virginica"]
     :pct     [33.3 33.3 33.3]}
    (pj/lay-bar :species :pct {:color "#a6cee3"})
    (pj/lay-text :species :pct {:text :pct :align-x :right})
    (pj/coord :flip))

speciespct33.333.333.3051015202530setosaversicolorvirginica
Swapping the two calls swaps which layer paints on top – paint order follows the order layers were added, not the layer type. Ask for the text first and the bars are drawn over the labels:

(-> {:species ["setosa" "versicolor" "virginica"]
     :pct     [33.3 33.3 33.3]}
    (pj/lay-text :species :pct {:text :pct :align-x :right})
    (pj/lay-bar :species :pct {:color "#a6cee3"})
    (pj/coord :flip))

title: 4  Poses
text:
Poses compose
The poses we have built so far are leaf poses – each has its own data, mapping, and layers, and draws one panel, which all of its layers share whatever columns they name (a facet multiplies the panel). A composite pose is a plain map that holds sub-poses under :poses and an optional :layout describing how to tile them. Each sub-pose is a cell of the composite. Composition functions take any pose and return a pose. Here is a two-panel composite written as an explicit map:

(def two-panel
  (pj/pose
   {:layout {:direction :horizontal}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :color :species}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width :color :species}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Data
The vocabulary you reach for daily: data, mappings, scope, layer types, and how they fit together. This chapter takes the mental model from Poses and turns it into a working reference you can scan while building a plot.
Read Poses first if you have not – this chapter builds on the pose vocabulary it introduces.
Plotje accepts plain Clojure data – maps, vectors of maps – or columnar datasets. No wrapping needed for simple cases. The Datasets chapter covers data formats and loading in detail.
We use the classic iris flower dataset throughout these examples. Each column has a name (a keyword like :sepal-length) and holds values of one type.
The dataset has 150 rows and 6 columns: a :rownames index plus four numerical measurements (in centimeters) and one categorical column (the species name – one of three strings).
Plotje treats numerical and categorical columns differently when choosing axes, colors, and statistical transforms.
Here is a scatter plot of sepal dimensions, colored by species:
Printed, the pose carries the data and the mapping of :x and :y at the top, and one point layer with its own layer-scoped :color:

Input formats
Plotje accepts several common Clojure data shapes and coerces them into a dataset internally.
Map of columns – keys are column names, values are sequences:

(-> {:height [1 2 3 4 5]
     :weight [2 4 3 5 4]}
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight123452345
Sequence of row maps – each map is one row:

(-> [{:city "Paris" :temperature 22}
     {:city "London" :temperature 18}
     {:city "Berlin" :temperature 20}
     {:city "Rome" :temperature 28}]
    (pj/lay-bar :city :temperature))

temperaturecityParisLondonBerlinRome0510152025
Sequence of row vectors – each vector is one row, and the columns are named by their place: 0, 1 and so on. Nothing has to be wrapped first:

(-> [[1 2] [3 4] [5 7]]
    pj/lay-point)

1012345234567
Those integer names are what the axes are titled with, and they can be mapped like any other column name. (tc/rename-columns ds [:height :weight]) gives them words. A vector of vectors given to pj/arrange means something else – rows of cells, each cell a column, a mapping or a pose. What tells the two apart is where the vector is written – in a mapping, or in pj/arrange’s list of cells – not what it holds.
When the dataset has 1, 2, or 3 columns, you can omit the column names entirely – they are inferred from the order of the columns: the first column becomes x, the second becomes y, the third becomes color. Here the first column is :weight, so :weight is on the x axis:

(-> {:weight [1 2 3 4 5] :height [2 4 3 5 4]}
    pj/lay-point)

heightweight123452345
With four or more columns no column is read by default: name the columns, in the pj/lay-* call or in pj/pose. See the Datasets chapter for loading from CSV, URLs, and other file formats.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Mappings and Layers
The Poses chapter introduced the mapping-vs-layer split (what vs how). This section is the practical follow-up: how the split plays out across multi-layer plots and explicit-vs-shorthand calls.
Declare a mapping once with pj/pose, then add layers with pj/lay-* – both layers share the same axes:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
One mapping, two layers: points and a regression line.
When pj/lay-* is called with columns, it creates a pose and attaches a layer in one step:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
We will revisit where mappings flow (to all layers or to a single one) in the Scope section below.
With multiple poses arranged side by side, use pj/arrange:

(def two-panel
  (pj/arrange
   [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
    (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))]))


two-panel

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5
Each sub-pose has its own data and layers, and here each layer names its own columns. pj/arrange produces a composite pose that contains the two sub-poses as siblings.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Scope
A mapping maps a column (or a written value) to a visual property – like mapping :species to color. Where you write a mapping determines which layers read it. There are two levels:



Where you write it
What it reaches




(pj/pose ... {:color :c})
All layers on this pose


(pj/lay-point ... {:color :c})
This layer only



This is lexical scope – the closest enclosing definition wins.

Pose-level mapping
pj/pose’s mapping flows to every layer attached to the pose:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Both point and smooth layers read :color :species. Three regression lines – one per species.


Layer-level mapping
A mapping in pj/lay-* scopes to that layer alone:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model})
    kind/pprint)

How scope is applied
The same scoping principle governs mappings, layers, data, row filters and plot options. Where two values for one key meet – a later pj/pose on the same pose, a layer under its pose, a cell under its composite – they combine the same way at every level. A key holds either one value, which the later or inner value replaces, or a map of independent settings, which combines key by key:

Mappings: pose and layer mappings merge; the innermost wins on conflict, and an explicit nil erases a mapping inherited from above. The one part that combines rather than being replaced is a mapping’s :scale: a scale set on a pose and a scale set on one of its layers combine key by key, and so do two scales that pj/pose writes into a pose that already has a mapping – see Scales.
Row filters: two :where maps combine column by column; a column named in both takes the later or inner value. A composite’s filter reaches every cell – see Pose Rules.
Plot options: the later or inner value wins, except :theme and :config, whose settings combine key by key.
Layers: every pj/lay-* adds a new layer; layers do not override one another.
Data: the first argument to pj/pose/pj/lay-* sets the pose-level dataset; writing :data in a layer’s mapping overrides it for that layer alone (innermost non-nil wins).

A series is the one mapping that reaches past its layer. A vector of columns written where one column goes, as in (pj/lay-line data :month [:rain :snow]), is drawn by reshaping the pose’s dataset into one row per column and value, and every layer of the pose reads the reshaped rows – see Series.


Layer-level data
Write :data in the mapping of pj/lay-* to give that layer its own dataset:

(def setosa
  (tc/select-rows (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                  #(= "setosa" (:species %))))


(def versicolor
  (tc/select-rows (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                  #(= "versicolor" (:species %))))


(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:data setosa})
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model :data versicolor}))

For layer data that differs per panel, build the panels with pj/arrange, so each cell is a pose with its own layer data – see Known Limitations.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Layer Placement
Scope determines which mappings each pose and layer reads. But how do layers find their pose? The rule depends on whether the pose is a leaf or a composite.
Two words name the parts of a plot with several sets of axes. A panel is a part of the drawing: one set of axes and the marks drawn against them. A cell is a part of the pose: one of the sub-poses pj/arrange is given, or the part of a facet over columns that draws one column. A pose without a facet draws one panel, and an arrangement draws a panel for each of its cells.
On a leaf, pj/lay-* adds the layer to that leaf. A leaf draws one panel, and its layers share it, whatever columns they name:

(-> {:cohort [:a :b :c] :growth [12 19 15] :tax [3 5 4]}
    (pj/lay-bar :growth :cohort)
    (pj/lay-bar :tax :cohort {:bar-width 0.4}))

cohortgrowth, taxgrowthtax024681012141618abc
Each layer takes a color and a legend entry naming its column, and the axis title names both columns. Separate panels come from pj/facet and pj/arrange – see Panels.
On a composite, and on the cells of a facet over columns, pj/lay-* adds the layer at the root. The layer is drawn in every cell that fits it. A cell fits the layer when two things hold: on each axis the layer names, the cell’s panel draws no other column, and the cell’s columns together with the layer’s are a number of columns the layer type reads – two for a scatter or a trend line, one for a histogram. Here the trend line names :sepal-width on :y, so it is drawn in the two cells that draw :sepal-width on :y, and not in the third:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
                 {:x :petal-length :y :sepal-width}
                 {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:y :sepal-width :stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal length682.02.53.03.54.04.5petal length246petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5
Where no cell fits the layer, the layer is drawn in every cell, beside each cell’s own layers, as the layers of a single pose share its panel. A pj/lay-* call never adds a cell; pj/arrange adds cells – see Panels and Rules LP1 to LP3 in Pose Rules.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
The Pose
The Poses chapter walked through the shape of a pose end to end. This is the per-field reference card – what each slot holds and which API call sets it:








Field
Contains
Set by




:data
the dataset
pj/pose, pj/lay-*, or pj/with-data


:mapping
pose-level mappings, and their scales, and a facet’s categories under :col and :row
pj/pose, pj/scale, pj/facet


:layers
layers attached to the pose
pj/lay-*


:facet
a facet over columns, when pj/facet is given them
pj/facet


:opts
title, width, theme, coordinate system
pj/options, pj/coord



A composite pose adds :poses (sub-poses) and optionally :layout and :share-scales; see the Composition chapter for that shape.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Mark, Stat, and Position
Each layer has a layer type – a rendering recipe with three parts:

Mark – the visual shape (point, bar, line, area, tile, …)
Stat – the computation before rendering (identity, bin, linear-model, density, …)
Position – how overlapping groups share space (identity, dodge, stack, …)

A keyword like :histogram or :point names a layer type – look it up to see its parts:

(pj/layer-type-lookup :histogram)


{:mark :bar,
 :stat :bin,
 :x-only true,
 :accepts [:normalize :bins :binwidth],
 :doc "Histogram -- bins numerical data into bars.",
 :column-counts #{1}}

A histogram: stat :bin computes ranges, mark :bar shows them:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))

countsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00510152025
A smoother: stat :loess fits a curve, mark :line draws it. (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}) replaces the stat with a straight-line fit, as in the examples above:

(pj/layer-type-lookup :smooth)


{:mark :line,
 :stat :loess,
 :accepts
 [:confidence-band
  :level
  :bootstrap-resamples
  :bandwidth
  :size
  :stroke-dash
  :dx
  :dy],
 :doc
 "Smoothed trend line -- defaults to LOESS; pass {:stat :linear-model} for OLS.",
 :column-counts #{2}}

Position :stack places groups on top of each other:

(-> {:day ["Mon" "Mon" "Tue" "Tue"]
     :count [30 20 45 15]
     :meal ["lunch" "dinner" "lunch" "dinner"]}
    (pj/lay-bar :day :count {:color :meal :position :stack}))

countdaymeallunchdinnerMonTue0102030405060
See the Layer Types chapter for complete tables of every mark, stat, and position.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Inference
Plotje makes small poses work without you having to specify everything. You give it what you know – a dataset, perhaps a column or two – and it fills in the rest by inspecting the data.
Wherever you make a choice it wins; wherever you don’t, the library picks something sensible.
Column inference applies when a dataset has up to three columns and you call pj/pose (or a pj/lay-*) without naming any column. Plotje pairs the columns with aesthetics in dataset order:



Columns in data
Inferred mapping




1
:x


2
:x, :y


3
:x, :y, :color



With four or more columns the library does not guess – you have to name the columns you want, and a layer that names none reports an error. Column inference is most useful for quick sketches of small, focused datasets.

(-> {:height [170 180 165 175] :weight [70 80 65 75]}
    pj/lay-point)

weightheight1661681701721741761781806668707274767880
Layer type inference happens when a pose has no explicit layer. The library inspects the types of the columns the mapping refers to and picks a chart type that fits. Two numerical columns produce a scatter plot:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
A single numerical column produces a histogram:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length))

countsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00510152025
In both cases the inferred plot is the same one you would get from pj/lay-point or pj/lay-histogram. Inference is a shorthand, not a separate rendering path. Every inferred choice can be overridden – see Inference Rules for the full decision logic and override settings, or Architecture for where in the pipeline each kind of inference happens.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Incremental Building
Because poses are plain data, you can save a partial plot and extend it later. Each call returns a new pose without changing the original.

(def scatter-base
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)))

Add a regression line:

(-> scatter-base (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Or a LOESS smoother instead:

(-> scatter-base pj/lay-smooth)

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Reusable Pose Templates
A pose does not need to carry data. (pj/pose) creates an empty pose you can evolve like any other – adding layers, options – and then attach a dataset at the end with pj/with-data. The result is a reusable pose that can be applied to many datasets:

(def scatter-with-regression
  (-> (pj/pose nil {:x :height :y :weight :color :cohort})
      pj/lay-point
      (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model})
      (pj/options {:title "Scatter with Regression"})))

Printed, the template has :data nil – a pose that carries mapping, layers, and options but no data yet:

(kind/pprint scatter-with-regression)


{:mapping {:x :height, :y :weight, :color :cohort},
 :layers
 [{:layer-type :point} {:layer-type :smooth, :stat :linear-model}],
 :opts {:title "Scatter with Regression"}}

Before it has data, the template draws an empty panel that reads “no data”, and prints a Note saying where to give the data:

scatter-with-regression

Scatter with Regressionweightheightno data0101
Apply to one dataset:

(-> scatter-with-regression
    (pj/with-data {:height [1 2 3 4 5 6]
                   :weight [2 4 3 5 6 8]
                   :cohort ["a" "a" "a" "b" "b" "b"]}))

Scatter with Regressionweightheightcohortab1234562345678
Apply the same template to a different dataset:

(-> scatter-with-regression
    (pj/with-data {:height [10 20 30 40 50 60]
                   :weight [15 18 22 20 25 28]
                   :cohort ["c" "c" "c" "d" "d" "d"]}))

Scatter with Regressionweightheightcohortcd10203040506016182022242628
pj/lay-* given nil in place of data also makes a template: (pj/lay-point nil :displ :hwy) is a pose with a point layer and no data. A template can also be a cell of an arrangement given data first – see Panels.
pj/with-data validates at attach time: if the dataset is missing a column the pose references, it reports an error naming the missing columns.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Color and Grouping
:color controls point and line colors. Its behavior depends on what you pass.
Categorical column – each unique value gets a distinct color. A legend maps labels to colors:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Numeric column – values map to a continuous gradient:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :petal-length}))

sepal widthsepal lengthpetal length2464.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Fixed color string – all points colored uniformly:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color "steelblue"}))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Coming from ggplot2. In ggplot2, colour="blue" is always a CSS color. In Plotje, {:color "blue"} is a column reference if a column with that exact name exists in the data, otherwise the CSS color. A keyword goes through the same two checks in the same order, so {:color :blue} is the column :blue where there is one and the color blue where there is not. Matching is strict: a string only matches a string column name, and a keyword only matches a keyword column name. Hex codes like "#0000ff" are practically unambiguous – the dataset is checked first for those too, but no dataset carries a column called #0000ff. To settle a genuine collision, say which you mean: {:color {:column "blue"}} or {:color {:value "blue"}}.
The disambiguation matters when the dataset uses string column names. With a string column named "blue", the column wins – three palette colors render, not a single blue:

(-> {"height" [1 2 3] "weight" [1 2 3] "blue" ["a" "b" "c"]}
    (pj/lay-point "height" "weight" {:color "blue"}))

weightheightblueabc123123
Same string :color, dataset without a "blue" column – “blue” parses as a CSS color:

(-> {"height" [1 2 3] "weight" [1 2 3]}
    (pj/lay-point "height" "weight" {:color "blue"}))

weightheight123123
A categorical color also creates groups. Each group is processed independently: it gets its own regression line, density curve, or boxplot:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-density :sepal-length {:color :species}))

densitysepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00.00.20.40.60.81.01.2
Other visual properties include :alpha (transparency), :size, and :shape. Each accepts a value or a column the same way :color does – {:shape :square} draws every point square, and {:shape :species} gives each category its own symbol.
Bubble plot – :size mapped to a numeric column gives each point a radius reflecting the value:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width
                  {:color :petal-length :size :petal-width :alpha 0.7}))

sepal widthsepal lengthpetal length246petal width0.511.522.54.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Shape by category – :shape mapped to a categorical column renders each group with a different marker, and a legend naming them. Useful for monochrome printing:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:shape :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
:color and :shape can take the same column at once. Each species then has its own color and its own marker, so a reader who cannot tell the colors apart can still tell the groups apart. The legend has one entry per species, and its key shows both:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species
                                              :shape :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
The :group aesthetic creates groups without changing colors:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width {:group :species})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Three regression lines but all the same color.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Plot Options and Reference Lines
The functions in this section set plot-level options: values that describe a plot rather than a layer. They are written on a pose and reach everything beneath it: written on the pose you are building they describe the whole plot, and written on one cell of a composite, that cell. See Options and Scopes for the full picture.
pj/options sets plot-level settings – title, axis labels, size, theme overrides:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/options {:title "Iris Measurements"
                 :color-values :dark2}))

Iris Measurementssepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Reference lines and shaded bands are themselves layers, added with pj/lay-rule-h, pj/lay-rule-v, pj/lay-band-h, pj/lay-band-v. Where each one draws comes from its mapping (:y-intercept / :x-intercept for rules; :y-min/:y-max or :x-min/:x-max for bands); appearance aesthetics like :color and :alpha work the same way they do on any other layer, and so does layer order – a rule added before the points is drawn under them.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-rule-h {:y-intercept 3.0})
    (pj/lay-band-v {:x-min 5.0 :x-max 6.0 :alpha 0.1}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Printed, the rule and the band hold the values they are drawn at (:y-intercept, :x-min, :x-max) and their appearance (:alpha) in their :mapping, the slot where the point layer holds its :color:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/lay-rule-h {:y-intercept 3.0})
    (pj/lay-band-v {:x-min 5.0 :x-max 6.0 :alpha 0.1})
    kind/pprint)

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Coordinates and Scales
pj/coord sets the coordinate system. :flip swaps the axes:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/coord :flip))

sepal lengthsepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica2.02.53.03.54.04.54.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.0
:fixed locks the aspect ratio so one data unit on x equals one data unit on y – useful for spatial data or when distances on the two axes should read the same. The canvas is made narrower or shorter until the panel has that ratio, so here, where both columns run from -1 to 1, the panel is square:

(-> {:east [-1 1 -1 1] :north [-1 -1 1 1]}
    (pj/lay-point :east :north)
    (pj/coord :fixed))

northeast-101-101
pj/scale changes how a numeric axis is shown. :log applies a logarithmic transformation:

(-> {:population [1000 5000 50000 200000 1000000 5000000]
     :area [2 8 30 120 500 2100]}
    (pj/lay-point :population :area)
    (pj/scale :x :log)
    (pj/scale :y :log))

areapopulation1000100001000001000000101001000
Both are written on the pose and reach every layer and panel beneath it. A mapping written out in full can name its own scale for one aesthetic, which takes precedence there.

title: 5  Core Concepts
text:
Panels
Faceting splits a pose into panels by a column’s values:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/facet :species)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/facet :species)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model})
    kind/pprint)

title: 6  Panels
text:
The panel of a leaf pose
A plot can be one set of axes or a grid of them, and which you get is never chosen directly. A pose draws one panel, however many layers it holds and whatever columns they name. More panels come from pj/facet, which splits a pose’s one panel, and pj/arrange, which places poses side by side.
Two things to compare are either two columns or two categories of one column, and they are drawn either inside one panel or in panels of their own. The table names the form that draws each combination:
A series is drawn by pivoting its columns into a key column, :series, mapped to :color, so two columns on one panel are drawn as two categories are: a color and a legend entry each. Series teaches the series, and Color and Grouping the :color aesthetic. This chapter shows the forms in the across-panels column of the table, and how they combine. Faceting and Composition teach each in depth.
Read Poses first for what a leaf is.
A pose built from one dataset with one mapping is a single leaf, and draws a single panel:
Adding a layer does not add a panel. The layers of a pose share its axes and are drawn over one another:
A layer naming other columns adds no panel either. The layer’s columns are drawn against the axes the panel already has, each axis covers every column drawn on it and is titled by all of them, and each layer takes a colour and a legend entry naming its columns:
How the colour of each layer is decided – a colour it specifies, a :color on the pose, or a layer coloured by a column – is in Pose Rules, and Inference Rules shows a colour specified on each layer and a layer coloured by a column.

title: 6  Panels
text:
(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight12341234


(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-line :height :weight))

weightheight12341234


(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-point :depth :weight))

weightheight, depthheightdepth1.01.52.02.53.03.54.04.51234


The panel’s columns
A pj/lay-* call keeps its columns on its own layer, so a pose built by such calls has no mapping of its own. The panel still has columns: on each axis, the column the pose names, and where the pose names none there, the column of the first layer that names one. A layer that names no columns reads both of the panel’s columns:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    pj/lay-smooth)

weightheight1.01.52.02.53.03.54.01.01.52.02.53.03.54.0
The layer that names no columns may be written first. A pj/lay-* call does not read the data’s columns when it is called; the layer is given its columns when the pose is drawn, so a later call may name them:

(-> measurements
    pj/lay-smooth
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight))

weightheight1.01.52.02.53.03.54.01.01.52.02.53.03.54.0
A layer that names one column reads the panel’s column on the other axis, where its layer type draws from two columns. The line below names :depth on :y and is drawn against the panel’s :height:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :depth}))

weight, depthheightweightdepth12341.01.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A layer type that can draw from one column is not given a second column. A rug draws from one column, so the rug below marks :depth along the :x axis and reads no :y:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-rug {:x :depth}))

weightheight, depthheightdepth1.01.52.02.53.03.54.04.51234

title: 6  Panels
text:
A panel per column
To draw the two columns apart, split the pose over them with pj/facet. Each layer naming one of the columns is drawn only in that column’s panel:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-point :depth :weight)
    (pj/facet {:x [:height :depth]}))

height12341234depth234weight
The cells of a facet over columns are made from the panel’s columns, and the facet replaces the column on the axis it names. Below, the point layer names :weight, so it is drawn in the :weight panel. The :depth panel keeps the panel’s :height on :x. No layer names :depth, so that panel draws the layer type inferred from :height and :depth, which is a scatter too:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/facet {:y [:weight :depth]}))

weight1234depth1234234height
Where one layer is meant for every column, name the columns in the facet alone. The panels share the axis they agree about, :weight, and title it once:

(-> measurements
    (pj/pose {:y :weight})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:x [:height :depth]}))

height12341234depth234weight

title: 6  Panels
text:
A matrix of columns
A facet over columns can cross a list of columns with itself: {:col {:x columns} :row {:y columns}} draws a panel for every pair of columns, the columns across drawn on :x and the same columns down drawn on :y. A layer naming no columns, added after it, is drawn in the panels that draw as many columns as its layer type reads – a point reads two, so it is drawn off the diagonal. A panel with the same column on both axes draws one column, and draws the layer type inferred for one column, a histogram:

(-> measurements
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:height :weight :depth]}
              :row {:y [:height :weight :depth]}})
    pj/lay-point)

242424242424heightweightdepthheightweightdepth
pj/matrix writes that facet from the list of columns:

(-> measurements
    (pj/matrix [:height :weight :depth])
    pj/lay-point)

242424242424heightweightdepthheightweightdepth

title: 6  Panels
text:
A panel per category
A facet over the categories of a column draws one panel per category, each drawing the rows of its category. Two species give two panels:

(-> measurements
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/facet :species))

weightheight123412341234ab
The panels share both axes, so the categories can be read against each other: species “a” spans 1 to 2 on :height and species “b” 3 to 4, and both panels run from below 1 to above 4.
Many categories make a long row of panels. {:cols n} wraps them into rows of n panels, as in (pj/facet pose :class {:cols 4}) – see Wrapping the panels into rows.

title: 6  Panels
text:
Arranging poses side by side
pj/arrange takes finished poses and makes each one a cell of a single composite:

(pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point measurements :height :weight)
             (pj/lay-point measurements :depth :weight)])

weightheight12341234weightdepth2341234
Each pose above carries the dataset, so each cell computes its own axes and titles weight beside its own panel. Given the dataset first, pj/arrange makes its cells parts of one dataset. Cells that draw the same column on an axis then share that axis, titled once beside the grid, as the panels of a facet are:

(-> (pj/arrange measurements [{:x :height :y :weight}
                              {:x :depth :y :weight}])
    pj/lay-point)

height12341234depth234weight
Composition gives the rule for which cells share an axis, and how :share-scales changes it.
A pj/lay-* call on an arrangement adds its layer at the root of the composite. The layer is drawn in every cell that fits it. A cell fits the layer when two things hold: on each axis the layer names, the cell’s panel draws no other column, and the cell’s columns together with the layer’s are a number of columns the layer type reads. In the arrangement above, pj/lay-point names no columns, and each cell draws two, so the points are drawn in every cell. Here the line of :weight against :depth is drawn in the second cell only:

(-> (pj/arrange measurements [{:x :height :y :weight}
                              {:x :depth :y :weight}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-line :depth :weight))

height12341234depth234weight
A call naming one column, of a layer type that draws from two columns, is drawn in every cell whose panel draws no other column on that axis, and reads the cell’s column on the other axis, as on a leaf.
Where no cell fits the layer, the layer is drawn in every cell, beside each cell’s own layers, as the layers of a single pose share its panel. A histogram reads one column, so beside cells that draw two columns it fits no cell, and it is drawn over the points of every cell. Each cell’s :y axis then reads a count beside a column, and drawing the plot prints a Note for each cell saying so:

(-> (pj/arrange measurements [{:x :height :y :weight}
                              {:x :depth :y :weight}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-histogram :height))

height123401234depth, heightdepthheight24weight
A pj/lay-* call never adds a cell. A histogram meant for a cell of its own is given that cell with pj/arrange, which adds the cells it is given to the arrangement’s list:

(-> (pj/arrange measurements [{:x :height :y :weight}
                              {:x :depth :y :weight}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/arrange [:height]))

weightheight241234depth24countheight24012
A cell may also be a template – a pose with layers and no data, as Reusable Pose Templates describes. When pj/arrange is given data first, the template cell draws from the arrangement’s data. Here a cell with layers of its own sits beside a cell drawn by inference:

(pj/arrange measurements [(-> (pj/lay-point nil :height :weight)
                              (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))
                          {:x :depth :y :weight}])

height12341.01.52.02.53.03.54.0depth234weight
A layer added at the root is drawn under a cell’s own layers, whatever order the calls come in. Below, the line added to the arrangement is drawn beneath the first cell’s points:

(-> (pj/arrange measurements [(pj/lay-point nil :height :weight)
                              {:x :depth :y :weight}])
    pj/lay-line)

height12341234depth234weight
A composite pose can also be written directly, which Composition covers. It is the same structure pj/arrange builds.

title: 6  Panels
text:
Cells that filter the data
A cell of pj/arrange may hold :where, a map from a column to a value, and draws only the rows that match. A cell is written as the argument after the data in pj/pose is written, so the cell {:where {:species "a"}} is read as it is read in (pj/pose nil {:where {:species "a"}}). Cells that split one dataset by the values of one column draw what pj/facet draws over that column:

(-> measurements
    (pj/pose {:x :height :y :weight})
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:species "a"}}
                 {:where {:species "b"}}])
    pj/lay-point)

weightheight123412341234ab
A layer naming columns is drawn in every cell that splits the data, as it is drawn in every panel of the facet. A line of :weight against :height added to the cells above draws a line in each cell:

(-> measurements
    (pj/pose {:x :height :y :weight})
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:species "a"}}
                 {:where {:species "b"}}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-line :height :weight))

weightheight123412341234ab
The Facet or Arrange section of Faceting compares a facet with cells that filter the data, and Pose Rules says how a filter on the pose combines with a cell’s.

title: 6  Panels
text:
Combining facets and arrangements
Columns and categories cross in one pj/facet call, the categories across and the columns down. Each entry under :col and :row is one of the two kinds of facet, as in the matrix above:

(-> measurements
    (pj/pose {:x :height})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:col :species :row {:y [:weight :depth]}}))

123412342341234heightabweightdepth
Two pj/facet calls, one over the categories and one over the columns, write the same grid, in either order:

(-> measurements
    (pj/pose {:x :height})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:weight :depth]})
    (pj/facet :species))

123412342341234heightabweightdepth
:col and :row are aesthetics, so a facet written on an arranged pose reaches every cell:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/pose measurements :height :weight)
                 (pj/pose measurements :depth :weight)])
    (pj/lay-point)
    (pj/facet :species))

weightheight24123424abweightdepth24123424ab

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
The words used here
This chapter explains how to say what a mapping means.
A mapping can always be written out in full. The full form answers two questions: where the values come from, and whether they are read through a scale. Answering both is never wrong, and it is never ambiguous.
Most of the time you do not write the full form. Plotje has conventions that supply the two answers from a shorter notation, and the shorter notation is what the rest of the book uses. Each convention is a shorthand for something you could have written out, not a rule of its own.
So this chapter goes in that order. First the full form, and the combinations of the two answers it can express. Then the conventions, and which combination each one produces. Then the cases where the conventions cannot decide, and you write the full form instead.
The terms below are used throughout this chapter. Each has a fuller entry in the Glossary.
An aesthetic is a visual property of a mark: where it sits (:x, :y), what color it is (:color), how large (:size), how opaque (:alpha), which symbol (:shape), what it says (:text). See Aesthetic.
A mapping says where one aesthetic gets its values. {:color :species} is a mapping. What it supplies may differ from row to row, or be a single value for the whole layer. A mapping is written either on a pose, where it reaches every layer of that pose, or in the mapping of a single layer, where it reaches only that layer. See Mapping.
A scale turns data into something visible. The color scale turns categories into colors; the size scale turns numbers into radii; the x scale turns data values into places across the panel. A scale is built from the data it is given, so it depends on the whole column and not on any one row. See Scale.
A legend is the key drawn beside the plot that explains a scale – which color stands for which category, which radius for which number. A legend appears when there is a scale to explain. See Legend.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
The data used here
Plants, measured. Two columns hold numbers, one holds category names, and one holds colors written as hex codes.

(def plants
  {:height  [12 25 18 31]
   :weight  [1.4 3.9 2.2 4.6]
   :species ["fern" "moss" "fern" "ivy"]
   ;; Deliberately nothing like the palette's first three colors, so
   ;; that a plot which scales this column and a plot which draws it
   ;; as it stands cannot be mistaken for each other.
   :shade   ["#EE7733" "#AA3377" "#EE7733" "#000000"]})


plants


{:height [12 25 18 31],
 :weight [1.4 3.9 2.2 4.6],
 :species ["fern" "moss" "fern" "ivy"],
 :shade ["#EE7733" "#AA3377" "#EE7733" "#000000"]}

The :shade column holds colors, and it is still a column of data like any other.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
A mapping written in full
The full form is a map with two keys, written where the shorter notation would otherwise go:
{:color {:column :species :scale true}}
The first key names the source – where the values come from. There are two possibilities and they are spelled differently:

:column names a column of the layer’s data. Every row supplies its own value, so the aesthetic can differ from mark to mark.
:value gives the value itself, written in the mapping. There is one of it, so it is the same for every mark in the layer.

A mapping names one or the other, never both. A third spelling, :from, leaves the choice to the data – the section Leaving the source to the data below covers it.
The second key, :scale, says whether that source is read through the aesthetic’s scale:

:scale true sends it through the scale. What you supplied is data, and the scale decides what is drawn for it.
:scale false draws it as it stands. What you supplied is already the visible thing, and no scale is involved.

The two keys are independent: either source can be read either way, which makes four combinations. The next four sections take them one at a time, each written in full.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: A column, read through the scale
text:
A column, read through the scale
{:column :species :scale true} says: take each mark’s value from the :species column, and send it through the color scale.
The color scale is built from every value in the column. There are three distinct species, so the scale assigns three colors from the palette, and a legend appears to explain which is which. Nothing about the drawn colors comes from the column – "fern" is not a color, and the scale is what supplies one for it.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:column :species :scale true}}))

weightheightspeciesfernmossivy121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: A column, drawn as it stands
text:
A column, drawn as it stands
{:column :shade :scale false} says: take each mark’s value from the :shade column, and draw it without a scale.
This only makes sense when the column already holds what the aesthetic draws, which for :color means colors. :shade holds hex codes, so each mark is drawn in the color its own row carries.
No legend appears. A legend explains a scale, and there is no scale here.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:column :shade :scale false}
                                   :size 9}))

weightheight121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
The first plant’s :shade is "#EE7733", and the first mark is drawn in exactly that color.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: A drawn column does not group
text:
A drawn column does not group
A color column read through its scale is data: each distinct value is a category, the rows are split into a group per category, every layer is computed once per group, and the legend says which group is which. A column drawn as it stands is not read that way. It holds drawn values already – the colors themselves – so no scale reads it, no categories come out of it, and the rows are not split. A bar keeps the whole of its band instead of sharing it with the other colors:

(-> {:cohort ["a" "b" "c"] :growth [10 20 30]
     :shade ["#EE7733" "#AA3377" "#000000"]}
    (pj/lay-bar :cohort :growth {:color {:column :shade :scale false}}))

growthcohortabc051015202530
The same column read through its scale would give three categories, so three groups, and three bars each a third of a band wide.
With no groups there is also no group color for a mark to take, which is why a drawn column reaches only the marks that draw one shape per row. A line drawn from every row, a histogram bar counting the rows in its bin and a boxplot summarizing a category can each be drawn in one color only, so Plotje reports an error instead of drawing it:

(try
  (-> {:day [1 2 3] :visits [4 5 6] :shade ["#EE7733" "#AA3377" "#000000"]}
      (pj/lay-line :day :visits {:color {:column :shade :scale false}})
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"A :scale false on :color draws the column's own values, one per row, and :line draws one shape from many rows, so it cannot read one. For one color over the layer, write the value itself. To split the data and color the parts, drop the :scale so the column is read through :color's scale."

The pose itself is well formed; the error comes when it is drawn. It names the mark and both ways out: write one color for the layer, or drop the :scale so the column is read through the color scale.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: A written value, drawn as it stands
text:
A written value, drawn as it stands
{:value "#0077BB" :scale false} says: use this one color, and draw it without a scale.
Every mark in the layer is drawn in it. There is one value, so there is nothing to tell marks apart by, and no legend.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:value "#0077BB" :scale false}
                                   :size 9}))

weightheight121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: A written value, read through the scale
text:
A written value, read through the scale
{:value "Model A" :scale true} says: treat this one value as data, and send it through the color scale.
One value repeated over every row is a column with one distinct value in it. The color scale is built from that, so it assigns one color, and a legend appears with one entry reading "Model A".
This is how a whole layer is given a name in the legend. The value is not a color – it is data, and the scale supplies the color.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:value "Model A" :scale true}
                                   :size 9}))

weightheightcolorModel A121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
The layers of a plot share one color scale, so a value read through it joins the categories the other layers supply. The points below take their color from the :species column, and the line is written as "ivy", which that column already holds. The line comes out in the color "ivy" was assigned, and the legend still has one row per species:

(-> plants
    (pj/pose :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-point {:color {:column :species :scale true} :size 9})
    (pj/lay-line {:color {:value "ivy" :scale true}}))

weightheightspeciesfernmossivy121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
So a layer with no column of its own can be drawn in the color the scale already gives a category. A value the column does not hold is a new category instead, and takes a color and a legend row of its own:

(-> plants
    (pj/pose :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-point {:color {:column :species :scale true} :size 9})
    (pj/lay-line {:color {:value "predicted" :scale true}}))

weightheightspeciesfernmossivypredicted121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
One scale per aesthetic is a plot-wide rule, not a rule about values; Scales states it and shows what happens when two layers ask for different ones.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
Source and :scale combined









Source
:scale
What you supply
What is drawn




:column
true
a column of data
one color per distinct value, from the palette, with a legend


:column
false
a column of colors
each row’s own color, no legend


:value
false
one color
that color for every mark, no legend


:value
true
one data value
one color from the palette, with a legend entry for that value



The rows naming a palette are the rows for a column of categories, which :species is. A column of numbers is read as a quantity instead and drawn through a gradient, with a bar in place of the per-value legend rows – :weight and :height on this data are both of those. The column’s type decides, as Column Types explains.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color :weight}))

weightheightweight234121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
The same four combinations exist for :size, where the scale turns numbers into radii, and for :alpha, where it turns numbers into opacities.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
The short form
A mapping may be written short – a bare column name, or the bare thing to be drawn – and Plotje supplies the two answers.

How the source is decided
The layer’s data decides. If the value names a column of that data, it is a column reference. If it does not, it is the value itself.
Matching is exact. A keyword finds a keyword-named column and a string finds a string-named one, so :species and "species" are not interchangeable. The Inference Rules chapter works through this in full.
So, on the plants data above, {:color :species} has the source of {:column :species}, because the data carries a :species column; and {:color "#0077BB"} has the source of {:value "#0077BB"}, because no column is named that.
A vector of column names where one column goes, as in {:y [:height :weight]}, is a series: the columns are drawn on one panel, each in a color of its own.


How the scale is decided
A column is read through the scale. That is the default, and :scale false overrides it. What the column holds makes no difference – :shade holds colors, and the short form {:color :shade} still sends it through the color scale, so three distinct values become three palette colors:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color :shade}))

weightheightshade#EE7733#AA3377#000000121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A written value is decided by what the aesthetic is for. The aesthetics fall into two groups here, and the two groups answer differently.
On the appearance aesthetics – :color, :size, :alpha, :shape – a written value is drawn as it stands. {:color "steelblue"} is that color and {:size 9} is that radius.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color "steelblue" :size 9}))

weightheight121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
On the positional aesthetics – :x, :y and the range endpoints :x-min, :x-max, :y-min, :y-max, :x-end and :y-end – a written value is read through the scale instead. It is a data value, so the axis takes it into account. The text below is placed at a :weight of 6.0, which is past the largest measured weight of 4.6, and the y axis stretches to reach it.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-text {:x 20 :y 6.0 :text "target"}))

weightheighttarget121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.55.05.56.0
The two groups differ because what people usually mean differs. A number written for :x or :y is usually a place in the data – a threshold to mark, a point to label – and only rarely a distance across the page. A number written for :size or :alpha is usually the appearance itself, and only rarely a measurement to be scaled. Each convention takes the common case, and writing :scale gives the less common reading where it is meant.
A layer’s :x and :y can both be given in drawing units at once, rather than one at a time, with {:in :drawing-area}, described in Placing Marks.


What the short forms come out as
Each short form below produces exactly the mapping beside it:



Short form
Full form




{:color :species}
{:color {:column :species :scale true}}


{:color :shade}
{:color {:column :shade :scale true}}


{:color "#0077BB"}
{:color {:value "#0077BB" :scale false}}



pj/svg-summary reports what a pose renders to, so the colors each pair draws can be read side by side. The pairs come out the same:

(defn drawn-colors
  "The colors a `:color` mapping draws on the plants scatter."
  [mapping]
  (-> plants
      (pj/lay-point :height :weight mapping)
      pj/svg-summary
      :colors
      (disj "none")))


{:species-short (drawn-colors {:color :species})
 :species-full  (drawn-colors {:color {:column :species :scale true}})
 :shade-short   (drawn-colors {:color :shade})
 :shade-full    (drawn-colors {:color {:column :shade :scale true}})
 :written-short (drawn-colors {:color "#0077BB"})
 :written-full  (drawn-colors {:color {:value "#0077BB" :scale false}})}


{:species-short #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :species-full #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :shade-short #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :shade-full #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :written-short #{"rgb(0,119,187)"},
 :written-full #{"rgb(0,119,187)"}}

The positional short form works the same way: {:y 6.0} is {:y {:value 6.0 :scale true}}, which is what stretched the y axis in the example above.


Naming the source without choosing the scale
The two keys can be written separately. A full form that names only a source leaves the scale to the convention, which is useful when the source is the ambiguous part and the scale is not.

{:column-alone   (drawn-colors {:color {:column :shade}})
 :column-scaled  (drawn-colors {:color {:column :shade :scale true}})
 :value-alone    (drawn-colors {:color {:value "#0077BB"}})
 :value-drawn    (drawn-colors {:color {:value "#0077BB" :scale false}})}


{:column-alone #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :column-scaled #{"rgb(228,26,28)" "rgb(55,126,184)" "rgb(77,175,74)"},
 :value-alone #{"rgb(0,119,187)"},
 :value-drawn #{"rgb(0,119,187)"}}



Leaving the source to the data
The third source key is :from. It names the source the way the plain form does – read the data, and take whichever reading it supports – while leaving room for a :scale, which a plain mapping has nowhere to put.
{:color {:from :shade}} and the plain {:color :shade} say the same thing, and draw the same plot:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:from :shade}}))

weightheightshade#EE7733#AA3377#000000121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
Writing it that way leaves room for a :scale. :shade holds colors, and the palette is drawn over them because a column passes through the color scale. :scale false draws them as they stand – and the plain form cannot say it:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:from :shade :scale false}}))

weightheight121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
{:column :shade :scale false} draws the same plot here, and the two differ on data that carries no such column. :column requires a column and reports it missing either way. :from falls back to reading the name as a value, exactly as the plain form does – so where the name is one a color can be made of, it draws that color:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:from :red} :size 9}))

weightheight121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
Where the name is not a color either – :shade on data without a :shade column – both report the column missing, since there is nothing else the name could be.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
The positional aesthetics (:x, :y) and :scale false
On :x and :y, :scale false means the value is a distance in drawing units measured from the top left of the panel background, rather than a data value. Drawing units are explained in Drawing Space.
:scale false is read for each axis on its own. Below, the note’s :x is a data value, so it sits at a :height value of 20; its :y is 14 drawing units down from the top of the panel, wherever the weights happen to run.

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight)
    (pj/lay-text {:x 20
                  :y {:value 14 :scale false}
                  :text "fixed to the panel"}))

weightheightfixed to the panel121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A value in drawing units informs no domain, which is why the y axis above still ends near the largest weight rather than stretching to 14. The marks that can read an axis in drawing units are the marks placed through the panel’s coordinates; a bar or a boxplot reads the axis scale directly and reports an error rather than ignoring the :scale false.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
When the conventions cannot decide
The source rule turns on one question: does this value name a column of the data? Two situations make that question the wrong one, and in both you write the full form.

A column named after a color
If the data carries a column called "blue", then {:color "blue"} names that column, and the color blue is out of reach through the short form.

(def named-after-a-color
  {:height [12 25]
   :weight [1.4 3.9]
   "blue"  ["p" "q"]})


named-after-a-color


{:height [12 25], :weight [1.4 3.9], "blue" ["p" "q"]}

{:value "blue"} is the color. One group, drawn blue, no legend.

(-> named-after-a-color
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:value "blue"} :size 9}))

weightheight121416182022241.52.02.53.03.54.0
{:column "blue"} is the column. Two groups, two palette colors, and a legend reading the column’s two values.

(-> named-after-a-color
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:color {:column "blue"} :size 9}))

weightheightbluepq121416182022241.52.02.53.03.54.0


Columns named by number
A dataset built without column names gets integer ones. A number on :x or :y then has both readings available – it could be a column name or a value to place a mark at – and the source rule decides between them the way it decides everywhere: by reading the data.

(def integer-named
  {0 [1 2 3]
   1 [4 5 6]})


integer-named


{0 [1 2 3], 1 [4 5 6]}

The data carries a column named 0, so the bare {:x 0} reads it. Its three values run from 1 to 3, so the x domain covers that range with the usual padding.

(-> integer-named
    (pj/lay-point {:x 0 :y 1}))

10123456
That is the reading the data gives it, not a reading of the number. On a dataset with no column named 0 the same mapping places every mark at an x of zero, and the domain is padded outward from that single value:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point {:x 0 :y :weight}))

weightx-1011.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
So the same code means different things on differently named data. Where that matters, write the mapping in full, and the data does not decide the source. {:column 0} reads the column even where one exists only by accident:

(-> integer-named
    (pj/lay-point {:x {:column 0} :y 1}))

10123456
and {:value 0} places every mark at zero even where a column named 0 is there to be read:

(-> integer-named
    (pj/lay-point {:x {:value 0} :y 1}))

1x-101456

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
What :scale accepts
true and false say which side of the scale a mapping is read through. :scale also accepts a scale type – linear or logarithmic, for instance – and a whole scale spec, the map that says which scale and how, and then it says which scale as well:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight {:size {:column :weight :scale :log}}))

weightheightweight23121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A spec is the same map pj/scale takes – the same keys, checked the same way – so a mapping can set the range an aesthetic spans as well as its type. The one below is twice the default at both ends, and every mark is drawn twice as wide:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point :height :weight
                  {:size {:column :weight :scale {:range [4 16]}}}))

weightheightweight1.522.533.544.5121416182022242628301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A type written here applies to that one mapping only. pj/scale sets the scale on the pose it is called on and everything below: called on the pose you are building, it covers the whole plot; called on one cell before the cells are arranged, that cell alone. Where both are written, the mapping is the narrower scope and wins, key by key – so a pose that sets a range and a mapping that names a type give a plot with both.
:scale true passes the value through whatever scale the aesthetic has, so a pj/scale above the mapping still decides the type.
Each aesthetic gets its own: (pj/scale pose :x :log) and (pj/scale pose :size :log) are separate decisions, and either can be made without the other. Which keys a spec may carry depends on the aesthetic – :size reads :range, :by and :from-zero beside :type and :domain, an axis reads :breaks and :tick-labels – and a key the aesthetic does not read reports an error rather than being dropped. Scales has each of them.

The axes take one scale per panel
:x and :y take a type or a spec like any other aesthetic:

(-> plants
    (pj/lay-point {:x {:column :height :scale {:type :log}} :y :weight}))

weightheight20301.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
A panel has one x axis and one y axis, and every layer is drawn against them, so a panel carries one scale per axis. Two layers naming different scales for one axis report an error; a layer naming no scale is drawn against whichever scale the panel has.

(try
  (-> plants
      (pj/pose :height :weight)
      (pj/lay-point {:x {:column :height :scale :log}})
      (pj/lay-line {:x {:column :height :scale :linear}})
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"Layers name different scales for the :x axis: [{:type :log} {:type :linear}]. A panel has one x axis, and every layer is drawn against it, so it can carry only one. Set it once with (pj/scale pose :x ...), or write the same :scale in each mapping."



Aesthetics with no scale
Two aesthetics have no scale at all, so a :scale written on either of them reports an error.
:text draws a label as it stands, whether the label comes from a column or is written in the mapping. :group splits a layer into one drawn group per value and draws nothing of its own.

(try
  (pj/lay-text plants :height :weight {:text {:column :species :scale false}})
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


":text {:column :species, :scale false} sets :scale, and :text has no scale to set. A label is drawn as it stands, whether it comes from a column or is written in the mapping, so there is no scale for it to pass through."

Both still take the full form’s source key, which is what settles a column name that could be read as a value.

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
section: What a distinction is put to work as
text:
What a distinction is put to work as
A distinction is a set of things to tell apart, and it is made of columns. Every aesthetic answers two questions about the distinction it is given: where the marks go, and how a reader tells them apart. The answer is the aesthetic’s role, and an aesthetic has one of four. A role is not a category – a category is a value a categorical column holds, which is what a role is given.
