 {:column-names [:aesthetic :role]
  :row-vectors (->> (pj/aesthetic-roles)
                    (sort-by (comp str key))
                    (mapv (fn [[k role]] [k role])))})

title: 7  Specifying Aesthetics
text:
Appendix: source and :scale in ggplot2
ggplot2 has all four combinations and reaches them through different syntax. The table uses :size as the example:







Plotje
ggplot2




{:size {:column :weight :scale true}}
aes(size = weight)


{:size {:column :radii :scale false}}
aes(size = radii) + scale_size_identity()


{:size {:value 7 :scale false}}
geom_point(size = 7)


{:size {:value 7 :scale true}}
aes(size = 7)



The table was checked by running each ggplot2 form on version 4.0.0 and comparing what it produced. What matches is which of the four combinations each form gives, not the sizes drawn: the two libraries spread a scaled column across different intervals of radii, so the same data draws different circles.
The difference is where the choice is written. In ggplot2 it is spread across three places – inside aes(), outside it, and in a scale_* call. In Plotje the two questions are answered in the mapping itself, by the two keys.
ggplot2 Equivalents collects the Plotje spellings of other ggplot2 functions – layers, scales, coordinates, facets and labels.

title: 8  Composition
text:
Side-by-Side via pj/arrange
Plotje’s poses let you combine whole plots into a single rendered image. A composite pose holds other poses and a layout; each sub-pose renders independently and the composite tiles them together.
This chapter walks through composition patterns from simple side-by-side arrangements to shared-scale marginal plots, using pj/arrange, pj/marginal and explicit composite-pose maps – compactly for simple cases, with a bit of literal map construction for nested layouts.
On a first read through the book you can skim or skip the later, deeper sections – Count and Density Axes, Cells Drawn Flipped, Cells That Line Up and Notes on the Current Implementation – and return when you build a composite that needs them.
The simplest composite: two independent poses, placed next to each other. pj/arrange takes a vector of poses and returns a composite. Each sub-pose has its own data, mapping, layers, and options. Coming from R, this is the same shape as patchwork’s p1 | p2 operator or cowplot’s plot_grid(p1, p2).
Pass {:cols 1} for a stacked arrangement (one column means each pose goes on its own row):
A vector of vectors gives one row per inner vector. nil in place of a pose is a cell left empty: it keeps its place in the layout and draws nothing, so the other cells stay where they are.
pj/arrange also takes data first. Each cell is then written as the argument after the data in pj/pose is written: a mapping such as {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} is a panel drawing those two columns, and a single column, :sepal-length, is a panel drawing that column. A vector in the list of cells is never a cell: it is a row of cells, or an arrangement of its own. The layers are added afterwards, once, and are drawn in every cell:
A layer that names columns is drawn in every cell that fits it: on each axis the layer names, the cell’s panel draws no other column, and the cell’s columns together with the layer’s are a number of columns the layer type reads. Below, the trend line names the first cell’s columns and is drawn there only:
The two cells read one dataset, so the two cells share the :x axis on which both draw :sepal-length, and that axis is titled once (see Shared Scales below). A layer that fits no cell is drawn in every cell, beside each cell’s own layers: a histogram naming :sepal-length fits neither cell, because each cell draws two columns and a histogram reads one, so it is drawn over the points in both. A layer added to the arrangement is drawn under the layers a cell holds of its own. See Rules LP2 and LP3 in Pose Rules and Panels.
A pj/lay-* call adds no cell. An arrangement is built in steps with pj/arrange: given an arrangement, it adds the new cells after its own and draws what one pj/arrange call with the longer list draws, so a third panel joins the row:
A cell can also hold a row filter, {:where {:species "setosa"}}, and draw the rows that match it, as Cells that filter the data shows.
pj/arrange divides space equally among its cells unless the plot options :col-weights or :row-weights give the columns and rows of cells unequal shares, as Panels of Unequal Size below shows.

title: 8  Composition
text:
Explicit Composite Poses
Under pj/arrange there is a plain-map composite pose. You can construct one directly when you want to write the tree of sub-poses as a literal map, with a weight for each sub-pose under :layout.
An explicit :layout accepts :direction (:horizontal or :vertical) and :weights (one weight per sub-pose). Here the first cell gets twice the width of the second:

(def weighted
  (pj/pose
   {:layout {:direction :horizontal :weights [2 1]}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}
            {:mapping {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))

pj/pose accepts a literal composite map and tags it for notebook auto-render – the same pose value the threaded API produces:

weighted

title: 8  Composition
text:
Panels of Unequal Size
A histogram beside a scatter plot reads well narrower than the scatter, and a plot printed beside others may need panels of an exact size. An arrangement’s columns and rows of cells are equal by default; two pairs of plot options change that.
:col-weights and :row-weights give each column and row of panels its share of the plot, which keeps its :width and :height. The tick labels, strips and titles take their room first, and the weights share out the rest, so [2 1] draws the first panel twice as wide as the second:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :displ :y :hwy} :hwy] {:col-weights [2 1]}))

hwydispl23456715202530354045counthwy2040010203040506070
:panel-width and :panel-height pin the panels in drawing units instead, and the plot’s size is worked out from them, as it is for a single plot. A number gives every column of panels the same width (or every row the same height), and a vector gives one value for each column (or row) in turn. Here the two columns are 300 and 150 wide, and the row is 200 high:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [{:x :displ :y :hwy} :hwy] {:panel-width [300 150] :panel-height 200}))

hwydispl246203040counthwy20400204060
Giving both kinds for one direction, :panel-width with :col-weights, reports an error. A facet over categories draws its panels at one size, so a vector there reports an error too; a facet over columns, such as a scatter plot matrix, takes them.

title: 8  Composition
text:
Shared Scales
Two cells that draw the same column are often read against each other – a marginal above a scatter, or one measurement shown for several groups – and then the two cells need one range on that axis. Whether cells share an axis by default depends on where they read their data. Cells that read the data of the pose holding them – a composite written with :data at its root, as above, or (pj/arrange data [...]) – share each axis on which they draw the same column, as the panels of a facet do. Cells that each carry data of their own, as in (pj/arrange [pose-a pose-b]), compute their own domains (the extent of data values each axis covers). :share-scales names the axes the cells share, whichever the default was, and the cells drawing the same column on such an axis are given one domain. Below, each cell holds the rows of one species, and :x is shared:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

56782.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.84.04.24.456782.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.8sepal lengthsepal width
Both cells are drawn on one :x range, and each cell keeps its own :y range, because :share-scales names :x only. Only cells drawing the same column on :x share that axis: two cells drawing different columns there each keep their own range.
A date column pools the same way – an axis holds a date as a number of milliseconds, so the union across cells is defined, and the cells are ticked over it rather than each over its own dates. See Change Over Time.

What a Shared Axis Covers
A shared axis covers what the cells sharing it draw. What a cell draws is not always what its column holds: a stack of bars reaches the total of its segments, an error bar reaches its ends, and a smoothed line can dip below or rise above the points it was fitted to. Plotje measures each cell after its statistics have run, pools the measurements of the cells sharing the axis, and pads the pooled extent once. Every sharing cell then draws the same axis, and no mark is cut off at the edge of a panel.
Two shops below sell the same drinks in two halves of a year. No value in the :sold column reaches the tallest stack, and the shared :y axis of both cells reaches past that stack:

(def north-shop
  {:drink ["tea" "tea" "coffee" "coffee"]
   :half ["first" "second" "first" "second"]
   :sold [30 45 20 25]})


(def south-shop
  {:drink ["tea" "tea" "cocoa" "cocoa"]
   :half ["first" "second" "first" "second"]
   :sold [60 70 10 15]})


(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-shop (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold {:color :half :position :stack}))
  (-> south-shop (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold {:color :half :position :stack}))]
 {:share-scales #{:y}})

teacoffee020406080100120teacocoadrinksoldhalffirstsecond
A rule or a band is covered too. A rule is drawn at a value written on its layer, which no column holds. Here one cell carries a limit beyond anything either species measures, and both cells reach it:

(def limit 8.5)


(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-rule-v {:x-intercept limit :color "firebrick"}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

56782.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.84.04.24.456782.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.8sepal lengthsepal width
A :domain that one cell specifies for a shared axis is the domain of every cell sharing that axis, since a shared axis is one axis. Below, the second cell specifies 0 to 10 for :x, and both cells are drawn on exactly that interval:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point {:x {:column :sepal-length :scale {:domain [0 10]}}
                     :y :sepal-width}))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

02468102.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.84.04.24.402468102.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.8sepal lengthsepal width
Two cells that specify different domains for one shared axis report an error naming both domains. To specify one domain for the cells, call pj/scale on the composite: (pj/scale composite :x {:domain [0 10]}) is the domain of every cell that specifies none of its own. On a shared axis, remove the :domain from the cells first: a cell that keeps its own domain reports the same error.


Columns That Share an Axis
A set of axes shares an axis among the cells that draw the same column on it. Two cells drawing different columns keep their own ranges, which is right when the columns are in different units and wrong when they measure one quantity. Highway mileage and city mileage are both in miles per gallon, and under #{:x :y} each panel still fits its own :y. Plotje prints a warning that no two cells share :y, naming the group form used next:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :displ})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales #{:x :y}}))

hwy203040cty1.52.02.53.03.54.04.55.05.56.06.57.0102030displ
The full form of :share-scales is a map from an axis to the columns that go together on that axis. Cells whose columns go together share the axis:

:same-column – each column goes with itself only, which is what the set says;
a vector of groups of columns, such as [[:hwy :cty]] – the columns of a group go together, and a column in no group goes with itself only;
:all – every column goes together, so every cell shares the axis.

An axis the map leaves out is not shared. Here :x is shared as before, and the two mileage columns share :y, so a point at the same height is the same mileage in both panels:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :displ})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:x :same-column
                                :y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

hwy10203040cty1.52.02.53.03.54.04.55.05.56.06.57.010203040displ
A group leaves the other columns alone. With engine displacement as a third panel, the mileage panels share a range and displacement keeps its own:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/pose {:x :year})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :cty :displ]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:x :same-column
                                :y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

hwy2040cty2040displ1999200020012002200320042005200620072008246year
The columns of a group may come from different datasets, which is how two poses that name one quantity differently are read against each other:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> {:day [1 2 3] :indoor [19.0 20.5 21.0]}
      (pj/lay-line :day :indoor))
  (-> {:day [1 2 3] :outdoor [4.0 9.5 14.0]}
      (pj/lay-line :day :outdoor))]
 {:share-scales {:y [[:indoor :outdoor]]}})

indoor123468101214161820outdoor123468101214161820day
Columns that go together have to hold one type of value: numbers with numbers, dates with dates, categories with categories. A group holding a numeric column and a categorical one reports an error:

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
      (pj/pose {:x :displ})
      pj/lay-point
      (pj/facet {:y [:hwy :drv]})
      (pj/options {:share-scales {:y :all}})
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e (ex-message e)))


":share-scales cannot share :y between these cells: columns :hwy, :drv have no one axis to be drawn on. The cells differ in column type: categorical and numerical. Cells sharing an axis must agree on the coordinate system, the column type (numerical, categorical or temporal) and the scale type (linear or log). Leave :y out of :share-scales, or name only the columns that go together."



A Shared Categorical Axis
A categorical axis is shared as the list of every category the sharing cells hold. A bar for tea then stands at the same place in each cell, and a cell with no rows for a category leaves the place of that category empty. The north shop sells no cocoa and the south shop no coffee; with :x shared, both cells list all three drinks. Each bar here is a drink’s total for the year:

(def north-totals
  {:drink ["tea" "coffee"] :sold [75 45]})


(def south-totals
  {:drink ["tea" "cocoa"] :sold [130 25]})


(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold))
  (-> south-totals (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold))]
 {:share-scales #{:x :y}})

teacoffeecocoa020406080100120teacoffeecocoadrinksold
The two cells above have data of their own, so the categories come in the order of the cells: the drinks of the first cell, then the drink the second cell adds. Cells that are parts of one dataset – the panels of a facet, or the cells of a pose arranged over its own data – list the categories in the order of that dataset’s rows, which is the order the same plot draws them in when it is not split.


Count and Density Axes
A histogram draws a count on :y, and no column holds that count. An axis like this is shared by what is counted. Two histograms of one column share their count axis:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))]
 {:share-scales #{:y}})

4.55.05.505101520255678sepal lengthcount
Histograms of different columns keep a count axis each under a set of axes, as cells drawing different columns do. A group naming the columns shares their count axes:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    pj/pose
    pj/lay-histogram
    (pj/facet {:x [:hwy :cty]})
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:y [[:hwy :cty]]}}))

counthwy203040010203040506070countcty102030
A count, a density and the values of a column are measured in different units, so an axis holding one is never pooled with an axis holding another. {:y :all} shares every count axis with the other count axes, every density axis with the other density axes, and the axes of columns with each other. Below, the two histograms share one count axis and the scatter keeps the axis of its :hwy column:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-histogram :hwy))
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-histogram :cty))
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy))]
 {:share-scales {:y :all}})

counthwy2040010203040506070countcty102030hwydispl24615202530354045
A histogram normalized with {:normalize :density} draws a density, and shares with a density curve of the same column. A layer type added by an extension takes part by declaring what its statistic computes; see Extensibility.


Cells Drawn Flipped
:share-scales names an axis as it is drawn: :x is the horizontal axis and :y the vertical one. Under (pj/coord :flip) the column mapped to :y runs across the page, and #{:x} shares the axis that column is drawn on. (pj/scale and :x-label name the column’s own axis, whichever way that axis is drawn.) The totals of the two shops as flipped bars, sharing the horizontal axis:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> north-totals
      (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold)
      (pj/coord :flip))
  (-> south-totals
      (pj/lay-bar :drink :sold)
      (pj/coord :flip))]
 {:share-scales #{:x}})

050100teacoffee050100teacocoasolddrink


Cells That Line Up
Each cell reserves the room its own y labels need, so a cell labelled in single digits comes out wider than a cell labelled in millions, and the axis the two share covers a different extent in each. :align-panels reserves the widest y-label pad and legend column any cell needs on all of them, so every cell gets the same drawing area:

(def readings
  {:t [1 2 3 4 5]
   :rate [1.0 2.0 3.0 2.0 4.0]
   :total [1200000.0 2400000.0 1800000.0 3100000.0 2600000.0]})


(pj/arrange
 [(-> readings (pj/lay-line :t :rate))
  (-> readings (pj/lay-line :t :total))]
 {:cols 1 :share-scales #{:x} :align-panels true})

rate1234total123451500000200000025000003000000t
Pair it with :share-scales where the cells are meant to be read against one another. pj/marginal sets both – What a marginal is made of takes one apart.


A Facet Placed as a Cell
A facet shares both axes across its panels by default. Placed as a cell of an arrangement, the facet takes the arrangement’s options wherever it writes none of its own, as any cell does – and :share-scales is one of those options. Below, the arrangement shares :x across all its cells, and the facet over :drv, which writes no :share-scales, takes {:x :all} as its own: its three panels share :x and each keeps its own :y range.

(def drv-facet
  (-> (pj/pose nil :displ :hwy)
      (pj/facet :drv)))


(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [[drv-facet]
                 [{:x :displ :y :cty} {:x :displ :y :hwy}]]
                {:share-scales {:x :all}})
    pj/lay-point)

hwy246203040246152025246152025f4rcty246102030hwy246203040displ
Written on the facet, :share-scales replaces the arrangement’s value for the facet’s own panels, and they share :y again:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/arrange [[(pj/options drv-facet {:share-scales #{:x :y}})]
                 [{:x :displ :y :cty} {:x :displ :y :hwy}]]
                {:share-scales {:x :all}})
    pj/lay-point)

hwy246203040246246f4rcty246102030hwy246203040displ

title: 8  Composition
text:
Marginal Plots
The classic “scatter with top density” – a distribution strip beside the main plot – has a function of its own. pj/marginal takes a leaf pose and puts a distribution of one of its columns in a thin panel against one edge: the :x column above the panel, the :y column to its right.

(def marginal
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
      (pj/marginal :top)))


marginal

density0.00.20.4sepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5sepal length
The strip shares the scatter’s x axis and keeps its own value scale. Its duplicate x ticks and axis title are dropped, since the axis below describes both panels, and the two drawing areas are aligned so a value sits at the same place in each – including here, where the scatter carries a legend and the strip does not.
The color mapping does not reach the strip. A marginal describes the pose’s :x column as a whole, so one grey curve is drawn over the three colored groups below it.
:histogram draws the distribution as bars instead of a curve, and :size sets the strip’s share of the height (0.25 by default):

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/marginal :top :histogram {:size 0.35}))

count020sepal width4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5sepal length

A marginal on the right
:right describes the pose’s :y column instead, in a strip beside the panel. The distribution is drawn under pj/coord :flip, so its value axis runs across the strip and its baseline stands at the left edge, against the scatter:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/marginal :right))

sepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica56782.02.53.03.54.04.5density0.00.51.0sepal width
The strip shares the panel’s vertical axis. pj/marginal writes {:share-scales #{:y}} for a marginal on the right, and under the flip the strip’s :x column is the column drawn along that axis.
A :top marginal and a :right one line up on different edges. Two panels in a column share their left and right edges, so what has to agree is the room reserved for the y title and for the legend; two panels in a row share their top and bottom edges, so what has to agree is the room below them. :align-panels reserves whichever the layout calls for.
:bottom and :left are not drawn: a strip there would sit between the panel and the axis that describes it.


Marginals on both sides
pj/marginal adds one strip. For a marginal on each side, write the grid with pj/matrix: nil in a list of columns leaves a place with no column on that axis, so that cell draws the distribution of the other column, and the corner, nil on both axes, is left empty. The weights draw the marginals a third the size of the scatter:

(pj/matrix (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) [:displ nil] [nil :hwy]
           {:col-weights [3 1] :row-weights [1 3]})

count02040hwydispl23456715202530354045count050


What a marginal is made of
A :top marginal is a vertical composite with a shared x, which can also be written out. Four things make it up: the weights, the shared scale, the ticks and axis title suppressed on the strip, and :align-panels. Here are the first three:

(def marginal-by-hand
  (pj/pose
   {:share-scales #{:x}
    :layout {:direction :vertical :weights [1 3]}
    :poses [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length}
             :opts {:suppress-x-ticks true :suppress-x-label true}
             :layers [{:layer-type :density}]}
            {:mapping {:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width :color :species}
             :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}]
    :data (rdatasets/datasets-iris)}))


marginal-by-hand

density0.00.20.4sepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5sepal length
So the two drawing areas do not line up: the strip draws no legend, reserves no column for one, and comes out wider than the scatter below it. The density then sits at a different scale from the points it describes.
That is the fourth part, and the one pj/marginal adds: :align-panels in the composite’s own :opts. It plans every cell twice, the second time with the widest pad any of them needed as a floor, so each cell reserves what the others do – the y-label pad and the legend column for a column of cells, the room below for a row of them. pj/arrange takes :align-panels among its options, as above, and a written-out composite carries it in its own :opts. pj/options does not accept it – it is a composite’s own setting rather than a plot option:

(assoc-in marginal-by-hand [:opts :align-panels] true)

density0.00.20.4sepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5sepal length
With the key in place the written-out form is the composite pj/marginal returns, up to the weights it computes from :size. Nothing in the shape is specific to distributions, so the same four parts serve any stack of panels read against one x axis.

title: 8  Composition
text:
A Small Dashboard
Composite poses can combine heterogeneous chart types. Here is a dashboard-style 2x2 layout: a histogram of sepal length, a boxplot of sepal width by species, a scatter of petal dimensions, and a density of petal length.
Each cell is built as its own leaf pose, then pj/arrange takes rows of cells and produces the 2x2 grid:

(def dashboard
  (pj/arrange
   [[(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))
     (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-boxplot :species :sepal-width {:color :species}))]
    [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color :species}))
     (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris) (pj/lay-density :petal-length {:color :species}))]]))


dashboard

countsepal length567801020sepal widthspeciesspeciessetosaversicolorvirginicasetosaversicolorvirginica234petal widthpetal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica246012densitypetal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica246012
Four panels, each its own layer type. pj/arrange stacks the rows vertically; each row is laid out horizontally.

title: 8  Composition
text:
Drawing Layers with Different Data
A layer can carry its own :data, written in the layer’s mapping. This is how reference lines, predictions drawn over the data, and small datasets of labels attach to a plot. The layer reads every column from its own data: the columns it names, and the columns the pose’s mapping names.
A layer with data of its own is drawn on the pose’s panel, like any other layer of the pose. A separate panel for it comes from pj/arrange.

On the same panel
Here a base scatter gets a second set of points from another dataset, whose columns are named :x and :y:

(def base-data
  {:fitted   [1 2 3]
   :residual [1 2 3]})


(def other-data
  (tc/dataset {:x [0.5 1.5 2.5]
               :y [1.5 2.5 3.5]}))


(-> base-data
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:color "#e6550d" :data other-data}))

residual, yfitted, x0.51.01.52.02.53.01.01.52.02.53.03.5
One panel with six points – three from each layer. Layers paint in the order they were added – see Poses – so add the layer you want on top last.
Each axis is titled by both columns drawn on it, fitted, x and residual, y. Where the incoming columns are the same quantity under another name, renaming them to the pose’s columns with tc/rename-columns draws the same marks under one name per axis:

(-> base-data
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual
                  {:color "#e6550d"
                   :data (tc/rename-columns other-data
                                            {:x :fitted :y :residual})}))

residualfitted0.51.01.52.02.53.01.01.52.02.53.03.5


A panel of its own
To draw the other dataset beside the base scatter, build each as a pose and arrange them:

(pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point base-data :fitted :residual {:color "#377eb8"})
             (pj/lay-point other-data :x :y {:color "#e6550d"})])

residualfitted123123yx121.41.61.82.02.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.6
Each panel has three points and its own axis titles: the first shows fitted against residual, the second x against y.

title: 8  Composition
text:
Panels Clip Their Own Content
Each panel confines its marks to its own rectangle. A layer whose data runs past the panel’s domain – a reference line drawn well beyond the visible range, say – is clipped at the panel edge rather than painting across its neighbours. The clip is applied per panel, so a stacked arrangement reports one clip region per panel.

(def bounded
  (-> {:x [1 2 3 4 5] :y [10 20 15 25 18]}
      (pj/lay-point :x :y)
      (pj/lay-line {:data {:x [1 5] :y [-200 300]}})
      (pj/scale :y {:type :linear :domain [0 30]})))


(pj/arrange [bounded bounded] {:cols 1})

yx123450102030yx123450102030

title: 8  Composition
text:
Notes on the Current Implementation
A few details about how composition renders today:

Cells with data of their own draw their own axes, titles and ticks, unless :share-scales names an axis for them to share. In (pj/arrange [pose-a pose-b] {:share-scales #{:x}}), and in cells that read the data of the pose holding them, as in (pj/arrange data [...]), a shared axis is titled once and its ticks are labelled on the outer cells only, as the panels of a facet do. Cells drawing different columns on one shared scale – under :all, or a group such as {:y [[:hwy :cty]]} – each keep their title and its tick labels. A cell drops its own with :suppress-x-ticks and :suppress-x-label in that cell’s :opts, which is what pj/marginal writes on the strip it builds. (A scatter plot matrix names its columns with strips in place of each panel’s axis titles, and labels its :x ticks along the bottom row only. A grid of cells written by hand gets these strips where it crosses a list of :x columns with a list of :y columns, as a matrix does: each grid column draws one :x column and each row one :y column. A grid whose grid columns each draw one :x column, while its rows do not each draw one :y column, titles that :x column once below each grid column, as a shared axis is titled.)
Plot-area edges may not line up across composite siblings, since each leaf reserves its own padding for axes and labels – two sub-poses with different label lengths, or one drawing a legend that its neighbour does not, produce visibly different panel widths. :align-panels on pj/arrange plans the cells against a common floor for both the y-label pad and the legend column, and pj/marginal turns it on (see Cells That Line Up).
Each cell has its own plot options. A cell is a pose, so pj/options, pj/scale and pj/coord written on it apply to that cell: one cell can be log-scaled and its neighbour linear, and each can have its own title. Written on the composite itself, a scale, a coordinate system or an option such as :x-label applies to every cell that does not set its own. The :title, :subtitle and :caption written there are drawn once, around the whole arrangement, and not in each cell. Two layers of one pose cannot read one aesthetic through different scales, and two cells can: to read an aesthetic through a second scale, put the layer in a cell of its own with pj/arrange.
Cells that map the same column share one scale and one legend. If every leaf maps an aesthetic to the same column (for example :color :species in all cells), each cell is given one scale for it – the categories of all the cells together, or the range of all their values – and a single legend is drawn for the composite. A category is then the same colour, and a value the same shade, in every cell, even where the cells hold different data. A legend is drawn once, so its scale has to hold in every cell; cells with data of their own share an axis only where :share-scales names that axis. A cell that writes its own scale for the aesthetic keeps it, and each cell then draws its own legend. When the mappings disagree – or when only some leaves carry the aesthetic, as in the dashboard above – each leaf with that aesthetic draws its own legend.
Rows of different poses go through pj/arrange. A row of rows is built by passing nested vectors of poses to pj/arrange (the dashboard example above shows the shape). A cell may be a composite itself, so an arranged pose can be arranged again and the cell draws its own grid. Cells of unequal size are written with :col-weights and :row-weights, or with :panel-width and :panel-height – see the section on panels of unequal size. A facet by one category is drawn in rows with :cols, as in (pj/facet pose :class {:cols 4}) – see Faceting.

Below, both cells map :color to :species, and they hold different rows: the left cell holds setosa and versicolor, the right cell versicolor and virginica. Versicolor is drawn in the same colour in both, and the one legend lists all three species:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(not= "virginica" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (tc/select-rows #(not= "setosa" (:species %)))
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))])

sepal widthsepal length5672.02.53.03.54.04.5sepal widthsepal length682.02.22.42.62.83.03.23.43.63.8speciessetosaversicolorvirginica
A cell that is itself a composite draws its own grid. Here the left cell holds two panels of its own and the right cell holds one, so the arranged pose draws three panels in two columns:

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/arrange
   [(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
    (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
        (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))]

      (pj/lay-histogram :sepal-length))])

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
Setup
Plotje has three kinds of values you set, each answering a different question:
Configuration holds the values that can meaningfully have a cross-plot default. A title cannot – each plot needs its own. A palette can – a whole project can share one. A layer’s color mapping is per-layer, but when several layers should share the mapping, you set it at a wider scope.
A helper to inspect pose structure. It prints :mapping, :layers, and :opts – everything except the :data field, which is omitted for readability.

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
(ns plotje-book.options-and-scopes
  (:require
   ;; Kindly -- notebook rendering protocol
   [scicloj.kindly.v4.kind :as kind]
   ;; Rdatasets -- standard datasets
   [scicloj.metamorph.ml.rdatasets :as rdatasets]
   ;; Plotje -- composable plotting
   [scicloj.plotje.api :as pj]))



(defn strip-data [pose]
  (cond-> (dissoc pose :data)
    (:layers pose) (update :layers (partial mapv #(dissoc % :data)))
    (:poses pose) (update :poses (partial mapv strip-data))))


(defn pose-summary
  "Print pose structure without :data (for readability)."
  [pose]
  (kind/pprint (strip-data pose)))

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
Mappings
The final argument of a pj/lay-* function is a map, the layer’s mapping. A layer’s mapping describes that layer, and it takes two kinds of key.
Aesthetics say how the layer maps data to visuals: :color, :size, :alpha, :shape, :group, plus mark-specific keys like :text and :fill. An aesthetic is either mapped from a column (:color :species) or given as a constant (:alpha 0.3).
Layer settings are the other keys of that map. A layer setting says how the layer is computed or drawn:

The parts of the layer type – the rendering recipe is a mark (point, line, bar, …), a stat (identity, linear-model, density, binning, …), and a position adjustment (dodge, stack, fill). The layer type is chosen by which pj/lay-* function you call, and the :mark, :stat, and :position keys override its parts.
Layer-type parameters – keys specific to one layer type, like :bandwidth for pj/lay-density or :bins for pj/lay-histogram.
Data – a per-layer :data key, if the layer should use a different dataset from the rest of the pose.

All of these are written in the one map passed to pj/lay-*. In the printed pose, the parameters of the layer type stay in the layer’s :mapping beside its aesthetics, while :mark, :stat, :position and :data are stored on the layer next to its :mapping:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :loess :bandwidth 0.5})
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
 :layers
 [{:layer-type :smooth, :mapping {:bandwidth 0.5}, :stat :loess}]}

An aesthetic written in the mapping of pj/lay-*:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
And the pose structure:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point, :mapping {:color :species}}]}


Scope: writing an aesthetic for several layers
An aesthetic can also be written at a wider scope when it should apply to more than one layer: pj/pose takes a mapping too, and a pose’s mapping takes aesthetics and :data. The parameters of a layer type and :mark, :stat and :position are written on the layer itself. For a single-panel plot the scope hierarchy has two levels, from narrow to broad:



Scope
Set via
Reaches




Layer
pj/lay-* mapping
that one layer


Pose
pj/pose mapping
every layer on this pose



When the same key is set at both scopes, the narrower one wins.
Composite poses introduce a third level: an outer pose’s mapping flows into each of its descendant leaves, where it combines with the leaf’s own mapping. See Pose Rule S1 for an example.
The layer type itself is chosen per layer – you pick which pj/lay-* to call. Core Concepts teaches where layers go and how values combine at each scope; Pose Rules S1 to S6 state the rules.

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
Plot Options
Plot options describe a plot as a whole: its title, labels, coordinate system, and how its panels share their axes. A single-panel plot has one of each. A composite has a scope for them: every cell is a pose, so each cell can have its own title and its own scales, and the options written on the composite itself apply to every cell that does not set them – except the title, subtitle and caption, which an arrangement draws once, above and below its cells.
Two functions are dedicated to plot options, and write them to the pose’s :opts field:

pj/options – plot text (title, subtitle, caption, axis and legend labels) and panel dimensions. It also accepts configuration keys as per-plot overrides (see Configuration below).
pj/coord – coordinate system (cartesian, flipped, polar, fixed).

pj/facet splits the plot into panels. A facet by category is a mapping: the column is written into the pose’s :mapping under :col or :row. A facet over columns, (pj/facet pose {:y [:hwy :cty]}), is kept under the pose’s :facet key. pj/facet takes a map of plot options as a last argument and passes that map to pj/options. pj/arrange takes the same map of plot options as its last argument.
pj/scale does not write to :opts: a scale belongs to the aesthetic it reads, so it is written into that aesthetic’s mapping. It takes an axis (:x, :y) or a visual aesthetic. Axis scales accept :linear, :log, :categorical; the continuous visual ones (:size, :alpha, :fill, :color) accept :linear and :log; :shape accepts :categorical. :group has no scale to set – it splits a layer into one drawn group per value and draws nothing of its own – so (pj/scale pose :group ...) reports an error.
Reference lines and shaded bands – pj/lay-rule-h, pj/lay-rule-v, pj/lay-band-h, pj/lay-band-v – are layers, not plot options. They are added like any other layer. On a pose with one panel the rule or band is drawn on that panel; columns named in the call that the panel does not draw are not read there, and a warning says so. On a composite pose the rule or band is added at the root and placed as any layer is (Rules LP2 and LP3 in Pose Rules): with no columns named, it is drawn in every cell whose panel draws two columns, and with columns named, in every cell whose panel draws no other column; where no cell qualifies, it is drawn in every cell.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/options {:title "Iris"})
    (pj/coord :flip))

Irissepal lengthsepal width2.02.53.03.54.04.54.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.0
And the pose structure:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/options {:title "Iris"})
    (pj/coord :flip)
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}],
 :opts {:title "Iris", :coord :flip}}

Both the title and the coordinate system landed in :opts. On a single-panel plot like this one they describe the whole plot; written on one cell of a composite they would describe that cell.
On a faceted plot, a scale has two parts:

Scale type (log, categorical, linear, and so on) is shared across all panels – if you set pj/scale :x :log on a faceted pose, every panel has a log x-axis.
Scale domain (the extent of values shown) is shared as well, so the panels can be compared. :share-scales names the axes the panels share – {:share-scales #{:x}} gives each panel its own :y domain, and {:share-scales #{}} its own on both axes – and the appearance aesthetics keep one domain either way.

pj/scale and pj/coord write at the pose they are called on and flow down from there, so called on the pose you are building they cover the whole plot, and called on one cell before the cells are arranged, that cell alone. A scale written in a mapping is the same setting written closer to the layer, and the two combine key by key. What has no spelling yet is a type that varies across the panels of a facet: those panels come from one pose, so they share it.
Other chapters call these values plot-level options. Plot-level here names a category, while pose-level (used for mappings) names a place in a scope hierarchy – the shared word “level” refers to different things. Putting a plot option inside a pj/lay-* mapping – for example {:title "Growth"} – is a category mistake: plot options belong in :opts via their dedicated functions above.
A scale is not a plot option at all. pj/scale writes the mapping the scale reads, so neither {:x-scale {:type :log}} nor any other *-scale key belongs in pj/options or in a mapping. Write (pj/scale pose :x :log), or say it in the mapping as {:x {:column :year :scale :log}}.

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
Configuration
Configuration controls the rendering defaults – palette, theme, default dimensions, color scale. A configuration value is resolved at render time from a layered stack of sources, from highest priority to lowest:

Plot options on the pose (pj/options) – a per-plot override that wins for that one plot.
Thread-local overrides via pj/with-config, for what is rendered inside its body. A pose returned from the body is drawn under the configuration in effect when it is shown, so end the body in pj/plot to keep the override.
Global overrides via pj/set-config!.
Project file (plotje.edn), if present.
Library defaults – the baseline included with Plotje.

Sources 2-5 sit outside any specific pose and carry across every plot you render. Source 1 lets a specific pose override a configuration key for itself – (pj/options {:color-values :dark2}) sets :color-values on one pose, and at render time wins over any palette set through the other four sources.
The Configuration chapter covers each source in depth and lists every configuration key.
pj/config returns the resolved configuration – the merged result of all five sources above.

(select-keys (pj/config) [:width :height :margin])


{:width 600, :height 400, :margin 10}

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
A Worked Example
The pose below touches two categories explicitly. The third, configuration, shows up at render time.

(def demo
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      ;; mapping: a color aesthetic at layer scope
      (pj/lay-point {:color :species})
      ;; plot options: stored in :opts
      (pj/options {:title "Iris measurements"})
      (pj/coord :flip)))

The rendered plot:

demo

Iris measurementssepal lengthsepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica2.02.53.03.54.04.54.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.0
The pose structure:

(pose-summary demo)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point, :mapping {:color :species}}],
 :opts {:title "Iris measurements", :coord :flip}}

Reading the summary:

:color :species is inside the layer’s mapping – an aesthetic at layer scope.
:title and :coord are in :opts – plot options, which on this single-panel plot describe the whole of it.
Configuration does not appear in the pose. (pj/config) supplies the theme, default dimensions and other defaults when the plot is drawn.

title: 9  Options and Scopes
text:
Coming from ggplot2
For readers familiar with ggplot2, the three categories map roughly as follows:







ggplot2 construct
Plotje category




geom_*(aes(...))
a layer’s mapping


ggplot(aes(...))
a pose’s mapping


+ geom_*()
a layer


+ coord_*()
plot option


+ scale_*()
a pose’s mapping: the aesthetic’s :scale (pj/scale)


+ facet_*()
a pose’s mapping: the panel aesthetics :col and :row (pj/facet); a facet over columns is kept beside the mapping, under :facet


+ labs(...), one-off + theme(...)
plot option


theme_set(...), options(...)
configuration



In ggplot2, these constructs are reached via separate function families (labs(), theme(), coord_*(), scale_*()). Plotje folds the plot-level concerns into one entry point: pj/options accepts title, axis labels, theme, legend position, dimensions, and other settings as keys in a single map. pj/scale, pj/coord, and pj/facet remain dedicated functions because each carries more structure, but everything else merges.
ggplot2 Equivalents gives the Plotje spelling of each of these ggplot2 constructs, one row each.

title: 10  Pose Rules
text:
Setup
Each rule below states one behaviour and shows it on a rendered pose, with the printed structure where the shape is the point.
The rules are organized into seven sections (Construction, Layer Placement, Inferred Columns, Scope, Options, Assembly, Layout) and cover the call shapes of pj/pose, pj/lay-*, pj/arrange, pj/options, pj/scale, pj/coord, and pj/facet.
Read Poses first. On a first read through the book you can skim or skip this chapter, and return when you want the precise rule behind a behavior.
A helper to inspect pose structure without :data – the dataset is heavy and not what we are checking. We strip :data from the pose and every nested sub-pose and layer.
The cells of a composite – its leaves, in reading order. pj/arrange puts its cells in rows, so they are not its :poses directly.

title: 10  Pose Rules
text:
(def iris (rdatasets/datasets-iris))



(defn strip-data [pose]
  (cond-> (dissoc pose :data)
    (:layers pose) (update :layers (partial mapv #(dissoc % :data)))
    (:poses pose) (update :poses (partial mapv strip-data))))


(defn pose-summary
  "Print pose structure without :data (for readability)."
  [pose]
  (kind/pprint (strip-data pose)))



(defn cells [pose]
  (filterv #(not (contains? % :poses)) (rest (tree-seq :poses :poses pose))))

title: 10  Pose Rules
text:
Overview
A pose is a plain Clojure map with a documented set of keys:








Key
On
Purpose




:data
leaf or any ancestor
dataset (Tablecloth)


:mapping
pose or layer
column-to-aesthetic mappings (on a layer, also the parameters of its layer type)


:layers
pose
per-scope layers


:poses
composite only
sub-poses


:layout
composite, or a leaf faceted by one category
on a composite, the direction of its rows and cells, weights, and :cols; on a faceted leaf, :cols (Rule L3)


:facet
leaf
a facet over columns, expanded into cells when the pose is drawn (Rule O3)


:opts
root
plot-level options (including composite-level keys like :share-scales)


:share-scales
composite
the axes the cells share; pj/arrange writes it under :opts, and pj/marginal writes it on the composite itself


:where
any pose
a map from a column to a value or a set of values; the pose draws only the rows that match



A leaf pose has :data, :mapping, :layers; no :poses. A composite pose has :poses, and a sub-pose may itself be a composite: pj/arrange wraps its cells in a row per line of the grid, so the composite it returns holds rows and each row holds cells. A composite the caller supplies is accepted the same way: pj/arrange given one among its inputs nests it (Rule C8), pj/facet called on one divides every cell of it (Rule O3), and a nested map written out and handed to pj/pose is read as written. So a grid inside a grid can be written directly. A layer is a map with :layer-type and an optional :mapping, plus sibling keys :stat, :position, :mark when the user provides them.

title: 10  Pose Rules
text:
Construction
How poses and composites come into existence: every pj/pose call shape, pj/arrange, and the facet that crosses two lists of columns.

Rule C1: pj/pose on raw data creates a leaf
Called with a dataset as first argument, pj/pose returns a leaf pose. The arity determines what’s in :mapping: a keyword is :x; two keywords are :x and :y; a final map is the mapping and contributes aesthetic keys.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}

With only :color in the mapping, the pose is a leaf that names no :x and no :y. On data of one to three columns, the columns are read by default when the pose is drawn (Rule LI1). Iris has more columns, so a layer added to this pose has to name its columns, or a later pj/pose call has to name them.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:color :species}, :layers []}



Rule C2: pj/pose on a leaf merges into its mapping
pj/pose called on a leaf merges the new mapping into the leaf’s own mapping, whatever the leaf or its layers already name. The leaf remains a leaf, and no composite is created.

(-> iris
    pj/pose
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
And an aesthetic-on-aesthetic extension merges with later-wins:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
Property P-C2 – construction commutativity. A mapping built over several pj/pose calls is equal to the same mapping written in one call.

(= (-> iris
       pj/pose
       (pj/pose {:color :species})
       (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width))
   (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))


true



Rule C3: pj/pose naming other columns replaces the leaf’s :x and :y
pj/pose writes one mapping and does not add a panel. Called with an :x or :y other than the one the leaf’s mapping has, it replaces that column, and the layers that name no columns of their own read the new columns. So a pose returned by a function can be pointed at other columns:

(defn trend-plot [data]
  (-> data
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      pj/lay-point
      pj/lay-smooth))


(-> (trend-plot iris)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width))

petal widthpetal length12345670.00.51.01.52.02.5

(-> (trend-plot iris)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width)
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point} {:layer-type :smooth}]}

A layer that names its own columns keeps them. The pose’s new :x and :y are then drawn by no layer, and drawing the pose prints a warning naming them:

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
For panels side by side, pj/arrange takes a cell for each panel, here a mapping naming the panel’s two columns:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point)

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5
Property P-C3 – writing the same columns again changes nothing. A pj/pose call naming the leaf’s own :x and :y returns the same pose.

(= (trend-plot iris)
   (pj/pose (trend-plot iris) :sepal-length :sepal-width))


true



Rule C4: pj/pose with no :x or :y merges into the leaf’s mapping
A pj/pose call naming no :x and no :y, on a leaf whose mapping names them, merges the aesthetic into the leaf’s :mapping. The leaf stays a leaf.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width, :color :species},
 :layers []}

Property P-C4 – the aesthetic may come in a second call. Adding the aesthetic in a second call equals writing it in the first.

(= (-> iris
       (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
       (pj/pose {:color :species}))
   (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species}))


true



Rule C5: pj/pose leaves the layers where they are
pj/pose changes only the mapping. The layers stay on the pose they were added to, and a layer that names no columns of its own reads the merged mapping.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/pose {:color :species}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width, :color :species},
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}



Rule C6: pj/pose on a composite merges into the root mapping
On a composite, pj/pose merges into the root :mapping, which reaches every cell that does not map the same aesthetic itself. So an aesthetic that no cell maps itself reaches every cell:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point)

sepal widthsepal length682.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5speciessetosaversicolorvirginica

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:color :species},
 :layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

An :x or a :y written on a composite whose cells each name their own :x and :y reaches none of the cells. The cells keep their columns, and drawing the pose prints a warning for each axis, saying that the column written on the composite is not drawn:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :petal-length)
    pj/lay-point)

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5


Rule C7: pj/pose with nothing new has no effect
(pj/pose pose) and (pj/pose pose {}), where pose is a leaf or a composite, return pose unchanged, and writing a mapping twice gives the pose that writing it once gives. So pj/pose is safe to use as a pipeline step that does nothing.
A leaf pose. First the rendered plot, then its structure:

(def leaf-pose (-> iris (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)))


leaf-pose

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

(pose-summary leaf-pose)


{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}

Wrapping it with pj/pose returns the same value:

(= leaf-pose
   (pj/pose leaf-pose)
   (pj/pose leaf-pose {}))


true


(= (pj/pose leaf-pose {:color :species})
   (pj/pose (pj/pose leaf-pose {:color :species}) {:color :species}))


true

A composite pose. The rendered plot, then its structure:

(def composite-pose
  (-> iris
      (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
      pj/lay-point))


composite-pose

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5

(pose-summary composite-pose)


{:layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

And again, pj/pose has no effect:

(= composite-pose
   (pj/pose composite-pose)
   (pj/pose composite-pose {}))


true



Rule C8: pj/arrange composes poses into a composite
pj/arrange returns a composite. It takes a vector of cells, or data or a pose first and then the cells. Each cell is written the way the argument after the data is written in pj/pose: a pose, a composite, a column (a panel of that column), or a mapping such as {:x :a :y :b} (a panel of the columns the mapping names). So a cell and (pj/pose nil cell) draw the same. nil is the exception: in pj/arrange it is a cell left empty, where after the data in pj/pose it names no column. A vector is never a cell. A vector in the cell list is a list of cells: a row, where the cell list is a list of rows, and otherwise an arrangement of its own. The cells are placed in rows: the composite’s :poses are the rows, and each row’s :poses are the cells of that row.

(pj/arrange
 [(-> iris
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      pj/lay-point)
  (-> iris
      (pj/pose :petal-length :petal-width)
      pj/lay-point)])

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5
A cell may itself be a composite, and nests rather than being flattened – which is the shape pj/arrange builds for itself, one row per line of the grid:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/arrange [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                              (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
                 (pj/pose iris :sepal-length :petal-length)])
    pj/lay-point)

sepal widthsepal length682.02.53.03.54.04.5petal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5petal lengthsepal length56781234567
Given data first, a list of vectors of columns is a list of rows, with a panel for each column, as a list of vectors of poses is:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [[:sepal-length :sepal-width] [:petal-length :petal-width]])
    pj/lay-histogram)

countsepal length567801020countsepal width2.02.53.03.54.04.502040countpetal length24602040countpetal width0.00.51.01.52.02.502040
pj/arrange writes the options it is given into the composite’s :opts: :title, :width, :height, :share-scales, and any plot option pj/options takes. :cols decides how many cells each row holds, and is written on the composite’s :layout rather than its :opts: an arrangement made from a flat list keeps it there, as :auto where no :cols was given, so that cells pj/arrange adds later are laid out the same way as if they had been in the original list.

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
  (pj/pose iris :petal-length :sepal-width)]
 {:title "Arranged"
  :share-scales #{:y}})

sepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.5petal length246sepal widthArranged


Rule C9: a facet crossing two lists of columns is a leaf pose
pj/facet given the map that crosses two lists of columns, {:col {:x cols} :row {:y cols}}, keeps that map on a leaf pose – no :poses – which the facet splits into a panel for every pair when the pose is drawn. A mapping written on the pose reaches every panel.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
               :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}}))

5678682.02.53.03.54.04.5234sepal lengthsepal widthsepal lengthsepal widthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica
Property P-C9 – the mapping can come first or last. A mapping written with pj/pose before the facet or after it gives an equal pose.

(let [a (-> iris
            (pj/pose {:color :species})
            (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
                       :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}}))
      b (-> iris
            (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}
                       :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]}})
            (pj/pose {:color :species}))]
  (= a b))


true

title: 10  Pose Rules
text:
Layer Placement
Where lay-* calls place the layer in the pose tree. The rules cover whether the call names :x and :y, whether the receiver is a leaf or a composite, which cells of a composite draw the layer, the raw-data convenience case, the panel the layers of a leaf share, and the columns a layer reads from that panel.
Where the columns are written: the columns a lay-* call names are written on the layer’s own :mapping, and only there; the pose’s :mapping is what pj/pose writes. The two meet by scope merge when the pose is drawn: a layer that names a column overrides the pose’s, and a layer that names none reads the pose’s.

Rule LP1: bare lay-* attaches at the current pose’s root
A lay-* call naming no columns attaches the layer to the current pose’s top-level :layers. On a leaf, that is the leaf’s own :layers. On a composite, it is the root :layers, and the layer is drawn in every cell whose number of columns is one its layer type draws from (Property P-LP1); where no cell has such a number of columns, it is drawn in every cell (Rule LP3) – a histogram added to two scatter cells draws a histogram of each cell’s :x column.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    pj/lay-point)

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5
On a composite, the same call attaches at the root, and here both cells draw it:

(-> (pj/arrange
     [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point)

(-> (pj/arrange
     [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)


{:layout {:direction :vertical, :cols :auto},
 :poses
 [{:layout {:direction :horizontal},
   :poses
   [{:mapping {:x :sepal-length, :y :sepal-width}, :layers []}
    {:mapping {:x :petal-length, :y :petal-width}, :layers []}]}],
 :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

Property P-LP1 – bare layers flow downward. After adding one bare layer to a composite, the composite’s root :layers holds that single entry. A cell that draws the root’s layer draws it first, underneath the cell’s own layers, and has no layer inferred for it.

(let [before (pj/arrange
              [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
               (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
      after  (-> (pj/arrange
                  [(pj/pose iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                   (pj/pose iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
                 pj/lay-point)]
  [(count (or (:layers before) []))
   (count (or (:layers after)  []))])


[0 1]



Rule LP2: on a composite, a lay-* naming columns is drawn in every cell that fits it
When a lay-* call names columns on a composite, the layer is added to the composite’s root :layers, as a bare layer is (Rule LP1), and its own :mapping carries the columns the call named. It is drawn in every cell that fits it; where no cell fits it, Rule LP3 applies. A cell fits the layer when two things hold. First, on each axis the layer names, the cell’s panel draws no other column than the layer names there; an axis the layer does not name is not compared. Second, the cell’s columns together with the layer’s are a number of columns the layer type draws from. So a trend line naming {:y :petal-width} fits every cell drawing :petal-width on :y, and a histogram naming :sepal-length does not fit a scatter cell of :sepal-length and :sepal-width, because the scatter cell’s two columns are more than the one a histogram draws from. Beside a cell of :sepal-length alone, the histogram is drawn in that cell only; where no cell fits it, Rule LP3 draws it in every cell. The columns of a cell’s panel are the :x and :y of the cell’s mapping after the mappings above the cell are merged in; where that mapping names no column on an axis, the panel’s column on that axis is the column of the cell’s first layer that names a column there. Matching is by strict equality: a column reference is the keyword or string the user typed, and the two forms are not interchangeable.
Here the trend line names the first cell’s columns, so it is drawn in the first cell only. The second cell draws the points added at the root:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth :sepal-length :sepal-width))

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:species "setosa"}}
                 {:where {:species "versicolor"}}
                 {:where {:species "virginica"}}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth :sepal-length :sepal-width))

(-> iris
    (pj/pose {:x :petal-length})
    (pj/facet {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width]})

A cell built by lay-* names its columns on its layer and not in its own mapping. The panel’s columns are the same either way, so the layer is drawn in the cell whose layers draw its columns:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                 (pj/lay-point iris :petal-length :petal-width)])

A lay-* call naming one column follows the same rule: it is drawn in every cell whose panel draws no other column on that axis, and reads that panel’s column on the other axis – as a layer naming one column on a leaf does (Rule LP6). Here a trend line naming only :sepal-width on :y is drawn in the first cell, against that cell’s :sepal-length:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width}
                 {:x :sepal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/lay-smooth {:y :sepal-width}))

Rule LP3: on a composite, a lay-* that fits no cell is drawn in every cell
When no cell fits a layer (Rule LP2 for a layer naming columns, Property P-LP1 for a bare one), the layer is drawn in every cell, as written, on that cell’s panel – the layers of a cell share its panel, as the layers of a leaf do (Rule LP5). A lay-* call adds no cell. Here the second layer names :sepal-length and :petal-length, which no cell draws together, so both cells draw it beside the points added at the root, and each axis is titled by every column drawn on it. A colour is written on each layer, as in the examples of Rule LP5, so no legend is added:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    (pj/lay-point {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :petal-length {:color "#999999"}))

A histogram naming :sepal-length fits no scatter cell – two columns are more than a histogram draws from – so it is drawn in both cells, over the points. Each cell’s :y axis then reads a count and a column, and drawing the plot prints a Note for each cell saying so:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])

Where a cell would then draw only that layer – the cell holds no layer of its own, and no other layer at the root fits it – and on :x or :y every cell draws another column than the layer names, the cell’s own columns would be drawn by no layer. That reports an error naming the columns, as it does on a facet over columns. A cell’s own columns are those its mapping or its own layers name:

(try
  (pj/plan (-> iris
               (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
               (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :petal-length)))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-point names :petal-length on :y, and no panel draws it: the panels draw :sepal-width and :petal-width on :y. Add :petal-length to the :y columns the panels are made from -- the facet's, or the cells given to pj/arrange -- and leave :y off the layer, or draw the layer on a pose of its own and put the two side by side with pj/arrange. A layer naming no column is drawn in every panel."

Each cell reads its own data, so a layer added to cells that carry their own data, under a root that has none, is drawn from each cell’s data:

(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point iris :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                 (pj/lay-point iris :petal-length :petal-width)])
    pj/lay-smooth)

A cell is added by pj/arrange: given an arrangement, it adds the cells it is given after the arrangement’s own, here as the third cell of the row. The root’s points are drawn in the new cell too, under its trend line:

(-> iris
    (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-smooth iris :sepal-length :petal-length)]))

Property: a split and an arrangement draw the same panels. Two layers on different columns, split over those columns with pj/facet, and the same layers attached to a composite built with pj/arrange (LP2 draws each in its matching cell) draw the same panels with the same marks. The pose values differ: the facet keeps one leaf and expands it into cells when it is drawn, while pj/arrange builds a composite.

(let [via-facet (-> iris
                    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width)
                    (pj/facet {:x [:sepal-length :petal-length]
                               :y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}))
      via-arrange (-> iris
                      (pj/arrange [{:x :sepal-length :y :sepal-width} {:x :petal-length :y :petal-width}])
                      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                      (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))
      drawn (fn [pose] (select-keys (pj/svg-summary pose) [:panels :points]))]
  {:via-facet-drawn (drawn via-facet)
   :via-arrange-drawn (drawn via-arrange)
   :via-facet-shape (if (:poses via-facet) :composite :leaf)
   :via-arrange-shape (if (:poses via-arrange) :composite :leaf)})


{:via-facet-drawn {:panels 2, :points 300},
 :via-arrange-drawn {:panels 2, :points 300},
 :via-facet-shape :leaf,
 :via-arrange-shape :composite}



Rule LP4: lay-* on raw data coerces the data into a leaf pose
lay-* called with a dataset as its first argument coerces the data into a leaf pose first, then applies the layer. The result draws what (-> data (pj/pose :x :y) pj/lay-point) draws. This keeps the convenience one-liner (-> data (pj/lay-point :x :y)) working as the shortest path from data to plot.

(def tiny
  {:a [1 2 3 4 5]
   :b [2 4 3 5 4]})


(-> tiny
    (pj/lay-point :a :b))

ba123452345
The explicit two-step form draws the same plot. The two poses differ in where the columns are written: the lay-* call above keeps them on its layer, and here pj/pose writes them on the pose, where every layer added afterwards reads them:

(-> tiny
    (pj/pose :a :b)
    pj/lay-point
    pose-summary)


{:mapping {:x :a, :y :b}, :layers [{:layer-type :point}]}

nil in place of the data, followed by columns or a mapping, is a template, as it is for pj/pose: a leaf pose holding the layer and no data, completed by pj/with-data or by an arrangement given data first. nil alone reports an error.

(pj/lay-point nil :a :b)

Rule LP5: the layers of a leaf share its panel
A leaf draws one panel, and every layer on it draws there, whatever columns it names. Its :x and :y stay on the layer’s own :mapping, and the leaf’s :mapping is left as it was.
Each axis is titled by every column drawn on it. A layer with no :color specified, on the pose or on the layer, also takes a color and a legend entry naming its columns by default, unless a layer of the panel is colored by a column. Each layer below specifies its color, so no color and no legend entry is added.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color "#377eb8"})
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:color "#e6550d"}))

A leaf that already carries columns, called with a lay-* that names different columns, keeps the layer with the columns the call named written on it. The pose stays a leaf, and the layer is drawn on the leaf’s one panel. The pose’s own columns are drawn only by layers that name none, so here only the petal columns are drawn, and drawing the pose prints a warning that the pose’s :x and :y are drawn by no layer:

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width))

petal widthpetal length12345670.00.51.01.52.02.5
Where the columns are written does not change the rule. A layer names its columns either in the call’s argument slots or in its mapping, and placement reads both alike: (pj/lay-line pose :sepal-length :petal-width) and (pj/lay-line pose {:x :sepal-length :y :petal-width}) add the same layer. A written value is not a column – it places a mark at that value – and the layer’s data decides which of the two a value is.
Two lines over one :x, each naming its own :y in its mapping, therefore draw on one panel, the y axis covering both columns:

(-> {:X [1 2 3 4 5] :Y [1 2 3 4 5] :Z [1 4 9 16 25]}
    (pj/pose :X)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :Y})
    (pj/lay-line {:y :Z}))

A written value in the same slot places a label. Here :x and :y are numbers on a dataset that has no column named 2, so the label is drawn at 2 and 4:

(-> {:X [1 2 3 4 5] :Y [1 2 3 4 5] :Z [1 4 9 16 25]}
    (pj/lay-point :X :Y)
    (pj/lay-text {:x 2 :y 4 :text "a note"}))

Separate panels for the layers of one leaf come from a split, (pj/facet pose {:x [...] :y [...]}), or from pj/arrange. Asking for them with {:overlay false} or (pj/overlay pose false) reports an error naming both:

(try
  (-> iris
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-point :petal-length :petal-width {:overlay false}))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-point -- :overlay is retired. The layers of a pose share one panel. To draw layers on separate panels, split the pose over the columns, as in (pj/facet pose {:y [:a :b]}), or give each layer a pose of its own and arrange the poses with pj/arrange."



Rule LP6: a layer reads the panel’s column where it needs one
The panel’s column on an axis is the column the pose names there, and where the pose names none, the column of the first layer that names one there. A layer reads the panel’s column on an axis where it names none and its layer type needs one: both columns for a layer naming none, and the other column for a layer naming one whose layer type draws from two.

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-line {:y :petal-width})
    pj/lay-smooth)

The columns stay on the layers. The pose’s own mapping is not written, so a layer type that can draw from one column reads no second column from a neighbouring layer:

(-> iris
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-rug {:x :petal-length}))

Property: column-existence safety check. When a lay-* call names a column on an axis where the pose already draws another column, it first checks that those columns exist in the data the layer would draw from – the layer’s own :data if present, otherwise the inherited data. A missing column is almost always a typing mistake, so the call reports an error at once, naming the columns the data has. A first lay-* call on raw data is not checked at the call; a missing column there reports an error when the pose is drawn.
The check at the call covers the columns written in the argument slots. A name written in the layer’s mapping may be a column or a value, which the data decides when the pose is drawn, so a name there that matches no column reports an error when the pose is drawn.

(try
  (-> iris
      (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/lay-point :nope :nada))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-point :x :nope names a column that doesn't exist in the data the layer would draw from. Available columns: [:petal-length :petal-width :rownames :sepal-length :sepal-width :species]. If you meant another dataset, pass `:data` on this lay-* call."

Supplying :data on the lay-* call satisfies the safety check: the layer draws its own data, on the leaf’s panel.

(-> iris
    (pj/pose :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/lay-point :foo :bar
                  {:data (tc/dataset {:foo [1 2 3] :bar [4 5 6]})}))
