Categories crossed with columns
Here the species run across and two measurements run down, each drawn against :sepal-length:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:col :species :row {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]}}))

234680126868sepal lengthsetosaversicolorvirginicasepal widthpetal width
The grid may also be written as two calls, one facet over the categories and one over the columns, in either order: (-> pose (pj/facet {:y [...]}) (pj/facet :species)). The categories go into the pose’s mapping and the columns under its :facet, and the two are crossed when the pose is drawn. When both directions are taken, a third facet reports an error that suggests a colour or pj/arrange instead.


Scatter plot matrix
A scatter plot matrix (SPLOM) draws every column of a list against every column of the same list, to show all their pairwise relationships at once. The same list under :col, on :x, and under :row, on :y, gives the matrix, and the panel of a column against itself draws that one column, as a histogram. The histogram is drawn within the column’s own range, so it shares its row’s :y axis and the row’s tick labels stand at the left edge; its bar heights are relative, with no count axis:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length]}
               :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length]}})
    pj/lay-point)

6823468246234246sepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthsepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica
pj/matrix writes this facet: (pj/matrix data cols) crosses a list of columns with itself, and the pose it returns is the one pj/facet returns for the map above.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/matrix [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length])
    pj/lay-point)

6823468246234246sepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthsepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica
Two different lists cross the same way: {:col {:x xs} :row {:y ys}}, or (pj/matrix data xs ys), draws each column of xs against each column of ys. Written without :col and :row, pj/facet given {:x xs :y ys} pairs the columns one by one instead, a panel per pair, as Layers on different columns, faceted shows below. A list of pairs given to pj/pose or to a pj/lay-* call is not read this way: it reports an error naming pj/arrange and pj/matrix. The Relationships chapter builds scatter plot matrices with more layers.

title: 25  Faceting
section: A facet over categories is a mapping
text:
A facet over categories is a mapping
The panel aesthetics :col and :row give each value of a column a panel of its own, told apart by a strip label – where :color tells the marks apart by colour on one panel. They are documented here, where they are written, rather than beside the keys of a layer’s mapping, because no pj/lay-* call accepts one.

(kind/table
 {:column-names [:aesthetic :what-it-reads]
  :row-vectors (mapv (fn [[k doc]] [k doc])
                     (sort-by (comp str key) pj/panel-aesthetic-docs))})






aesthetic
what-it-reads




col
A column of the pose's data, or a vector of them, giving each value a panel of its own, laid out across. A vector unites the columns into a compound key, so a panel is drawn for each combination the data holds. Written by (pj/facet my-pose col), and by (pj/facet my-pose {:col col :row ...}) for a grid, where the other entry may be categories or a map of columns.


row
A column of the pose's data, or a vector of them, giving each value a panel of its own, laid out down. The same readings as :col. Written by (pj/facet my-pose {:row col}), and by (pj/facet my-pose {:col ... :row col}) for a grid, where the other entry may be categories or a map of columns.





pj/facet writes :col into the pose’s mapping. Here is the plot, and then the pose that draws it.

title: 25  Faceting
text:
What the scope rules give
Mappings flow downward: a mapping written on a pose reaches every layer and every sub-pose below it, and a sub-pose that writes its own key overrides what it inherits. A panel aesthetic is a mapping, so all of that applies to faceting.

A composite can be faceted
A facet written on an arranged pose divides every cell of it.

(-> (pj/arrange [[(pj/pose (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :sepal-length :sepal-width)]
                 [(pj/pose (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :petal-length :petal-width)]])
    (pj/lay-point)
    (pj/facet :species)
    (pj/options {:width 700 :height 560}))

sepal widthsepal length56782.02.53.03.54.04.556785678setosaversicolorvirginicapetal widthpetal length2460.00.51.01.52.02.5246246setosaversicolorvirginica
Two cells, three species, six panels. pj/arrange takes one vector per row, so [[a] [b]] stacks the two cells and each has the full width for its three panels.
A facet over columns is not a mapping, so it does not reach into a composite: pj/facet given an arranged pose and a map of columns reports an error naming the spellings that draw – a facet on each cell, or the columns arranged as cells.


One cell can be faceted differently from another
A cell that writes its own :col overrides the one it inherits, which is the rule for every mapping key. Here the top cell is divided by species and the bottom cell is not divided at all.

(-> (pj/arrange [[(-> (pj/pose (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                      (pj/facet :species))]
                 [(pj/pose (rdatasets/datasets-iris) :petal-length :petal-width)]])
    (pj/lay-point)
    (pj/options {:width 700 :height 560}))

title: 25  Faceting
text:
Several columns as one key
Under some aesthetics, several columns in a vector are one distinction made of those columns united – a compound key. That is what {:group [:a :b]} means, and the panel aesthetics read a vector the same way. pj/compound-key-aesthetics names the aesthetics that read a vector of columns as a compound key. Plotje checks a vector against this set, so under an aesthetic outside the set, several columns where one goes report an error rather than being united:

(pj/compound-key-aesthetics)

title: 25  Faceting
text:
Free Scales (Independent Axis Ranges)
By default the panels of a facet share each axis on which they draw the same column. In a facet over categories every panel draws the same columns, so the panels share both axis ranges, and a mark at the same height stands for the same value in every panel. In a facet over columns, the panels drawing different columns keep an axis range each. The :share-scales option names the axes the panels share, as a set. An axis left out of the set is fitted to the rows of each panel. A map, as in {:y :all}, shares an axis between panels that draw different columns, as the Series chapter shows. An axis the map leaves out is not shared: on a facet over columns, {:y :all} alone leaves :x unshared, so every panel labels its own :x ticks, and {:x :same-column :y :all} keeps :x shared among the panels drawing the same column, labelled once.
Both axes shared – the default, written out:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/facet :species)
    (pj/options {:share-scales #{:x :y}}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica682.02.53.03.54.04.56868setosaversicolorvirginica
Only :x shared – each panel has its own y range:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/facet :species)
    (pj/options {:share-scales #{:x}}))

#{:y} shares :y and fits :x to each panel, and #{} fits both axes to each panel. In a grid of categories too, an axis left out of the set is fitted to each panel, where ggplot2’s facet_grid(scales = "free_y") fits it to each row of panels.
The options of a faceted plot may also be written in the facet call, in a map after the column. pj/facet passes that map to pj/options, so the two spellings build the same pose:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/facet :species {:share-scales #{:x}}))

A shared axis covers what the panels sharing it draw, and is padded once. So the panels of a facet read on the axes the same plot has when it is not split:

(let [whole (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width))
      domains (fn [pose] (mapv (juxt :x-domain :y-domain) (:panels (pj/plan pose))))]
  {:not-split (first (domains whole))
   :each-panel (distinct (domains (pj/facet whole :species)))})


{:not-split [[4.12 8.08] [1.88 4.5200000000000005]],

A shared axis of categories lists every category the panels hold, in the order of the data, so a category sits at the same place in every panel. The panels of a faceted histogram share their count axis.
pj/arrange takes the same option for its cells, where it can also say which columns share an axis; see Composition and, for what a shared axis covers, What a Shared Axis Covers.

title: 25  Faceting
text:
Appearance Aesthetics Across Panels
:share-scales is about the axes, and the axes alone. A :size or :alpha column is read against every value the plot holds, whichever panel a mark sits in, so one value is one size everywhere and the legend explains every panel at once.
Below, the left panel’s values run from 1 to 3 and the right panel’s from 4 to 10, so every mark on the left is smaller than every mark on the right:

(def per-panel
  {:g ["L" "L" "L" "R" "R" "R"]
   :x [1 2 3 1 2 3]
   :y [1 1 1 1 1 1]
   :n [1 2 3 4 7 10]})


(-> per-panel
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n})
    (pj/facet :g))

The legend lists the categories in the order the rows of the data hold them, whichever panel a row is drawn in, so a category has the colour it has in the same plot drawn without the facet. Below, the first panel holds some of the classes and not others, and the legend is the legend of the unfaceted plot:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy {:color :class})
    (pj/facet :drv))

title: 25  Faceting
section: A panel aesthetic on a layer is an error
text:
A panel aesthetic on a layer is an error
A facet divides every layer of the pose alike, and a panel aesthetic is read from a pose’s mapping and not from a layer’s, so a panel aesthetic belongs on the pose. Written in a pj/lay-* mapping, a panel aesthetic reports an error, and the message names the places to write it instead.

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:col :species})
      pj/plan)
  (catch Exception e (ex-message e)))


"A panel aesthetic col was written in a layer's mapping. A facet divides every layer of the pose, and a panel aesthetic is read from a pose's mapping and not from a layer's, so write it on the pose: (pj/facet pose :species), or in the pose's mapping. On a composite, write it on the cell whose panels it divides."

A second facet in the same direction on one pose is reported rather than replacing the first. A facet written on a cell of a composite overrides the facet the cell inherits, by the scope rules.

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/facet :species)
      (pj/facet :sepal-length))
  (catch Exception e (ex-message e)))


"pj/facet was given :sepal-length for :col, which this pose already facets by :species. A pose divides its panels once per direction: write the other direction, (pj/facet pose {:row :sepal-length}), which with the earlier facet draws a grid, or leave out the earlier facet and write one compound key in its place -- (pj/facet pose [:species :sepal-length])."

The map given to pj/facet says where the panels come from, and takes no other key. A plot option written inside it is reported, and the message says to write the option in a map of its own, after the first:

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
      (pj/facet {:col :species :share-scales #{:x}}))
  (catch Exception e (ex-message e)))


"pj/facet was given {:col :species, :share-scales #{:x}}, and the map has unexpected key(s): [:share-scales]. It takes [:col :row]. :share-scales is a plot option: write it in a map of its own after this one, as in (pj/facet pose {...} {:share-scales ...})."

Where a facet’s column holds so many values that each panel would be narrower than the smallest panel size, the error names the column and the number of its values, and suggests wrapping the panels with :cols and a height the rows fit in, as in “Wrapping the panels into rows” above:

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
      (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
      (pj/facet :model)
      pj/plan)
  (catch Exception e (ex-message e)))


"Each panel would be 15 wide, which is below the smallest panel size, 20. The plot's width, 600, less 38 for its labels and legend (38 for the y axis labels), leaves 562 for 38 columns of panels. Increase :width, set :panel-width directly, or lower :min-panel-size for a sparkline-sized plot. The panels are those of a facet by :model, which holds 38 values and draws them in one row. For several rows of panels, give the facet across a number of panels per row with :cols, and the plot a height its rows fit in: (pj/facet pose :model {:cols 4 :height 1200})."

title: 25  Faceting
text:
Facet or Arrange
pj/facet and pj/arrange both draw several panels, and many plots can be written with either call. Which call fits depends on where the panels come from. A facet generates its panels from one pose: a panel for each category of a column, or a panel for each column the facet names, all drawn from the same data with the same layers. An arrangement lists its cells, and each cell is a pose of its own, with its own mapping and layers. The cells read the data the arrangement is given, or each holds data of its own.
Cells that each hold data of their own share no axis. Here three cells each hold the rows of one kind of drive, and each :y axis covers only its own cell’s rows:

(pj/arrange (vec (for [drive ["4" "f" "r"]]
                   (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
                       (tc/select-rows #(= drive (:drv %)))
                       (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
                       (pj/options {:title drive})))))

4hwydispl246121416182022242628fhwydispl24202530354045rhwydispl46161820222426
{:share-scales #{:y}} in the arrangement’s options gives the three cells one :y axis, as the Shared Scales section of the Composition chapter shows.
A facet over :drv divides one dataset, so its three panels share both axes:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/facet :drv))

hwydispl24615202530354045246246f4r
A facet over categories draws what an arrangement of :where cells draws: one cell per category, each holding the whole data and a :where, the row filter that keeps the rows of that category. Written out by hand, the cells draw the same plot as the facet:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:drv "f"}} {:where {:drv "4"}} {:where {:drv "r"}}]))

The cells are parts of the arrangement’s data, so they share both axes, as the panels of the facet do – the cells holding data of their own, above, share none.
The plots agree and the poses do not: the arrangement holds its cells under :poses, and the faceted pose holds no :poses. A layer added afterwards is drawn alike in both. Added to the facet, (pj/lay-point :displ :cty) draws in each of the three panels, in a second colour:

    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/facet :drv)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :cty))

hwy, ctydisplhwycty2461015202530354045246246f4r
Added to the arrangement, the same layer is drawn in each of the three cells, since no cell draws another column on :x or :y, and the plot is the facet’s:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:drv "f"}} {:where {:drv "4"}} {:where {:drv "r"}}])
    (pj/lay-point :displ :cty))

The cells of an arrangement can also be plots of different kinds, which the panels of a facet cannot. Here a cell naming two columns draws a scatter, and a cell naming one column draws a histogram:

(pj/arrange (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg) [{:x :displ :y :hwy} :hwy])

An arrangement wraps its cells into rows with :cols, as a facet wraps its panels. {:cols 2} places the three :where cells in two columns, and draws what the facet by :drv given {:cols 2} draws. Each cell keeps its strip, and the cells still share both axes:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/arrange [{:where {:drv "f"}} {:where {:drv "4"}} {:where {:drv "r"}}]
                {:cols 2}))

203040f2464246203040rdisplhwy
So write pj/facet when the panels are parts of one plot: one dataset and the same layers, divided by the categories of a column or across columns. A facet also reaches every cell of an arrangement it is written on, as “A composite can be faceted” above shows. Write pj/arrange when the cells are different plots – different data, different layers, a dashboard – or when the layout needs what only a list of cells can say: an empty cell written nil, rows of different lengths, or one arrangement placed inside another. A layer holding data of its own is drawn whole in every panel of a facet, so a reference line computed for each category needs an arrangement, as Known Limitations says.

title: 25  Faceting
text:
The Order of the Calls
pj/facet may be written anywhere in a pipeline. pj/options, pj/scale and pj/coord written before the facet give the pose they give written after it, and a layer added before or after the facet draws the same plot. These two pipelines write the same calls in different orders:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    (pj/facet :drv)
    (pj/scale :y {:domain [0 50]})
    pj/lay-smooth)

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
    (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
    pj/lay-smooth
    (pj/scale :y {:domain [0 50]})
    (pj/facet :drv))

hwydispl24605101520253035404550246246f4r
The same holds under a facet over columns, where a layer added before or after the facet gives an equal pose.

title: 25  Faceting
text:
Coming from ggplot2
A reader who knows ggplot2 looks for its faceting functions by name. Each has a Plotje spelling, or none:







ggplot2
Plotje




facet_wrap(~ drv)
(pj/facet pose :drv), which draws the panels in one row


facet_wrap(~ class, ncol = 4)
(pj/facet pose :class {:cols 4})


facet_grid(cyl ~ drv)
(pj/facet pose {:col :drv :row :cyl})


facet_wrap(scales = "free")
{:share-scales #{}} in the options map after the facet, which fits each panel to its own rows


facet_grid(scales = "free")
{:share-scales #{}}, which fits :x and :y to each panel; ggplot2 fits :x to each column of panels and :y to each row, which has no Plotje spelling


facet_grid(scales = "free_y")
{:share-scales #{:x}}, which fits :y to each panel rather than to each row


GGally::ggpairs(data, columns = cols)
(pj/matrix data cols), which writes the facet {:col {:x cols} :row {:y cols}}: a scatter off the diagonal and a histogram on it


facet_grid(labeller = label_both)
{:strip-labels :both} in the options map after the facet


facet_grid(margins = TRUE)
no option; stack the data with a copy labelled "(all)", as below



Panels follow the order the data holds the values. ggplot2 sorts a text column and follows the levels of a factor; (pj/scale pose :col {:domain [...]}) plays the part of factor(levels = ...), as the section on ordering the panels shows.
ggplot2 Equivalents collects the ggplot2 spellings outside faceting – layers, scales, coordinates, labels – with the Plotje spelling of each.

A panel for all rows
ggplot2’s margins = TRUE adds a panel that draws every category together, so each panel can be compared with the whole. The same panel comes from the data: stack the dataset with a copy of itself whose facet column reads "(all)", and facet the stacked rows. The copy is the last value the data holds, so its panel comes last:

(let [mpg (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)]
  (-> (tc/concat mpg (tc/add-column mpg :drv "(all)"))
      (pj/lay-point :displ :hwy)
      (pj/facet :drv)))

hwydispl24615202530354045246246246f4r(all)
Each row is drawn twice, in its own panel and in the "(all)" panel. For a grid, stack a copy for each direction and one more for the corner, where both columns read "(all)".

title: 26  Series
text:
The data
A table often carries one measure per column. Writing several of those columns where one goes reads them as several series of one layer: Plotje pivots them, invents a key column naming which measure a row holds and a value column holding the number, and maps the key column to :color. Because the measures are labelled, they can be placed against each other by a position adjustment.
The sections up to Examples teach the main ideas in order: what a series is, what the pivot makes of the columns it reads, where a series may be written, how the measures are placed against each other, how a series on each axis is read in pairs, and the limits a series has.
One row per quarter, one column per measure – the wide shape a series reads.
The same measures split by region and outlet, for the examples that divide the canvas as well as the band. A mark draws one shape per row, so a pose reading this one without a panel or a group per region would draw the two regions on top of each other.

title: 26  Series
text:
Several measures on one panel
A bar divides its band between the series, so each quarter’s band holds one bar per measure.

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180

title: 26  Series
section: A series is a layer per column
text:
A series is a layer per column
A series draws what one layer per column draws. The three layers below share the pose’s one panel, and each takes a colour and a legend entry naming its column, as the measures of the series do – the two plots are equal, titles and legend included:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :revenue)
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :cost)
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :tax))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
The series is the shorter spelling, and the one that names the measures as one group: a position adjustment can place them against each other in a band, and a facet can split them by the key column, as the sections below show.

title: 26  Series
section: The same plot from long data
text:
The same plot from long data
A series is the wide-side spelling of something the long shape already writes. Pivoting the measures into a key column and a value column, then mapping the key column to :color, draws the same marks:

(-> sales
    (tc/pivot->longer #{:revenue :cost :tax}
                      {:target-columns :series :value-column-name :value})
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter :value {:color :series :position :dodge}))

valuequarterseriesrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180
The titles differ. The long table’s columns were named in the tc/pivot->longer call, so value titles the axis and series the legend. A series names no column of its own: its axis is titled by the columns it reads, and its legend has no title, since the entries already name the columns.
The legend takes a title where one is specified, as any colour legend does: the :color-label option, or a :label in the colour scale.

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/options {:color-label "Measure"}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterMeasurerevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
An adjustment divides a band between labelled competitors, and the pivot gives the measures their labels, so the adjustments below apply to a series.

title: 26  Series
text:
Naming the key column
A series can be written out as a map rather than a bare vector. The reason to write it out is to name the key column the pivot invents, which then titles the legend.

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost :tax] :as :measure}
                {:position :dodge})
    (pj/options {:y-label "Euros"}))

EurosquartermeasurerevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180

title: 26  Series
text:
The keys a series takes
A series written out takes three keys: :series for the columns it reads, :as for the key column the pivot invents, and :scale for the scale its value column is read through. Any other key reports an error, so a misspelled :as is caught at the call that writes it rather than leaving the legend untitled.

(try
  (-> sales
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost] :label :measure}))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-bar was given a series with unexpected key(s): [:label]. A series names the columns it reads with :series, the key column the pivot invents with :as, and the scale its value column is read through with :scale."

title: 26  Series
text:
Where a series is written
A series goes wherever a column goes. Written on the pose it reaches every layer below it, which is what scope does for every other mapping – the pivot reshapes the dataset the pose carries, and each layer then reads the columns it invented:

(-> sales
    (pj/pose :quarter [:revenue :cost])
    pj/lay-line
    pj/lay-point)

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q490100110120130140150160170180190
One pivot per plot, though. A series written in a lay-* call on a pose that already reads one is two reshapes of one dataset, and the second would name columns the first consumed, so it is reported:

(try
  (-> sales
      (pj/pose {:x :quarter :y [:revenue :cost]})
      (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :tax]))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-line was given a series on :y, and the pose it is added to already reads one on :y. A series pivots the data into one value column, and two pivots have no shared shape. Read one of them: drop the series from the pj/lay-line call to use the pose's, or build the layer on a pose of its own."

Within the lay-* call a series goes wherever a column goes – as an argument, or written under :x or :y in a map. The two spellings draw the same plot:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar {:x :quarter :y [:revenue :cost :tax]}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180
A series goes where a column goes on an axis, so it can be written on :x as readily as on :y. On :x the measures run along the horizontal axis and the quarters go up the vertical one:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point {:series [:revenue :cost :tax]} :quarter))

quarterrevenue, cost, taxrevenuecosttax20406080100120140160180Q1Q2Q3Q4
The bare vector means on :x what it means on :y:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point [:revenue :cost :tax] :quarter))

quarterrevenue, cost, taxrevenuecosttax20406080100120140160180Q1Q2Q3Q4
For bars, write the series on :y and turn the plot with pj/coord as the Sideways example below does. A bar drawn from a category on :y is supported less fully – see Known Limitations.

title: 26  Series
section: Placing the measures against each other
text:
Placing the measures against each other
:identity draws every series at the same place, so the bars overlap. It is the one that differs from the bar’s own default. Three partly transparent bars drawn from zero make a third tone wherever they cross, which reads as a stack – the axis is what tells the two apart, since here it reaches the largest measure and under :stack below it reaches their total:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :identity}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180
:dodge gives each series a slot of the band, which is what a bar does without being asked:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180
:stack piles the series, so the band’s height is their total:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :stack}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150200250300350
:fill piles them and normalizes, so each band reads as shares between zero and one:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :fill}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q40.00.10.20.30.40.50.60.70.80.91.0

title: 26  Series
text:
The columns the pivot invents
The pivot drops the columns it reads and puts two columns in their place: :value holds the number, and the key column holds which measure a row came from. The key column is named :series unless :as names it otherwise.
Where the data already carries a column of one of those names, the pivot reports an error instead of overwriting the column:

(try
  (-> {:quarter ["Q1" "Q2"]
       :revenue [120 150]
       :cost    [90 100]
       :series  ["a" "b"]}
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost]))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-bar cannot pivot these columns: the pivot names its key column :series, and the data already has a :series column. Name the key column something else -- {:series [:revenue :cost] :as :measure} -- or rename the column in the data."

:as gives the key column a name the data does not use. A data column named :value has to be renamed in the data instead, since :as does not reach the value column.

(-> {:quarter ["Q1" "Q2"]
     :revenue [120 150]
     :cost    [90 100]
     :series  ["a" "b"]}
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost] :as :measure}))

revenue, costquartermeasurerevenuecostQ1Q2020406080100120140

title: 26  Series
text:
A series on each axis
Two measures recorded at different times each have a time column of their own. Below, :reading-a was taken at the times in :time-a, and :reading-b at the times in :time-b. To draw both on one panel, write a series on :x and another on :y. They are read in pairs: the first :x column with the first :y column, the second with the second, and so on. Each pair is one series of the layer, labelled with both column names, and the pivot invents two value columns, :x-value and :y-value, one for each axis. Each axis is titled by the columns it reads.

(-> {:time-a    [0 1 2 3]
     :time-b    [0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5]
     :reading-a [2 3 5 4]
     :reading-b [1 2 2 3]}
    (pj/lay-line [:time-a :time-b] [:reading-a :reading-b]))

reading a, reading btime a, time btime a / reading atime b / reading b0.00.51.01.52.02.53.03.512345
Titles of your own are written with :x-label and :y-label:

(-> {:time-a    [0 1 2 3]
     :time-b    [0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5]
     :reading-a [2 3 5 4]
     :reading-b [1 2 2 3]}
    (pj/lay-line [:time-a :time-b] [:reading-a :reading-b])
    (pj/options {:x-label "Time (s)" :y-label "Reading"}))

ReadingTime (s)time a / reading atime b / reading b0.00.51.01.52.02.53.03.512345
The same pairs can be written in the pose’s mapping, as {:x [...] :y [...]}, and there :as names the key column – here :sensor, which titles the legend:

(-> {:time-a    [0 1 2 3]
     :time-b    [0.5 1.5 2.5 3.5]
     :reading-a [2 3 5 4]
     :reading-b [1 2 2 3]}
    (pj/pose {:x [:time-a :time-b]
              :y {:series [:reading-a :reading-b] :as :sensor}})
    pj/lay-line)

reading a, reading btime a, time bsensortime a / reading atime b / reading b0.00.51.01.52.02.53.03.512345
The two series take as many columns each, since each :x column needs a :y column to be paired with:

(try
  (-> {:time-a [0 1] :time-b [2 3] :reading-a [1 2] :reading-b [3 4]}
      (pj/lay-line [:time-a :time-b] [:reading-a :reading-b :time-a]))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-line was given 2 columns on :x, [:time-a :time-b], and 3 on :y, [:reading-a :reading-b :time-a]. Two series are read in pairs, the first :x column with the first :y column, so they take as many columns each."

Every :x column against every :y column is the product of the two lists. It is useful where the columns share units, so that each pair can be compared on one set of axes. A for over the two lists returns the product as a sequence of pairs, (apply map vector) turns the pairs into the list of :x columns and the list of :y columns, and apply passes the two lists to the lay-* call. Here the two lengths of an iris flower are drawn against its two widths, all in centimetres:

(->> (for [x [:sepal-length :petal-length]
           y [:sepal-width :petal-width]]
       [x y])
     (apply map vector)
     (apply pj/lay-point (rdatasets/datasets-iris)))

sepal width, petal widthsepal length, petal lengthsepal length / sepal widthsepal length / petal widthpetal length / sepal widthpetal length / petal width24680.00.51.01.52.02.53.03.54.04.5
For a panel per pair in place of one panel, give the two lists to pj/matrix as (pj/matrix data xs ys): each column of xs is drawn against each column of ys in a panel of its own. The scatter plot matrix in Relationships crosses one list of columns with itself.

title: 26  Series
text:
One series per pose
A series pivots the data of the pose it is on, so a second, different series on the same pose is reported at the call that adds it:

(try
  (-> sales
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost])
      (pj/lay-line :quarter [:tax :units]))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-line reads [:tax :units] as series, and a layer on the same pose already reads [:revenue :cost]. A series pivots the pose's data into one value column, and two pivots have no shared shape. Give each series a pose of its own and arrange the poses."

Give each series a pose of its own and arrange the poses:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> sales
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :dodge}))
  (-> sales
      (pj/lay-line :quarter [:tax :units]))])

revenue, costquarterQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180tax, unitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q412141618202224262830revenuecosttaxunits

title: 26  Series
text:
Examples
Each example below combines a series with one more thing – another mark, a scale, the key column in another role, panels, another layer, a composite. The last group lists the series that report an error, and the vectors that are not series at all.

Other marks

Lines and points

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180


Areas and steps

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-area :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :stack}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150200250300350

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-step :quarter [:revenue :cost]))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q490100110120130140150160170180190
An area normalizes under :fill the way a bar does, so each quarter reads as shares between zero and one:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-area :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :fill}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q40.00.10.20.30.40.50.60.70.80.91.0


Marks that take a series
Any mark drawing from a value column takes a series. The five above are bars, lines, points, areas and steps; a lollipop is another:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-lollipop :quarter [:revenue :cost]))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180
The pivot does not change what a mark’s stat requires. A smooth needs a numeric x column and reports when it is drawn, since the quarter column is categorical whether the measures are pivoted or not:

(try
  (pj/plot (-> sales (pj/lay-smooth :quarter [:revenue :cost])))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"Stat :loess requires a numeric column for :x, but :quarter is categorical. A stat that bins or smooths reads numbers; a column of text names groups instead. Dates written as text stay categorical until they are parsed with tc/convert-types."



A stat over a series
A stat runs after the pivot, so it reads one series at a time. Each measure of each quarter has a row per region in sales-by-region, and pj/lay-summary draws the mean of those rows with a standard-error bar around it – one mean per quarter per measure:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-summary :quarter [:revenue :cost]))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q480100120140160180200


A series along a date axis
The pivot reshapes the measures and leaves the axis column as it was, so a date axis stays a date axis. Two columns of the economics dataset hold counts of people in thousands – the population and the number of them unemployed – which a log scale brings onto one axis:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-economics)
    (pj/lay-line :date {:series [:pop :unemploy] :scale {:type :log}}))

pop, unemploydatepopunemploy197019801990200020103000500010000200003000050000100000200000300000
A stat needing a numeric axis column reported an error on the quarters above, and runs on these dates, since a date is not a category – one smooth per measure:

(-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-economics)
    (pj/lay-smooth :date {:series [:pop :unemploy] :scale {:type :log}}))

pop, unemploydatepopunemploy19701980199020002010500010000200003000050000100000200000300000



Scales and colours

A scale on the value axis

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost :tax]
                            :scale {:type :log}}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4203050100200
pj/scale on the axis the series is written on says the same thing, so the scale can go in either place:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/scale :y {:type :log}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4203050100200


A domain on the value axis

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost])
    (pj/scale :y {:domain [0 250]}))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220240


Choosing the colours

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/scale :color {:values ["#377eb8" "#e6550d" "#4daf4a"]}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
A scale set on the pose carries down to every panel, so the same three colours are used in each:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/scale :color {:values ["#377eb8" "#e6550d" "#4daf4a"]})
    (pj/facet :region))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180200Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS


The order of the series
The order the measures are drawn in – the legend’s order, the order of the slots in a dodged band, and the order a stack piles them – is the order they are written in:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:tax :revenue :cost] {:position :stack}))

tax, revenue, costquartertaxrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150200250300350
A :domain on the colour scale sets the order, since the key column is the column the colour reads:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :stack})
    (pj/scale :color {:domain [:tax :revenue :cost]}))

tax, revenue, costquartertaxrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150200250300350



Column names and missing values

Column names that look like numbers
A wide table often names its measures by year. tc/pivot->longer reads a column name that looks like a number as one, so the key column comes out holding numbers rather than text – and the pivot says that it holds column names, by writing :color-type :categorical beside the colour it maps them to. Without it, the colour would read the years as a quantity and draw one gradient over the lot, with every measure in one colour and no legend entry naming either year.

(-> {"country" ["a" "b" "c"]
     "2019"    [10 20 30]
     "2020"    [12 25 28]}
    (pj/lay-line "country" ["2019" "2020"]))

2019, 2020country20192020abc1012141618202224262830
The pivot happens when the pose is drawn, so the :color-type it writes is visible in the draft:

(-> {"country" ["a" "b" "c"]
     "2019"    [10 20 30]
     "2020"    [12 25 28]}
    (pj/lay-line "country" ["2019" "2020"])
    pj/draft
    :layers
    first
    (select-keys [:color :color-type])
    kind/pprint)


{:color :series, :color-type :categorical}

A series whose columns are named in words needs none of this, and carries no :color-type. The dataset the pose holds is what tc/pivot->longer returns either way : the key column keeps the type Tablecloth gave it, and :color-type changes only how the colour reads the key column.


A measure with no value
A cell left empty in the wide table has no value to pivot, so that observation is not drawn. Two quarters and two measures are four observations, and three are drawn:

(-> {:quarter ["Q1" "Q2"]
     :revenue [120 nil]
     :cost    [90 100]}
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost]))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q29095100105110115120
Plotje says how many went, naming the columns read as series:

(with-out-str
  (pj/plan (-> {:quarter ["Q1" "Q2"]
                :revenue [120 nil]
                :cost    [90 100]}
               (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost]))))


"Warning: Removed 1 row with a missing value among the columns read as series (:revenue, :cost).\n"

The pivot is tc/pivot->longer with Tablecloth’s own defaults, so the dataset the pose carries is what Tablecloth gives for the same columns, and a row with no value is not in it. Writing the data long by hand reaches the same plot, and Plotje reports the same observation at a later stage and in its own words:

(with-out-str
  (pj/plan (-> {:quarter ["Q1" "Q1" "Q2" "Q2"]
                :measure ["revenue" "cost" "revenue" "cost"]
                :value   [120 90 nil 100]}
               (pj/lay-point :quarter :value {:color :measure}))))


"Warning: Removed 1 row with non-finite values: 1 missing (nil/NaN).\n"




The key column elsewhere

Panels from the key column
Faceting a series by its key column draws one panel per measure: each panel draws one column, is titled by that column, and has a value axis of its own.

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/facet :series))

revenueQ1Q2Q3Q4120130140150160170180190costQ1Q2Q3Q49095100105110115120taxQ1Q2Q3Q418202224262830quarter
Two other spellings draw the same plot: a facet over the three columns, placed across with :col, and an arrangement of three mappings, each naming :quarter and one of the columns.

(-> sales
    (pj/pose {:x :quarter})
    pj/lay-line
    (pj/facet {:col {:y [:revenue :cost :tax]}}))

revenueQ1Q2Q3Q4120130140150160170180190costQ1Q2Q3Q49095100105110115120taxQ1Q2Q3Q418202224262830quarter
The panels have value axes of their own because they draw different columns, and the series keeps the names of the columns it reads. A table pivoted by hand with tc/pivot->longer and faceted by its key column draws one column, :value, in every panel, so its panels share one value axis.
To read the measures against each other, share the value axis between the columns with :share-scales:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/facet :series)
    (pj/options {:share-scales {:y :all}}))

revenueQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180costQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180taxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180quarter
With :as, the facet names the key column by its new name:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost :tax] :as :measure})
    (pj/facet :measure))

revenueQ1Q2Q3Q4120130140150160170180190costQ1Q2Q3Q49095100105110115120taxQ1Q2Q3Q418202224262830quarter


The key column on the axis
Naming the key column on an axis draws the measures against each other rather than along the quarters. The pivot runs before the axis is read, so the column is there by the time the mark is drawn: one box per measure, from every row that measure has.

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-boxplot :series [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxseriesrevenuecosttaxrevenuecosttax20406080100120140160180200
A violin over the same three measures:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-violin :series [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxseriesrevenuecosttaxrevenuecosttax20406080100120140160180200


Another aesthetic from the key column
The layer that writes a series may map the key column again. Shape beside colour separates the measures twice over, which survives printing in one colour. Colour and shape share one legend, each entry drawn in its colour and its shape:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:shape :series}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
:tooltip reads the key column as readily, so in the HTML rendering of this page hovering a point says which measure it holds:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:tooltip :series}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180

:size and :alpha draw a magnitude, and a measure’s name is not one, so a series key on either reports an error:

(try
  (pj/plot (-> sales
               (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]
                             {:size :series})))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"Aesthetic :size needs a numeric column, but :series holds categories. :size draws a magnitude, so there is nothing for a category to be. To tell categories apart, map the column to :color (a palette) or to :group (one drawn group each)."




Another column beside the series

Series and a grouping column
A grouping column keeps its own marks separate, so each measure is drawn once per region: two measures across two regions give four lines, coloured by measure.

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:group :region}))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q480100120140160180200
On a bar, a dodge gives every combination of the measure and the grouping column a slot of its own, so each quarter draws four bars – but the grouping column draws no legend, so the two bars of one measure share its colour and nothing says which region each is:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:group :region}))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220
Facet on the column instead, as the panel sections below do, so each region’s bars are labelled by a strip.


Colouring by another column
The pivot maps the key column to :color, which is what gives each measure a colour of its own. Where the layer maps :color itself, the pivot maps the key column to :group instead. The measures stay separate marks, and the colour shows the region: still four lines, two of them red and two blue.

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:color :region}))

revenue, costquarterregionEUASQ1Q2Q3Q480100120140160180200
The same layer in panels, one per outlet:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:color :region})
    (pj/facet :outlet))

revenue, costquarterregionEUASQ1Q2Q3Q480100120140160180200Q1Q2Q3Q4webshop
A :color written on the pose does not reach the marks. The pivot writes :color on the layer that writes the series, and a layer’s own mapping wins over the pose’s, so the region separates nothing and each line runs through both regions – the same plot as one with no :color on the pose at all. Write :color on the layer, as the two examples above do:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/pose {:color :region})
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost]))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q480100120140160180200



Panels and turned plots

Sideways

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge})
    (pj/coord :flip))

quarterrevenue, cost, taxrevenuecosttax020406080100120140160180Q1Q2Q3Q4


Series in panels

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge})
    (pj/facet :region))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :stack})
    (pj/facet {:col :region :row :outlet}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttax0100200300Q1Q2Q3Q40100200300Q1Q2Q3Q4EUASwebshop


Series in each panel, drawn as lines
Each region has all four quarters, so each panel draws a line per measure across the whole axis. Faceting on region and outlet together would leave two quarters per panel, so each line would join only two points.

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/facet :region)
    (pj/options {:title "Measures by region"}))

Measures by regionrevenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180200Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS


Dodged series, drawn sideways, in panels

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :dodge})
    (pj/coord :flip)
    (pj/facet :region))

quarterrevenue, costrevenuecost0100200Q1Q2Q3Q40100200EUAS


Shares, drawn sideways
Normalizing and turning the plot compose, so each quarter becomes a bar of shares running left to right:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :fill})
    (pj/coord :flip))

quarterrevenue, cost, taxrevenuecosttax0.00.20.40.60.81.0Q1Q2Q3Q4


A named series, scaled and in panels
The written-out form composes with the rest. Here the key column is named, the value column is read through a log scale, the value axis is relabelled, and the canvas is divided by region:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-point :quarter {:series [:revenue :cost :tax]
                            :as :measure
                            :scale {:type :log}})
    (pj/facet :region)
    (pj/options {:y-label "Euros"}))

EurosquartermeasurerevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4203050100200Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS



Other layers beside a series

Two marks over one series
A second mark over the same measures is written as a second series naming the same columns. Each layer draws its own series, in the same colours, on the pose’s one panel:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/lay-point :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
The pivot replaces the pose’s data when the pose is drawn, so a second layer may also read the columns it invented – :value for the number and :series for the key – and draws the same series in another mark. The key column is mapped to :color on the layer that asked for the series, so a second layer names it to be coloured the same way.

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/lay-point :quarter :value {:color :series}))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180
A layer naming no columns reads the columns of the panel – those of the series layer, :quarter and :value – so it draws at the same places. It does not read the series layer’s :color: the key column is mapped to :color on the layer that asked for the series alone, so the twelve points come out one colour:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax])
    (pj/lay-point))

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180


Series beside a layer on another column
A layer naming a column the pivot did not consume is drawn on the series’ panel, its column on the axis of the series’ values. The axis title names the layer’s column after the columns of the series. With no :color specified, the layer takes a colour and a legend entry named after its column, beside the entries of the series:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :stack})
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :units))

revenue, cost, unitsquarterrevenuecostunitsQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150200250300
A count of units and an amount of money do not belong on one axis, and Plotje prints a Note that :units takes a small part of the axis. Here the two belong in panels of their own, arranged one above the other:

(pj/arrange [(pj/lay-bar sales :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :stack})
             (pj/lay-line sales :quarter :units)]
            {:cols 1})

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q40100200300unitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q412141618


A rule across every panel of a series
A layer naming no columns of its own is drawn on every panel.

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :dodge})
    (pj/facet :region)
    (pj/lay-rule-h {:y-intercept 120}))

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS



Composites

Nested poses
pj/arrange places poses side by side. Each input is a pose, so a series pose goes in a cell like any other.

(pj/arrange
 [(-> sales
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge}))
  (-> sales
      (pj/lay-line :quarter :units))])

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180unitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q41213141516171819
A cell may be a composite itself, so an arranged pose can be arranged again and the cell draws its own grid.

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/arrange
   [(-> sales
        (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :dodge}))
    (-> sales
        (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :stack}))]
   {:cols 1})
  (-> sales
      (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))])

revenue, costquarterQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150revenue, costquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40100200300revenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q420406080100120140160180revenuecosttax


Sub-plots of faceted panels of series

(pj/arrange
 [(-> sales-by-region
      (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge})
      (pj/facet :region))
  (-> sales-by-region
      (pj/lay-line :quarter :units)
      (pj/facet :region))]
 {:width 900})

revenue, cost, taxquarterrevenuecosttaxQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220Q1Q2Q3Q4EUASunitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q4101214161820Q1Q2Q3Q4EUAS


Sub-plots read against one axis

(pj/arrange
 (vec (for [r ["EU" "AS"]]
        (-> sales-by-region
            (tc/select-rows (fn [row] (= r (:region row))))
            (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :dodge})
            (pj/options {:title r}))))
 {:share-scales #{:y}
  :align-panels true})

EUQ1Q2Q3Q4020406080100120140160180200220ASQ1Q2Q3Q4quarterrevenue, cost, taxrevenuecosttax


A written-out composite of series

(pj/pose
 {:layout {:direction :vertical :weights [2 1]}
  :poses [(-> sales
              (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position :stack}))
          (-> sales
              (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost]))]})

revenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40100200300revenue,costquarterQ1Q2Q3Q4100150revenuecosttax


Three levels of nesting

(pj/arrange
 [(pj/arrange
   [(-> sales
        (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :dodge}))
    (-> sales
        (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost]))]
   {:cols 1})
  (pj/arrange
   [(-> sales
        (pj/lay-area :quarter [:revenue :cost] {:position :stack}))
    (-> sales
        (pj/lay-point :quarter :units))]
   {:cols 1})]
 {:title "Measures four ways"})

revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4050100150revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q4100150revenue, costquarterrevenuecostQ1Q2Q3Q40100200300unitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q412141618Measures four ways


A titled grid of series

(pj/arrange
 (vec (for [pos [:identity :dodge :stack :fill]]
        (-> sales
            (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax] {:position pos})
            (pj/options {:title (name pos)}))))
 {:cols 2})

identityrevenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40100dodgerevenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40100stackrevenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40200fillrevenue, cost, taxquarterQ1Q2Q3Q40.00.51.0revenuecosttax


A grid of panels of series
A grid of panels of series is an arrangement of series poses, each pose reading its own columns:

(pj/arrange
 [(-> sales (pj/lay-line :quarter [:revenue :cost]))
  (-> sales (pj/lay-line :quarter [:tax :units]))])

revenue, costquarterQ1Q2Q3Q490100110120130140150160170180190tax, unitsquarterQ1Q2Q3Q412141618202224262830revenuecosttaxunits
pj/facet splits a series into panels by a column, as in Panels from the key column; pj/arrange places series poses that read different columns, as here.



Errors and look-alikes

Series that report an error
The sections above show the errors a writer meets most often. The rest of the set, with the message each one gives:

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["written" "what it reports"]
  :row-vectors
  (mapv (fn [[written f]]
          [(kind/code written)
           (try (do (pj/plot (f)) "draws")
                (catch Throwable e (first (str/split (ex-message e) #"\. "))))])
        [["{:color [:revenue :cost :tax]}"
          #(-> sales (pj/lay-point :quarter :revenue {:color [:revenue :cost :tax]}))]
         ["{:series [:revenue]}"
          #(-> sales (pj/lay-bar :quarter {:series [:revenue]}))]
         ["[:revenue 42]"
          #(-> sales (pj/lay-bar :quarter {:series [:revenue 42]}))]
         ["[:revenue :nope]"
          #(-> sales (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :nope]))]
         ["a mapping already naming a consumed column"
          #(-> sales (pj/pose :quarter :revenue)
               (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))]
         ["a series on a composite pose"
          #(-> (pj/arrange [(pj/lay-point sales :quarter :revenue)])
               (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost :tax]))]
         ["a pose carrying no data"
          #(-> (pj/pose) (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :cost]))]
         ["{:y-min [:cost :tax]}"
          #(-> sales (pj/lay-errorbar :quarter :revenue {:y-min [:cost :tax]}))]
         ["[:revenue :outlet]"
          #(-> sales-by-region (pj/lay-bar :quarter [:revenue :outlet]))]])})










written
what it reports





{:color [:revenue :cost :tax]}

pj/lay-point :color was given several columns, [:revenue :cost :tax]



{:series [:revenue]}

pj/lay-bar was given 1 column in a slot where several are read as several series: [:revenue]



[:revenue 42]

pj/lay-bar was given [:revenue 42], and 42 is not a column reference -- a keyword or a string naming a column of the data.



[:revenue :nope]

pj/lay-bar was given several columns to read as series, and the data does not have [:nope]



a mapping already naming a consumed column

this pose's mapping names :revenue on :y, a column that a series on this pose has already read: the series pivots [:revenue :cost :tax] into a key column and a value column, so the rows it draws have no column :revenue



a series on a composite pose

pj/lay-bar was given several columns to read as series, on a composite pose



a pose carrying no data

A pose reads several columns on :y as series and has no data to pivot



{:y-min [:cost :tax]}

pj/lay-errorbar :y-min was given several columns, [:cost :tax]



[:revenue :outlet]

The series [:revenue :outlet] on :y holds values of different types: ["Long" "String"]







What is not a series
A vector on :group is one compound key rather than several series. Region combined with outlet gives four keys, so the line is drawn in four pieces:

(-> sales-by-region
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :revenue {:group [:region :outlet]}))

revenuequarterQ1Q2Q3Q4100120140160180200
A vector whose elements are not column references is whatever the aesthetic it is written on reads it as. A dash pattern is two lengths, not two columns to pivot:

(-> sales
    (pj/lay-line :quarter :revenue {:stroke-dash [5 5]}))

revenuequarterQ1Q2Q3Q4120130140150160170180190

title: 27  Polar Coordinates
text:
Polar Scatter
For polar coordinates, (pj/coord :polar) maps x to angle and y to radius. Bars become arc-interpolated wedges (rose charts), and scatter points wrap onto a polar plane. The angular spread is set by the x-column’s domain, so a narrow domain produces a wedge cluster rather than a full circle. Supported marks today are :point, :bar, :rect, :text, and :rug; other marks report an error. The :x title below the panel names the column drawn as the angle, and its tick labels stand around the circle, one at each spoke of the grid. The :y title beside the panel names the column drawn as the radius, and its tick labels stand at the left edge, each level with the top of its circle of the grid. Legends render as they would on Cartesian coordinates – a :color mapping produces a normal legend that can be repositioned via :legend-position (see Customization).
The same scatter plot, wrapped onto a polar plane. x maps to angle (clockwise from 12 o’clock), y maps to radius (center = minimum, edge = maximum). Iris’s :sepal-length spans roughly 4.3 to 7.9 – a narrow interval of values – so the points cluster in an arc rather than spreading across the full circle.

text:
(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/coord :polar))

Rose Chart (Coxcomb Diagram)
A bar chart in polar coordinates produces a rose chart – wedge area encodes count. Bars are arc-interpolated for smooth curved edges.

    (pj/lay-bar :species)
    (pj/coord :polar))

Wind Rose
A bar chart with a y column (value bars) in polar makes a wind rose – each direction gets a wedge proportional to wind speed.

    (pj/lay-bar :direction :speed)

Polar Histogram
A histogram in polar wraps bins around the circle. Useful for circular distributions, such as time of day or compass bearing.

title: 27  Polar Coordinates
text:
Facets on Polar Coordinates
pj/facet splits a polar plot into panels as it does a Cartesian one, and each panel draws its own circle. The circle fits the shorter side of its panel’s drawing area, so three panels side by side on the default canvas are tall and narrow and draw small circles. A wider, shorter canvas gives each circle more room:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/coord :polar)
    (pj/facet :species)
    (pj/options {:width 900 :height 340}))

sepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica567823456785678setosaversicolorvirginica

title: 27  Polar Coordinates
text:
Explicit Labels with Polar
The axis titles name the angle’s column and the radius’s column, as on Cartesian coordinates. pj/options replaces them, and sets a title, as it does on Cartesian coordinates:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/coord :polar)
    (pj/options {:title "Iris in Polar Space"
                 :x-label "Sepal length (angle)"
                 :y-label "Sepal width (radius)"}))

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Tooltips
Plotje produces SVG hiccup, and offers interaction in two ways:
The static Markdown render of this notebook shows the SVGs as flat images. Open the HTML rendering to see the interactions live.
Both kinds of interaction run in a browser reading the figure, so SVG is the only format that carries them – see Formats that draw interaction at the end of the chapter.
Pass :tooltip true to pj/options and every point gets a data-tooltip attribute holding its column values. A small embedded script renders the tooltip on hover – no extra setup. pj/lay-point and pj/lay-interval-h are the two marks that carry a tooltip, whether the text is the built-in one or a mapped column; a tooltip written on any other layer type is accepted and draws none, which Known Limitations records.

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/options {:title "Hover over a point for column values"
                 :tooltip true
                 :height 320}))

Hover over a point for column valuessepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5


Writing the tooltip yourself
The built-in text names the columns the layer drew and their values, which is right for exploring and wrong as soon as the numbers need presenting – a currency sign, a thousands separator, a percentage, 1,653,346 read as 1.7M, or a column the plot does not draw at all.
Rather than a formatting option per case, :tooltip is an aesthetic like any other, mapped to a column whose values are the text each point shows. Building that column is ordinary data work, with the whole language available.

(def sales
  (tc/dataset {:month   ["Jan" "Feb" "Mar" "Apr"]
               :revenue [1653346 2410880 987654 3120500]
               :margin  [0.184 0.223 0.161 0.207]}))

(def sales-labelled
  (tc/add-column sales :hover
                 #(map (fn [month revenue margin]
                         (str month "\n"
                              (format "%.1fM" (/ (double revenue) 1e6))
                              " at " (format "%.1f%%" (* 100.0 margin))))
                       (:month %) (:revenue %) (:margin %))))

Map that column to :tooltip:

    (pj/lay-point :margin :revenue {:tooltip :hover})
    (pj/options {:title "Hover for the month, revenue and margin"
                 :height 320}))

Hover for the month, revenue and marginrevenuemargin0.160.170.180.190.20.210.2210000001500000200000025000003000000

Three things follow from :tooltip being an aesthetic rather than a plot option.

The month is in the tooltip and on neither axis. A tooltip column is built from whatever the dataset holds.
Writing it turns tooltips on. {:tooltip true} in pj/options is the switch for the built-in text, and is not needed beside a mapping.
It scopes like every mapping. On the pose it covers each layer; on one layer it covers that layer, and the nearer one wins.

A written string rather than a column gives every mark of the layer the same tooltip: {:tooltip "one reading per bar"}.


Tooltips with markup
A tooltip may hold hiccup instead of a string, for a label that carries a heading, an emphasis or a table rather than a line of text. A column of hiccup gives each mark its own markup, and a written hiccup vector gives every mark of the layer the same markup, exactly as a column of strings and a written string do.

(def sales-rich
  (tc/add-column sales :hover
                 #(map (fn [month revenue margin]
                         [:div
                          [:b month]
                          [:br]
                          "revenue " [:code (format "%.1fM" (/ (double revenue) 1e6))]
                          [:br]
                          "margin " [:code (format "%.1f%%" (* 100.0 margin))]])
                       (:month %) (:revenue %) (:margin %))))

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Brush selection
:brush true enables drag-to-select. While dragging, a shaded rectangle follows the cursor; on release, points inside keep full opacity and points outside dim to 0.15. A short drag (less than 3 CSS pixels each side – the unit a mouse event reports, not a drawing unit) clears the selection. Selection is keyed by row index, so it tracks the same rows across every panel in the pose.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
    (pj/options {:title "Drag a rectangle to highlight a region"
                 :brush true
                 :height 320}))

Drag a rectangle to highlight a regionsepal widthsepal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.02.02.53.03.54.04.5

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Cross-panel linked highlighting
Brush selection is keyed by data-row-idx, the row of the pose’s dataset a mark was drawn from. A facet keeps that number when it splits the data, so a row drawn in several panels carries one number in all of them, and selecting it in one panel highlights it in the others. Below, each flower is drawn twice, once against its sepal width and once against its petal width. Drag over the setosa cluster in the top panel, and the same flowers light up in the bottom one.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:x :sepal-length})
    pj/lay-point
    (pj/facet {:y [:sepal-width :petal-width]})
    (pj/options {:title "Brush on one panel, see linked points in the other"
                 :brush true
                 :tooltip true
                 :height 420}))

sepal width234petal width4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.0012sepal lengthBrush on one panel, see linked points in the other


A series links its columns the same way: both points drawn from one row carry that row’s number. The cells of an arrangement drawn from one dataset link the same way, and so do the panels of a scatter plot matrix, which is a facet over columns. A facet over the categories of a column draws each row in one panel only, so there a selection stays in the panel it was made in.

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Interval (Gantt) tooltips
lay-interval-h participates in the same tooltip/brush system. Each rectangle’s tooltip names the lane, the start, the end, and the color label; on temporal axes the start and end are formatted as date strings rather than raw epoch-milliseconds.

(-> {:start [#inst "2024-01-01" #inst "2024-02-15" #inst "2024-04-01"
             #inst "2024-05-10" #inst "2024-06-20"]
     :end   [#inst "2024-03-15" #inst "2024-04-20" #inst "2024-06-30"
             #inst "2024-07-10" #inst "2024-08-30"]
     :task  ["Design" "Build" "Test" "Deploy" "Document"]
     :team  ["UX" "Eng" "QA" "Eng" "UX"]}
    (pj/lay-interval-h :start :task {:x-end :end :color :team})
    (pj/options {:title "Hover for task: start -> end, team"
                 :tooltip true
                 :height 320}))

Hover for task: start -> end, teamtaskstartteamUXEngQAJanMarMayJulDesignBuildTestDeployDocument

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Custom wrapper: save as PNG
Browsers can serialize an SVG element to a PNG via a <canvas> round-trip. The wrapper below adds a “Save PNG” button that renders the current SVG into a canvas and triggers a download.

(let [plot-svg (pj/plot
                (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
                    (pj/options {:title "Click 'Save PNG' to download the rendering"
                                 :height 320})))
      attrs (second plot-svg)
      body (drop 2 plot-svg)
      plot-id (str "pj-png-" (System/nanoTime))
      btn-id (str plot-id "-save")
      script (str "document.getElementById('" btn-id "').addEventListener('click',function(){"
                  "var svg=document.getElementById('" plot-id "');"
                  "var w=svg.clientWidth||" (or (:width attrs) 600) ","
                  "h=svg.clientHeight||" (or (:height attrs) 400) ";"
                  "var data=new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(svg);"
                  "var img=new Image();"
                  "img.onload=function(){"
                  "var c=document.createElement('canvas');c.width=w;c.height=h;"
                  "c.getContext('2d').drawImage(img,0,0,w,h);"
                  "var a=document.createElement('a');"
                  "a.href=c.toDataURL('image/png');a.download='plotje.png';"
                  "document.body.appendChild(a);a.click();a.remove();};"
                  "img.src='data:image/svg+xml;base64,'+btoa(unescape(encodeURIComponent(data)));"
                  "});")]
  (kind/hiccup
   [:div
    [:button {:id btn-id
              :style "margin-bottom:6px; padding:4px 12px;"}
     "Save PNG"]
    (into [:svg (assoc attrs :id plot-id)] body)
    [:script script]]))

title: 28  Interactivity
text:
Formats that draw interaction
A tooltip and a brush are behaviours a browser runs over the figure, so they reach a reader only where the figure is SVG. A plot rendered to :bufimg, or saved as a PNG, carries neither: a raster image is finished before anyone hovers over it, and has no elements for a script to attach to.
A tooltip or a brush requested on such a format prints a warning, and the figure still renders without them. One warning covers the plot, naming both requests where both were written, the format, and the formats that draw interaction:

(with-out-str
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
      (pj/options {:tooltip true :brush true})
      (pj/plot {:format :bufimg})))


"Warning: :tooltip and :brush asked for, and the :bufimg format draws no interaction. The formats that do: :svg. The request is accepted and draws nothing.\n"

pj/save to a PNG prints the same warning, since a PNG file is that format written to disk. Saving the SVG keeps the attributes on the marks, and a browser opening the file runs the script that reads them.

title: 29  Troubleshooting
text:
Column Not Found
Common mistakes and how to fix them.
Symptom: "Column :foo (from :x) not found in dataset" error, listing the available columns at the end of the message.
Cause: The column reference does not match a dataset column name. Matching is strict – :foo matches keyword column :foo only, and "foo" matches string column "foo" only. The two forms do not interchange. Three common triggers:
1. Typo. A misspelled column name. Check the spelling against the dataset’s columns:
2. Keyword vs string. A CSV loaded without :key-fn keyword produces string column names; using a keyword reference against that dataset throws:
The fix is to either pass {:key-fn keyword} when loading the CSV (so the dataset has keyword columns) or to use string references everywhere.
3. Whitespace or punctuation mismatch. A column literally named "sepal length" (with a space) does not match :sepal-length (with a hyphen):
:key-fn keyword on "sepal length" produces :sepal length – a keyword whose printed form contains a space, not the hyphenated form a Clojure reader would normally produce. Spaces and other special characters in CSV headers usually need a custom :key-fn, e.g. (comp keyword #(clojure.string/replace % " " "-")).
