title: 37  Extensibility
text:
layer->membrane
Renders a plan layer descriptor into membrane drawable primitives. This is the “membrane path” – used when the target format goes through membrane, as SVG does.
Dispatch function: (fn [layer ctx] (:mark layer))
The rendering context ctx carries, among other keys:

:coord-fn – takes an :x and a :y value in data space and returns the point [px py] in drawing units, through the panel’s coordinate system. A renderer that places its marks through coord-fn is drawn correctly under (pj/coord :flip); one that calls the scales directly is not. On a categorical axis a number is a place among the categories, counted from one, so coord-fn also places the edges of a band.
:sx, :sy – the two scales themselves, for a renderer that needs a scale object, such as the width of a band
:coord-type – :cartesian, :flip, :polar or :fixed

The Waterfall Extension chapter draws its bars through coord-fn and shows them flipped.

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["Dispatch value" "Membrane output"]
  :row-maps
  (->> (methods mark/layer->membrane)
       keys
       (filter keyword?)
       (remove #{:default})
       sort
       (mapv (fn [k] {"Dispatch value" (kind/code (pr-str k))
                      "Membrane output" (pj/membrane-mark-doc k)})))})










Dispatch value
Membrane output





:area

Closed filled polygons with baseline



:band-h

One filled rectangle across the panel between two written y values



:band-v

One filled rectangle down the panel between two written x values



:bar

Filled polygons (histogram bars)



:boxplot

Box + whiskers + median line + outlier points



:contour

Stroked iso-density polylines



:errorbar

Vertical lines with caps



:interval-h

Filled rectangles spanning x to x-end at categorical y



:line

Stroked polylines



:lollipop

Stems with dots at category positions



:point

Translated colored rounded-rectangles



:pointrange

Point at mean + vertical SE line



:rect

Filled polygons (categorical/value bars)



:ridgeline

Overlapping filled density curves



:rug

Short stroked tick marks at axis margins



:rule-h

One stroked line across the panel at a written y



:rule-v

One stroked line down the panel at a written x



:segment

Straight lines from (x, y) to (x-end, y-end), with optional arrow heads



:step

Stroked step polylines



:text

Translated text labels, on a rounded background box when one is asked for



:tile

Translated colored rectangles (heatmap cells)



:violin

Mirrored filled density polygon






Drawing an aesthetic the layer type declares it varies
A layer type says which appearance aesthetics its mark varies from row to row under :varies, and that declaration earns the layer a legend. Drawing them is the renderer’s half, and it has to agree with the legend: both read the column’s values through the same scale, and a mark that spreads the values itself instead will draw sizes its own legend does not explain.
layer-type/aesthetic-magnitude-fn is that shared function. It turns a value from the layer’s per-row buffers into the drawn size – for the :point mark, a radius for :size and an opacity for :alpha:

(def bubble-layer
  (-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [1 2 3] :n [1 4 9]}
      (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n})
      pj/plan
      :panels
      first
      :layers
      first))


(let [groups (:groups bubble-layer)
      radius-of (layer-type/aesthetic-magnitude-fn bubble-layer :size
                                                   (keep :sizes groups))]
  (mapv radius-of [1 4 9]))


[2.0 5.674234614174766 8.0]

It returns identity where the mapping gives the column’s values as they stand ({:scale false}), so a renderer applies the result either way, and nil where the layer carries nothing to draw.
A layer type of your own declares :varies, and lists the same aesthetic under :accepts, so that its mapping takes the key at all:
Pseudocode:
(layer-type/register! :blob
  {:mark :point
   :stat :identity
   :varies {:size :radius}
   :accepts [:size]})
Without :accepts, {:size :n} on that layer prints a warning that the key is not recognized, and is dropped. The stat has to attach the per-row values to each group, as :sizes; :identity does. A mark that declares an aesthetic and then draws no per-row values for it prints a warning at pj/plan, naming the mark and the aesthetic.


How to extend: add a new mark type
Adding a new mark, such as a :dumbbell that joins two values per row, requires methods on both extract-layer and layer->membrane.
Pseudocode:
;; 1. Extract geometry from stat result
(defmethod extract/extract-layer :dumbbell [draft-layer stat all-colors cfg]
  {:mark :dumbbell
   :style {:opacity 0.8}
   :position (:position draft-layer)
   :groups (vec (for [{:keys [color xs ys]} (:points stat)]
                  {:color (extract/resolve-color all-colors color
                                                 draft-layer cfg)
                   :label color
                   :xs xs
                   :ys ys}))})

;; 2. Render to membrane drawables, placing each point with coord-fn
(defmethod mark/layer->membrane :dumbbell [layer ctx]
  (let [{:keys [coord-fn]} ctx]
    ...))


How to extend: register a layer type and create a pose-compatible layer function
After defining compute-stat and extract-layer for your custom mark, register a layer type and create a convenience function that works with the pose API. The Waterfall Extension chapter evaluates the same steps.
Pseudocode:
;; Register the layer type
(layer-type/register! :waterfall
  {:mark :waterfall
   :stat :waterfall
   :doc "Waterfall -- running total with increase/decrease bars."})

;; Users can then call:
;; (pj/lay pose :waterfall)

;; Or create a convenience function using lay:
(defn lay-waterfall
  ([pose]
   (pj/lay pose :waterfall))
  ([data x y]
   (-> data
       (pj/pose x y)
       (pj/lay :waterfall)))
  ([data x y mapping]
   (-> data
       (pj/pose x y)
       (pj/lay :waterfall mapping))))
pj/lay given the key checks the mapping’s keys against the layer type’s, and prints a warning naming a key it does not recognize. A layer type whose mapping takes a key of its own lists the key under :accepts, as in {:mark :dumbbell :stat :dumbbell :accepts [:y-end]}; without it, {:y-end :after} on that layer prints the same warning.
Users can then call (lay-waterfall data :category :amount).
If your custom mark is not one of the built-in marks, you also need a layer->membrane defmethod for the SVG renderer. Without one, the library throws an error explaining which defmethod to add.


A mark placed at a written value
Four marks – :rule-h, :rule-v, :band-h, :band-v – draw one shape at a value written on the layer rather than at values read from its rows. They are ordinary marks: they travel on a panel’s :layers in the order they were written, and they have the two defmethods this chapter has been describing.
stat/written-extent reports the extent the mark covers – the written value on the axis the mark names, and the layer’s column on the axis it spans – instead of grouping rows into :points. Its extract-layer method then reads the written value straight off the draft layer, so the plan layer carries a number rather than a group of buffers:

(let [layer (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
                (pj/lay-rule-h {:y-intercept 3.0})
                pj/plan
                :panels
                first
                :layers
                last)]
  layer)


{:mark :rule-h,
 :style {:stroke-width 1.5, :opacity 1.0},
 :color [0.2 0.2 0.2 1.0],
 :y-intercept 3.0,
 :y-domain [2.0 4.4],
 :x-domain [4.3 7.9]}

A custom mark placed the same way follows the same three steps: a stat that reports an extent, an extract-layer method that carries the written value onto the plan layer, and a layer->membrane method that draws it.

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
mark-clip-region
Each panel clips its marks so geometry past the domain cannot paint outside the panel. The region a mark clips to is itself an extension point: mark-clip-region (in render/mark.clj, dispatching on the :mark key) names the region, and the panel renderer resolves it to a rectangle and clips the mark to it. (The clip itself is a Membrane scissor; the Membranes chapter shows the mechanism.)
Two regions exist:

:drawing-area (the default) – the grey panel background. Data marks clip here, so geometry past the domain is masked at the plotting edge and nothing spills into the axis margin.
:panel-box – the wider panel rectangle including the axis margin, for marks that draw in the margin on purpose. The built-in :rug mark uses it so its ticks are not cut at the drawing-area edge.


(mark/mark-clip-region :point)


:drawing-area


(mark/mark-clip-region :rug)


:panel-box


How to extend: a mark that draws in the margin
A custom mark that paints in the axis margin (a marginal density, an axis-edge glyph) registers a mark-clip-region defmethod returning :panel-box, so the renderer does not clip it at the drawing-area edge. Without this, a margin-drawing mark defaults to :drawing-area and is cut off.

(defmethod mark/mark-clip-region :margin-glyph [_] :panel-box)


(mark/mark-clip-region :margin-glyph)


:panel-box

Cleanup – remove the example defmethod:

(remove-method mark/mark-clip-region :margin-glyph)


#object[clojure.lang.MultiFn 0x62398874 "clojure.lang.MultiFn@62398874"]


(contains? (methods mark/mark-clip-region) :margin-glyph)


false

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
plan->plot
Orchestrates the full path from plan to plot. The :svg implementation goes through the membrane path: plan, then membrane, then plot. Other renderers can skip membrane and go directly from plan to their target format.
Dispatch function: (fn [plan format opts] format)







Dispatch value
Path




:svg
plan, then membrane, then membrane->plot :svg


:bufimg
plan, then membrane, then membrane->plot :bufimg (raster image)



pj/save’s :png file format is not a separate dispatch value – it routes through the :bufimg path internally and encodes the resulting BufferedImage as PNG bytes on disk. The save-side keyword names the file format; the dispatch-side keyword names the JVM render target.
Using plan->plot directly:

(def my-plan
  (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
      (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width {:color :species})
      pj/plan))


(first (pj/plan->plot my-plan :svg {}))


:svg

The same plan can be rendered to different formats:

(def my-figure (pj/plan->plot my-plan :svg {}))


(vector? my-figure)


true


How to extend: add a new direct format
To add a Plotly renderer that reads plan data directly (no membrane needed), register a plan->plot defmethod.
Pseudocode:
(ns mylib.render.plotly
  (:require [scicloj.plotje.impl.render :as render]))

(defmethod render/plan->plot :plotly [plan _ opts]
  ;; Read plan domains, layers, legend, layout
  ;; Build a Plotly.js spec directly -- no membrane needed
  {:data (mapcat plan-layer->plotly-traces
                 (:layers (first (:panels plan))))
   :layout {:xaxis {:title (:x-label plan)}
            :yaxis {:title (:y-label plan)}}})
Then users opt in by requiring the namespace, and call the format through pj/plan->plot:
(require '[mylib.render.plotly])
(-> pose
    pj/plan
    (pj/plan->plot :plotly {}))
pj/plot always renders through the membrane, so (pj/plot pose {:format :plotly}) reports an unknown format for a format registered on plan->plot alone. pj/save writes :svg and :png only.

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
membrane->plot
Converts a PlotjeMembrane into a plot for a given format. This is the extensibility point for membrane-based output formats – formats that consume the same drawable tree but walk it differently. The Membranes chapter walks the PlotjeMembrane record itself and the Membrane UI protocols it implements.
Dispatch function: (fn [membrane-tree format opts] format)







Dispatch value
Output




:svg
SVG hiccup wrapped in kind/hiccup


:bufimg
Java BufferedImage wrapped in kind/buffered-image (raster)



pj/plan->membrane builds the membrane, pj/membrane->plot converts it. The record carries plan-derived dimensions as fields and the title as :plotje/title, so pj/membrane->plot reads them off the value directly:

(def my-membrane (pj/plan->membrane my-plan))


(pj/membrane? my-membrane)


true


(membrane.ui/width my-membrane)


600


(first (pj/membrane->plot my-membrane :svg {}))


:svg

The shorter shortcut pj/membrane runs the full chain from a pose to a membrane in one call – the natural starting point for a custom backend that consumes membranes:

(def shortcut-membrane
  (pj/membrane (-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
                   (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width
                                 {:color :species}))))


(pj/membrane? shortcut-membrane)


true


How to extend: add a new membrane-based format
To add a format that reuses the membrane tree, such as Canvas or PDF, register a membrane->plot defmethod. The defmethod reads canvas dimensions via the Membrane UI protocols and the title via :plotje/title, so it operates without the plan:
Pseudocode:
(ns mylib.render.canvas
  (:require [membrane.ui :as ui]
            [scicloj.plotje.impl.render :as render]
            [scicloj.plotje.render.membrane :as membrane]))

(defmethod render/membrane->plot :canvas [membrane-tree _ opts]
  (let [w     (ui/width membrane-tree)
        h     (ui/height membrane-tree)
        title (:plotje/title membrane-tree)]
    ;; Walk the drawable tree (via membrane.ui/children), emit
    ;; canvas draw calls at the correct canvas size
    (canvas-walk membrane-tree w h title)))

;; Optionally register plan->plot for users who call
;; pj/plan->plot with this format; pj/plot and pj/membrane do not
;; need it -- they go through plan->membrane and membrane->plot.
(defmethod render/plan->plot :canvas [plan _ opts]
  (-> plan
      (membrane/plan->membrane opts)
      (render/membrane->plot :canvas opts)))

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
make-scale
Builds a wadogo scale from a domain and a drawing-space range.
The scale types are a fixed set: pj/scale and a scale spec accept the three types below and report an error for any other, so a defmethod on make-scale for a new type is never called. This section shows how the built-in scales are made.

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["Dispatch value" "Scale type"]
  :row-maps
  (->> (methods scicloj.plotje.impl.scale/make-scale)
       keys
       (filter keyword?)
       sort
       (mapv (fn [k] {"Dispatch value" (kind/code (pr-str k))
                      "Scale type" (pj/scale-doc k)})))})










Dispatch value
Scale type





:categorical

Band scale (one band per category)



:linear

Continuous linear mapping



:log

Logarithmic mapping





Dispatch: inferred from the domain type and scale spec. Categorical domains dispatch to :categorical. Numerical domains default to :linear, overridden to :log by (pj/scale pose :x :log).

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
make-coord
Builds a coordinate function that maps data-space (x, y) to drawing units (px, py).
The coordinate systems are a fixed set: pj/coord accepts the four below and reports an error for any other, so a defmethod on make-coord for a new coordinate system is never called. This section shows how the built-in coordinate systems are made.

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["Dispatch value" "Behavior"]
  :row-maps
  (->> (methods scicloj.plotje.impl.coord/make-coord)
       keys
       (filter keyword?)
       (remove #{:default})
       sort
       (mapv (fn [k] {"Dispatch value" (kind/code (pr-str k))
                      "Behavior" (pj/coord-doc k)})))})










Dispatch value
Behavior





:cartesian

Standard x-right, y-up mapping



:fixed

Fixed aspect ratio (1 data unit = 1 data unit)



:flip

Swap x and y axes



:polar

Radial mapping: x->angle, y->radius





All four use the same scales – :flip swaps which scale maps to which drawing-space axis, and :polar maps x to angle and y to radius.

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
make-inverse
The other direction: canvas coordinates back to data-space x and y. pj/to-data reads it, and so does anything answering which value sits under a pointer. The built-in coordinate systems that can be inverted coordinate by coordinate have a method here:

(->> (methods scicloj.plotje.impl.coord/make-inverse)
     keys
     (filter keyword?)
     (remove #{:default})
     sort
     vec)


[:cartesian :fixed :flip]

:polar registers none, so it falls to the default, which returns nil. A panel under a coordinate system with no inverse reports :invertible? false in pj/frames, and pj/to-data throws for it rather than answering with a value that is only sometimes the one asked about. A custom coord that can be inverted should register a method; one that cannot needs no action.
A flipped bar chart uses :flip coordinates:

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-bar :species)
    (pj/coord :flip))

speciescount05101520253035404550setosaversicolorvirginica

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
apply-position
Adjusts the plan layers of one panel that share a :position value – :dodge places groups side by side in a band, :stack and :fill pile them. It runs after extract-layer, on the layers that method returned.
Dispatch function: (fn [position layers] position). It returns the vector of adjusted layers.

(kind/table
 {:column-names ["Dispatch value" "What it does"]
  :row-maps
  (->> (methods position/apply-position)
       keys
       (filter keyword?)
       (remove #{:default})
       sort
       (mapv (fn [k] {"Dispatch value" (kind/code (pr-str k))
                      "What it does" (pj/position-doc k)})))})










Dispatch value
What it does





:dodge

Shift groups side-by-side within a band



:fill

Stack normalized to [0, 1] (proportions)



:identity

Plot at exact data coordinates (groups overlap)



:stack

Pile groups cumulatively, the first group on top





The adjustment reads the plan layer’s own :position, so an extract-layer method copies (:position draft-layer) onto the layer it returns. :dodge then writes a :dodge-idx on each group and a :dodge-ctx on the layer, and the renderer reads the two to place each group in its share of the band. A dodged point layer:

(-> {:site ["north" "north" "south" "south"]
     :yield [3 5 4 6]
     :year ["2024" "2025" "2024" "2025"]}
    (pj/lay-point :site :yield {:color :year :position :dodge})
    pj/plan
    :panels
    first
    :layers
    first
    ((juxt :position :dodge-ctx #(mapv :dodge-idx (:groups %)))))


[:dodge {:n-groups 2} [0 1]]

title: 37  Extensibility
text:
Self-Documenting Extensions
Every generated dispatch table in this notebook is built by introspecting multimethod keys at render time. When you extend a multimethod, your new dispatch value automatically appears in the table. You can also register a [:key :doc] defmethod to provide a description.

Adding a documented extension
Register both the implementation and a [:key :doc] defmethod:

(defmethod stat/compute-stat :quantile [draft-layer]
  {:points [] :x-domain [0 1] :y-domain [0 1]})


(defmethod stat/compute-stat [:quantile :doc] [_]
  "Quantile regression bands")

The doc helper picks it up immediately:

(pj/stat-doc :quantile)


"Quantile regression bands"

If you skip the [:key :doc] defmethod, the table still renders – the description falls back to “(no description)” instead of throwing an error. With the doc defmethod removed:

#object[clojure.lang.MultiFn 0x68a932fe "clojure.lang.MultiFn@68a932fe"]


(pj/stat-doc :quantile)


"(no description)"

(remove-method stat/compute-stat :quantile)

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Sample Data
This notebook walks through building a custom chart type from scratch – a waterfall chart that shows running totals as colored bars (green for increases, red for decreases).
It uses all three extension points needed for a new mark:
A simple profit-and-loss waterfall: revenue flows through costs to net income.

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
(def pnl-data
  {:category ["Revenue" "COGS" "Gross Profit" "OpEx" "Tax" "Net Income"]
   :amount   [500       -300   200            -120   -30   50]})

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Step 1: The Stat
compute-stat transforms raw data into the shape the extractor needs. For a waterfall, we compute running totals and determine the start and end of each bar.
The stat must always return :x-domain and :y-domain. Beyond that, the shape is a contract between the stat and the extractor that reads it – here we use :waterfall-bars.

(defmethod stat/compute-stat :waterfall [{:keys [data x y x-type] :as draft-layer}]
  (let [clean (tc/drop-missing data [x y])
        categories (vec (distinct (clean x)))
        values (vec (clean y))
        ;; Running total: each bar starts where the previous ended
        ends (vec (reductions + values))
        starts (vec (cons 0 (butlast ends)))
        bars (mapv (fn [cat s e v]
                     {:category cat
                      :start (double s)
                      :end (double e)
                      :value (double v)})
                   categories starts ends values)
        y-min (min 0.0 (apply min (concat starts ends)))
        y-max (apply max (concat starts ends))]
    {:waterfall-bars bars
     :categories categories
     :x-domain categories
     :y-domain [y-min y-max]}))

Test the stat in isolation:

(stat/compute-stat {:stat :waterfall :data (tc/dataset pnl-data) :x :category :y :amount :x-type :categorical})


{:waterfall-bars
 [{:category "Revenue", :start 0.0, :end 500.0, :value 500.0}
  {:category "COGS", :start 500.0, :end 200.0, :value -300.0}
  {:category "Gross Profit", :start 200.0, :end 400.0, :value 200.0}
  {:category "OpEx", :start 400.0, :end 280.0, :value -120.0}
  {:category "Tax", :start 280.0, :end 250.0, :value -30.0}
  {:category "Net Income", :start 250.0, :end 300.0, :value 50.0}],
 :categories
 ["Revenue" "COGS" "Gross Profit" "OpEx" "Tax" "Net Income"],
 :x-domain ["Revenue" "COGS" "Gross Profit" "OpEx" "Tax" "Net Income"],
 :y-domain [0 500]}

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Step 2: The Extractor
extract-layer converts the stat output into a plan layer descriptor – a plain map with :mark, :style, and geometry data. Colors are resolved here using the library’s color system.
We color bars green for positive amounts and red for negative.

(defmethod extract/extract-layer :waterfall [draft-layer stat all-colors cfg]
  (let [bars (:waterfall-bars stat)
        green [0.2 0.7 0.3 1.0]
        red [0.85 0.25 0.25 1.0]]
    {:mark :waterfall
     :style {:opacity 0.85}
     :categories (:categories stat)
     :bars (mapv (fn [{:keys [category start end value]}]
                   {:category category
                    :start start
                    :end end
                    :color (if (>= value 0) green red)})
                 bars)}))

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Step 3: The Renderer
layer->membrane turns the plan layer into membrane drawable primitives. The rendering context (ctx) provides:

:coord-fn – takes an :x and a :y value in data space and returns the point [px py] in drawing units, through the panel’s coordinate system, so a mark drawn through it is flipped under (pj/coord :flip)
:sx, :sy – the two scales, for a mark that needs a scale itself, such as the width of a band
:coord-type – :cartesian, :flip, :polar or :fixed

On a categorical axis a number is a place among the categories, counted from one, so bar i spans the places from i + 0.6 to i + 1.4 – four fifths of its band. The renderer gives coord-fn the four corners of each bar in data space:

(defmethod mark/layer->membrane :waterfall [layer ctx]
  (let [{:keys [bars style]} layer
        {:keys [coord-fn]} ctx
        {:keys [opacity]} style]
    (vec
     (for [[i {:keys [start end color]}] (map-indexed vector bars)
           :let [[cr cg cb ca] color
                 place (inc i)
                 left (- place 0.4)
                 right (+ place 0.4)]]
       (ui/with-color [cr cg cb (or opacity ca)]
         (ui/with-style :membrane.ui/style-fill
           (ui/path (coord-fn left start)
                    (coord-fn right start)
                    (coord-fn right end)
                    (coord-fn left end))))))))

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Step 4: Register and Plot
Register the layer type, so that pj/lay accepts :waterfall:

(layer-type/register! :waterfall
                      {:mark :waterfall :stat :waterfall
                       :doc "Waterfall -- running total with increase/decrease bars."})


:waterfall

Now we can plot it using the pose API. There is no built-in pj/lay-waterfall, so pj/lay takes the registered key.
The plan and the plot are both computed here, while the extension’s methods exist; the cleanup section at the end of this notebook removes them.

(def waterfall-bars
  (-> pnl-data
      (pj/pose :category :amount)
      (pj/lay :waterfall)
      pj/plan
      :panels
      first
      :layers
      first
      :bars))


(-> pnl-data
    (pj/pose :category :amount)
    (pj/lay :waterfall)
    (pj/options {:title "Profit & Loss Waterfall"
                 :width 500 :height 350})
    pj/plot)

Profit & Loss WaterfallamountcategoryRevenueCOGSGross ProfitOpExTaxNet Income0100200300400500
Six bars – one per category. Green for positive amounts (Revenue, Gross Profit, Net Income), red for negative (COGS, OpEx, Tax).
Because the renderer places each bar through coord-fn, (pj/coord :flip) turns the waterfall on its side:

(-> pnl-data
    (pj/pose :category :amount)
    (pj/lay :waterfall)
    (pj/coord :flip)
    (pj/options {:title "Profit & Loss Waterfall"
                 :width 500 :height 350})
    pj/plot)

Profit & Loss Waterfallcategoryamount0100200300400500RevenueCOGSGross ProfitOpExTaxNet Income

title: 38  Waterfall Extension
text:
Optional: Convenience Function
To make the call read like a built-in layer, wrap the pattern in a pose-compatible function:

(defn lay-waterfall
  ([pose]
   (pj/lay pose :waterfall))
  ([data x y]
   (-> data
       (pj/pose x y)
       (pj/lay :waterfall)))
  ([data x y mapping]
   (-> data
       (pj/pose x y)
       (pj/lay :waterfall mapping))))

Now the call matches any built-in layer type:

(-> pnl-data
    (lay-waterfall :category :amount)
    (pj/options {:width 500})
    pj/plot)

title: 39  Edge Cases
text:
Data Shape
This chapter tests how Plotje handles unusual or boundary inputs – missing values, extreme numbers, degenerate datasets, and uncommon configurations.

title: 39  Edge Cases
text:
Missing Data
Rows with nil values are dropped before rendering.

(def with-missing
  {:x [1 2 nil 4 5 nil 7]
   :y [3 nil 5 6 nil 8 9]})


(-> with-missing
    (pj/lay-point :x :y))

yx12345673456789


Infinite Values
Rows with Double/POSITIVE_INFINITY or Double/NEGATIVE_INFINITY are filtered automatically with a warning – similar to log-scale filtering.

(def with-infinity
  {:x [1 2 3 4 5]
   :y [10.0 Double/POSITIVE_INFINITY 30.0 Double/NEGATIVE_INFINITY 50.0]})


(-> with-infinity
    (pj/lay-point :x :y))

yx12345101520253035404550


Single Point
A lone data point should render without errors.

(-> {:x [3] :y [7]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y))

yx234678


Two Points with Regression
Regression requires at least 3 points. With only 2, the line is omitted and the points still render.

(-> {:x [1 10] :y [5 50]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

yx123456789105101520253035404550


Three Points with Regression
With 3 points, the regression line appears.

(-> {:x [1 5 10] :y [5 25 50]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/lay-smooth {:stat :linear-model}))

yx123456789105101520253035404550


Constant X
All x values are the same – the plot should still render.

(-> {:x [5 5 5 5 5] :y [1 2 3 4 5]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y))

yx45612345


Constant Y
All y values are the same.

(-> {:x [1 2 3 4 5] :y [3 3 3 3 3]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y))

yx12345234

Position and Layout

Stacked bar – single group
Stack with only one color value, so nothing is stacked.

(-> {:category ["a" "b" "c"]
     :count [10 20 15]}

Dodge – missing category in one group
Group “g1” has data for “a” and “b”, but “g2” only has “a”. Dodge should still align correctly.

One group has zero count for a category. Fill should handle the zero without error.

title: 39  Edge Cases
text:
Scale and Coordinate

Log scale with clean powers of 10

(-> {:x [1 10 100 1000 10000]
     :y [2 20 200 2000 20000]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/scale :x :log)
    (pj/scale :y :log))

yx11010010001000010100100010000


Log scale spanning decimals to large values

(-> {:x [0.001 0.01 0.1 1 10 100]
     :y [1 2 3 4 5 6]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/scale :x :log))

yx0.0010.010.1110100123456


Log scale with non-positive values
Non-positive values are filtered on log-scaled axes, since log requires positive inputs. Here x includes 0 and -1:

(-> {:x [0 -1 1 10 100] :y [1 2 3 4 5]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/scale :x :log))

yx110100345


Continuous color – constant value
All points have the same numeric color value. The gradient should still render and not divide by zero.

(-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [4 5 6] :c [5 5 5]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:color :c}))

yxc5123456


Diverging color with midpoint at zero

(-> {:x (range 20)
     :y (map #(- % 10) (range 20))
     :val (map #(- % 10.0) (range 20))}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:color :val})
    (pj/options {:color-range :diverging :color-midpoint 0}))

yxval-10-505024681012141618-10-8-6-4-202468


Dates with very narrow range (two days apart)

(-> {:date [(jt/local-date 2025 1 1)
            (jt/local-date 2025 1 2)]
     :val [10 20]}
    (pj/lay-point :date :val))

valdateWed 00:00Wed 06:00Wed 12:00Wed 18:00Thu 00:001011121314151617181920


Sub-day precision (LocalDateTime spanning hours)
LocalDateTime values preserve sub-day precision. Tick labels show HH:MM format when the range is less than a day.

(-> {:time (dt-dt/plus-temporal-amount
            (dtype/const-reader (jt/local-date-time 2025 3 15 8 0) 24)
            (map #(* (long %) 15) (range 24)) :minutes)
     :value (map #(+ 18.0 (* 4.0 (Math/sin (* % 0.3)))) (range 24))}
    (pj/lay-line :time :value)
    pj/lay-point)

valuetime08:0009:0010:0011:0012:0013:00141516171819202122


Instant with sub-day precision
java.time.Instant values are converted to LocalDateTime (UTC) for calendar-aware tick formatting. Tick labels show hours when the range spans less than a day.

(-> {:time (dt-dt/plus-temporal-amount
            (dtype/const-reader (jt/instant 1750003200000) 12)
            (range 12) :hours)
     :temp (map #(+ 20.0 (* 5.0 (Math/sin (* % 0.5)))) (range 12))}
    (pj/lay-line :time :temp)
    pj/lay-point)

temptime16:0018:0020:0022:0000:0002:001516171819202122232425


Multi-year date range
With a date range spanning several years, tick labels show year values.

(-> {:date (dt-dt/plus-temporal-amount
            (dtype/const-reader (jt/local-date 2020 1 1) 20)
            (map #(* (long %) 120) (range 20)) :days)
     :value (map #(+ 100 (* 50 (Math/sin (* % 0.4)))) (range 20))}
    (pj/lay-line :date :value)

valuedate20202021202220232024202520265060708090100110120130140150


Polar with many categories

(-> (let [r (rng/rng :jdk 12)]
      {:cat (map #(str "cat-" %) (range 12))
       :val (repeatedly 12 #(rng/irandom r 100))})
    (pj/lay-bar :cat :val)
    (pj/coord :polar))

valcatcat-0cat-1cat-2cat-3cat-4cat-5cat-6cat-7cat-8cat-9cat-10cat-11050100


Log scale + coord flip combined
When log scale and coord flip are both applied, the panel should have log ticks on the (now vertical) axis and the domain should reflect the flipped layout.

(-> {:x [1 10 100 1000] :y [2 4 8 16]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/scale :x :log)
    (pj/coord :flip))

xy2468101214161101001000


Scale with explicit domain

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/lay-point :sepal-length :sepal-width)
    (pj/scale :y {:domain [0 6]}))

sepal widthsepal length4.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.00123456


A size scale anchored at zero, on data holding a zero
:from-zero makes the area proportional to the value, so a value of zero gives a radius of zero and that mark is not visible. This is the correct result for a proportional scale, and ggplot2’s scale_size_area behaves the same way, but a row can disappear without anything being wrong.

(-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [1 2 3] :n [0 5 10]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n})
    (pj/scale :size {:from-zero true}))

yxn246810123123


A size scale anchored at zero, on data holding a negative
Anchored at zero, the distance from zero decides the size, so a value of -5 is drawn the size a value of 5 is drawn. The mark stays on the panel and keeps its place on the axis; only its size stops distinguishing the two directions. Where the sign matters, map it to another aesthetic – :color splits the two apart.

(-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [1 2 3] :n [-5 5 10]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n})
    (pj/scale :size {:from-zero true}))

yxn246810123123


A size domain with no spread
When every value is equal there is nothing to compare, so every mark is drawn halfway across the domain rather than at one of its ends. Halfway is read through the scale’s own spread method (:by – how the values spread across the range), so a constant column and a nearly-constant one are drawn alike.

(-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [1 2 3] :n [5 5 5]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n}))

yxn5123123


A size range written backwards
[8 2] runs from large to small. This reverses the encoding rather than raising an error: the largest value is drawn smallest.

(-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [1 2 3] :n [1 5 10]}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y {:size :n})
    (pj/scale :size {:range [8 2]}))

yxn246810123123


Fixed aspect ratio with extreme domain ratio

(-> {:x (range 100) :y (range 0 10 0.1)}
    (pj/lay-point :x :y)
    (pj/coord :fixed))

yx01020304050607080901000510


Full grid – a matrix of columns
A facet crossing a list of columns with itself draws a panel for every pair of the columns – the pose pj/matrix returns, so (pj/matrix data [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length]) draws the same grid. Each column is named once above its column of panels and once beside its row of panels, and a panel with one column on both axes draws a histogram of that column.

(-> (rdatasets/datasets-iris)
    (pj/pose {:color :species})
    (pj/facet {:col {:x [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length]}
              :row {:y [:sepal-length :sepal-width :petal-length]}}))

6823468246234246sepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthsepal lengthsepal widthpetal lengthspeciessetosaversicolorvirginica

title: 39  Edge Cases
text:
Error Messages
Plotje reports an error for these common mistakes.

Non-existent column

(try
  (-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [4 5 6]}
      (pj/lay-point :nonexistent :y)
      pj/plot)
  (catch Exception e
    (ex-message e)))


"Column :nonexistent (from :x) not found in dataset. Available: (:x :y) To place the mark at :nonexistent itself rather than read a column, write {:x {:value :nonexistent}}."



Non-existent color column

(try
  (-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [4 5 6]}
      (pj/lay-point :x :y {:color :bogus})
      pj/plot)
  (catch Exception e
    (ex-message e)))


"Column :bogus (from :color) not found in dataset. Available: (:x :y)"



A layer with its own :data that lacks the panel’s columns
A layer that names no columns reads the panel’s columns. When the layer carries its own :data and that data lacks one of them, the error names the column and says to set the axis on the layer call, to a column of the layer’s data. This error covers a second layer attached with its own dataset whose columns do not match the panel’s axes, a pattern common in ggplot2.

(try
  (-> (tc/dataset {:fitted [1 2 3] :residual [1 2 3]})
      (pj/lay-point :fitted :residual)
      (pj/lay-text {:data (tc/dataset {:x    [1 2 3]
                                       :y    [1 2 3]
                                       :text [:a :b :c]})})
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-text :y :residual, the panel's column or the layer's own, names a column absent from this layer's :data. Available columns: [:text :x :y]. Set :y on the layer call to a column that exists in :data."



Unsupported polar mark

(try
  (-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [4 5 6]}
      (pj/lay-line :x :y)
      (pj/coord :polar)
      pj/plot)
  (catch Exception e
    (ex-message e)))


"Mark :line is not supported with polar coordinates. Supported polar marks: (:bar :point :rect :rug :text)"



Mismatched mark and stat

(try
  (-> {:x [1 2 3]}
      (pj/pose :x)
      (pj/lay {:mark :boxplot :stat :bin})
      pj/plot)
  (catch Exception e
    (ex-message e)))


"Stat result for :boxplot mark must contain :boxes, got keys: (:bins :max-count :x-domain :y-domain)"



A layer naming a column no cell of an arrangement draws
A pj/lay-* call on an arrangement adds no cell: a layer that fits no cell is drawn in every cell. Where the cells hold no layers of their own and the layer names a column that no cell draws, each cell would draw only that layer and leave its own columns unread, so drawing the pose reports an error. The error names the columns, and suggests adding the column to the cells or drawing the layer on a pose of its own beside the others with pj/arrange:

(try
  (-> (rdatasets/ggplot2-mpg)
      (pj/arrange [{:x :displ :y :hwy} {:x :displ :y :cty}])
      (pj/lay-point :cty :hwy)
      pj/plan)
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-point names :cty on :x, and no panel draws it: the panels draw :displ on :x. Add :cty to the :x columns the panels are made from -- the facet's, or the cells given to pj/arrange -- and leave :x off the layer, or draw the layer on a pose of its own and put the two side by side with pj/arrange. A layer naming no column is drawn in every panel."



A second column given to a layer type that draws from one column
A histogram, a density and a rug each draw from one column. Naming a second column, in the arguments or in the mapping, reports an error:

(try
  (-> {:x [1 2 3] :y [4 5 6]}
      (pj/lay-histogram :x :y))
  (catch clojure.lang.ExceptionInfo e
    (ex-message e)))


"pj/lay-histogram draws from one column, and was given :x on :x and :y on :y. Name one column; to draw the layer on its side, name the column on :y, as in (pj/lay-histogram data {:y :x})."

A bar is not among these layer types: (pj/lay-bar data :x :y) draws a bar for each row, whose length is that row’s :y value. To draw a histogram on its side, name the column on :y in the layer’s mapping:

(pj/lay-histogram (rdatasets/datasets-iris) {:y :sepal-length})

sepal lengthcount05101520254.55.05.56.06.57.07.58.0

REPL Setup
How to set up a development environment, run tests, author notebooks, and release new versions.
Start an nREPL server with the :dev alias, which adds notebooks, tests, Clay, and related dependencies to the classpath. One way to start the server is the following:

title: 40  Development
text:
Namespace Structure
The source is split by pipeline stage (see Architecture). In the diagram, an arrow runs from a namespace to a namespace it requires, and the dashed arrow points to a namespace that is loaded the first time it is needed. The diagram leaves out helper namespaces such as impl/text.clj and impl/rowid.clj.

graph TD
  API["api.clj"] --> POSE["impl/pose.clj"]
  API --> RES["impl/resolve.clj"]
  API --> PL["impl/plan.clj"]
  API --> COMP["impl/compositor.clj"]
  POSE --> RES
  COMP --> POSE
  COMP --> PL
  PL --> RES
  PL --> STAT["impl/stat.clj"]
  PL --> SCALE["impl/scale.clj"]
  PL --> DEFAULTS["impl/defaults.clj"]
  PL --> PS["impl/plan_schema.clj"]
  PL --> LAYOUT["impl/layout.clj"]
  API --> FRAMES["impl/frames.clj"]
  API --> IMEM["impl/membrane.clj"]
  API --> RENDER["impl/render.clj"]
  API --> SVG["render/svg.clj"]
  SVG --> RENDER
  BUFIMG["render/bufimg.clj"] --> RENDER
  RENDER -.->|loaded on first use| BUFIMG
  SVG --> MEMBRANE["render/membrane.clj"]
  BUFIMG --> MEMBRANE
  MEMBRANE --> IMEM
  MEMBRANE --> FRAMES
  MEMBRANE --> LAYOUT
  MEMBRANE --> PANEL["render/panel.clj"]
  PANEL --> MARK["render/mark.clj"]
  PANEL --> SCALE
  PANEL --> COORD["impl/coord.clj"]
  API --> RC["render/composite.clj"]
  RC --> MEMBRANE
  RC --> IMEM
  style API fill:#c8e6c9
  style COMP fill:#d1c4e9
  style PL fill:#d1c4e9
  style SVG fill:#f8bbd0
  style MEMBRANE fill:#f8bbd0
  style RC fill:#f8bbd0

impl/pose.clj holds the pose operations: resolve-tree (merges mappings, data and options from the root down to every leaf), elaborate (writes in what the draft chooses), expand-facet-nodes (a facet over columns as cells), fit-layers (the cells of a composite, or of a facet over columns, that draw each layer), shared-axis-groups (which cells share an axis), and leaf->draft (the leaf flattening that the public pj/pose->draft calls).
impl/compositor.clj handles composite framing layout, composite-pose->draft, and composite-draft->plan – pure data-side, no membrane dependency.
impl/plan.clj holds the leaf-plan computation (domains, ticks, legends, layout) that the public pj/draft->plan calls.
impl/layout.clj sizes the canvas: the room the axes, titles and legends take, and the size of each panel. impl/frames.clj turns a plan into the rectangles each panel occupies on the canvas, which pj/frames returns.
impl/membrane.clj defines the PlotjeMembrane record, the value of the membrane stage.
impl/resolve.clj defines the Plan, CompositePlan, LeafDraft, CompositeDraft, PlanLayer, and LayerType records, and holds resolve-draft-layer (single draft layer resolution, column type inference, grouping).
The impl/ directory holds data with no Membrane dependency, except impl/membrane.clj, whose PlotjeMembrane is a Membrane component by definition. The render/ directory uses Membrane for drawing and for SVG and raster conversion; render/bufimg.clj, the raster backend, is loaded the first time a :bufimg or :png plot is rendered. render/composite.clj carries the composite plan->membrane defmethod and the membrane drawables for composite framing (title, strip labels, shared legend).

title: 40  Development
text:
Running Tests
The test suite runs via cognitect test-runner:
./run_tests.sh
This is equivalent to:
clojure -M:dev:test -m cognitect.test-runner
There are two kinds of tests:

Hand-written tests in test/scicloj/plotje/ – unit tests for core logic (pose resolution, plan resolution, rendering, and more)
Generated tests in test/plotje_book/ – produced from notebooks every time Clay renders notebooks using Clay’s test generation. Every kind/test-last form in a notebook becomes an assertion in the corresponding *_generated_test.clj file.

title: 40  Development
text:
Notebook Authoring
Notebooks live in notebooks/plotje_book/ and are Clojure source files with ;; comment blocks for prose (rendered as Markdown by Clay).
You can explore the data visualizations interactively with Clay.
To add assertions that verify computed values, use kind/test-last with a function in a vector:
(+ 1 2)

(kind/test-last [(fn [v] (= 3 v))])
You may also add arguments after the function:
(+ 1 2)

(kind/test-last [= 3])
kind/test-last forms are invisible in rendered output – they only generate test assertions.

title: 40  Development
text:
Regenerating Tests
After editing a notebook, you may regenerate its test file by rendering it:
(require '[dev :as dev])
(dev/make-gfm! "plotje_book/relationships.clj")
This updates test/plotje_book/relationships_generated_test.clj. The generated test files are checked into version control.
To regenerate all notebooks at once:
(require 'dev)
(dev/make-gfm!) ; in Github Flavored Markdown format
;; or:
(dev/make-book!) ; as an HTML book

title: 40  Development
text:
Building the Book
The full HTML book is rendered through Clay and Quarto:
(require '[dev :as dev])
(dev/make-book!)
Chapter ordering is defined in notebooks/chapters.edn. The output goes to the docs/ directory and is published to scicloj.github.io/plotje.

title: 40  Development
text:
Generating the README
The README.md is generated from notebooks/readme.clj using Clay’s GFM (GitHub-Flavored Markdown) output. The notebook contains live code examples that produce SVG plots, so the README always shows current output.
(require '[dev :as dev])
(dev/make-readme!)
This produces:

README.md at the repository root
readme_files/*.svg – rendered plot images referenced by the README

The book’s index.clj reads README.md and copies readme_files/ into notebooks/ so that the book’s front page shows the same images. Run make-readme! before make-book! when the README content changes.

title: 40  Development
text:
Building a JAR
The build uses tools.build with deps-deploy:
clojure -T:build ci                 # run tests + build JAR
clojure -T:build ci :snapshot true  # build snapshot JAR
The JAR is written to target/.

title: 40  Development
text:
Deploying to Clojars
Two convenience scripts handle the full build-and-deploy workflow:
./release.sh    # test + build + deploy release
./snapshot.sh   # test + build + deploy snapshot
Both run tests first, then build the JAR, then deploy to Clojars. Deployment requires CLOJARS_USERNAME and CLOJARS_PASSWORD environment variables (or a ~/.m2/settings.xml with credentials).

title: 40  Development
text:
Continuous Integration
GitHub Actions runs the test suite on every push and pull request to main (see .github/workflows/tests.yml). The workflow uses Java 21 (Temurin) and the latest Clojure CLI.
